title: Small-n Approaches to Impact Evaluation
text:
1.1 A way through the book
The book starts from the causal claim rather than a sample-size threshold. It then examines the methods that can support that claim, the assumptions that remain, and the practical work of commissioning and using the evidence.

title: Small-n Approaches to Impact Evaluation
text:
1.2 Three causal claims, connected evidence
Each method chapter identifies the claim it addresses, the inferential operation it uses, and the evidence it requires. The categories overlap in applied work, but they should not be treated as interchangeable.



Difference-making


1.2.1 Effects
Did outcomes differ under intervention from what would plausibly have happened otherwise? Within-unit counterfactual designs are the primary home for this question.




Set relations


1.2.2 Configurations
Which conditions, alone or in combination, are necessary or sufficient for an outcome? Configurational approaches compare cases as combinations rather than as isolated variables.




Process evidence


1.2.3 Mechanisms
What process links an intervention to an outcome, and how do the available observations alter confidence in that account? Process tracing, contribution analysis, realist evaluation, and diagnostic updating contribute here.

title: Small-n Approaches to Impact Evaluation
text:
1.5 How to use this book
Read from the beginning when the framework is new: later chapters rely on distinctions established in the foundations. Use the part cards to enter a particular method family, then return to the decision framework when several approaches are feasible. Commissioners can begin with the method-selection aid and the practice chapters, but should use the linked methods chapters to assess the claims a proposed design can support.

title: 2  Introduction
text:
2.1 Impact evaluation and causal claims
Some interventions provide only one or a few independent units for evaluating effects. National policy changes and capacity-building programmes in single organisations are common examples. White & Phillips (2012) describe these as small-n settings when there are too few units of assignment to test differences between treatment and comparison groups. The same difficulty can arise with several treated units if no comparison units represent a credible alternative to the intervention.
The number of respondents does not resolve this problem. A programme assigned across four districts may survey thousands of people, but the intervention still varies across four units. A national reform may generate many administrative records while providing no untreated version of the same country. Repeated observations, staggered implementation, or other forms of evidence may create useful comparisons, but their contribution depends on the causal claim and the design.
This book concerns causal inquiry under those constraints. It examines evaluations that seek to establish whether an intervention made a difference, which combinations of conditions contributed to an outcome, or how a causal process operated in a particular setting. Chapter 3 defines small n through the inferential constraint that is binding, including the number of independent intervention units, support for a counterfactual comparison, repeated temporal observations, and diversity across cases. No fixed sample-size threshold applies across these designs.
Small n does not justify a lower standard of evidence. It requires the evaluator to state what is being inferred, identify the variation or observations bearing on that claim, and explain the assumptions connecting the evidence to the conclusion. In some settings, the available evidence will not support an effect estimate. The evaluation may still examine implementation or a proposed mechanism, but those findings should not be reported as an answer to the unobserved effect question.
The appropriate response to this limit is not to abandon causal inquiry or to attach causal language to evidence that cannot bear it. It is to distinguish the questions that remain open from those the evaluation can address. An implementation record can establish whether activities occurred, who received them, and where delivery differed. Process evidence can examine whether the events expected under a proposed explanation took place and whether rival explanations fit the record better. Cross-case comparison can examine whether outcomes appear under particular configurations of conditions. These findings may be useful for management and policy. They do not become an estimate of an effect unless the evaluation also provides a defensible contrast with the relevant alternative state.
This distinction has practical consequences from the first discussion of an evaluation. A commissioner may ask whether a programme should be extended, while the available records allow only an account of implementation. An evaluation team may be able to introduce repeated outcome measurement but not randomise delivery. A programme may have enough variation across sites for a configurational analysis but not enough comparable units for a conventional regression. In each case, the design should state the claim it can support and the decision for which that claim will be used. The later chapters develop the relevant methods; the point here is that a method cannot repair an unspecified or infeasible causal question.
The term impact evaluation is used in this book for evaluations that make causal claims about an intervention and its outcomes. These claims include attribution, where the object is an effect associated with a specified intervention contrast, and causal contribution, where the object is the intervention’s role within a configuration or process. Description of outcomes, implementation, or participant experience may be necessary to an impact evaluation, but description alone does not establish causation.
These two claims, together with the evidence and inferential operations that support them and the roles of participation and modelling, are organised in this book into a single framework, developed fully in Chapter 4.
This usage is narrower than the OECD-DAC impact criterion, which asks what difference an intervention makes and includes positive and negative, intended and unintended, higher-level effects (OECD-DAC Network on Development Evaluation, 2019). The OECD-DAC criteria are intended to be selected and applied in relation to an evaluation’s purpose, users, and context. An evaluation may therefore examine impact without estimating a treatment effect, but any causal conclusion still requires evidence appropriate to the claim.
This narrower usage also has a specific history. The OECD-DAC’s impact criterion, part of its evaluation framework since the 1991 Principles for Evaluation of Development Assistance, was never tied to a particular design; it asked whether an intervention produced higher-level effects, not how that determination should be reached. The equation of impact evaluation with counterfactual, and increasingly experimental, designs took shape later, in the mid-2000s. The Evaluation Gap Working Group, convened by the Center for Global Development, argued that a chronic shortage of rigorous counterfactual evidence was limiting what could be learned about development effectiveness, and called for an independent body to fund and synthesise such evidence (The Evaluation Gap Working Group, 2006); that recommendation informed the case for 3ie, founded in 2008. Around the same period, randomised evaluations conducted through the Abdul Latif Jameel Poverty Action Lab and Innovations for Poverty Action established randomisation as the reference design against which quasi-experimental alternatives were increasingly judged. White & Phillips (2012) and Department for International Development (2012) belong to a subsequent correction against that narrowing, arguing for a wider range of designs and methods under the impact evaluation label, while Deaton & Cartwright (2018) questions the definitional authority that randomisation had by then acquired. The usage adopted in this book sits inside that unsettled range: narrower than the OECD-DAC criterion, because it requires a causal claim, and broader than the usage associated with J-PAL and IPA, because it treats causal contribution, not only counterfactual attribution, as a legitimate route to that claim.
At small n, the inferential problem differs by design rather than admitting a single description. Few independently assigned clusters limit precision and narrow the range of feasible design-based tests, while weak overlap with untreated units undermines the credibility of whatever comparison those clusters could support. Short or unstable outcome series pose a different constraint, limiting what a temporal design can establish rather than what a cross-sectional comparison can, and configurational analysis has its own failure mode, becoming underdetermined when the cases at hand display too little diversity relative to the conditions under examination. None of this points to one alternative method; each constraint identifies a specific piece of information the evaluation lacks.
The distinction between attribution and contribution should therefore not be used to lower the standard for either claim. An attribution claim needs a contrast that represents what would have happened without, or under a different form of, the intervention. A contribution claim needs an account of how the intervention entered a process or configuration, evidence on the expected links, and serious attention to other plausible causes. The two claims may be pursued in the same evaluation, but they should retain their own warrants. Calling a mechanism account an attribution study does not create a counterfactual; reporting an effect estimate does not explain the process that generated it.
The availability of suitable methods affects whether interventions generate evidence that can later be appraised or used. Chapter 17 places this issue within an evidence-informed policymaking framework. The connection is limited but direct: commissioners and evaluation teams need the capability to identify feasible causal claims and designs before evidence can enter wider processes of interpretation and decision-making. The framework does not establish that adopting a particular vocabulary or method will increase policy use.

title: 2  Introduction
text:
2.2 Existing guidance
Development evaluation already has substantial guidance on causal inference beyond conventional experiments. The NONIE guidance reviewed experimental, quasi-experimental, and non-experimental approaches without treating one design as suitable for every question (Leeuw & Vaessen, 2009). The DFID report Broadening the Range of Designs and Methods for Impact Evaluations distinguished experimental, statistical, theory-based, case-based, and participatory approaches and argued for designs fitted to the intervention and evaluation purpose (Department for International Development, 2012). The World Bank Independent Evaluation Group later provided a broader overview of approaches used to evaluate international development interventions (Vaessen et al., 2020).
Two guides address the small-n problem more directly. White & Phillips (2012) examine attribution when units of assignment are too few for conventional treatment–comparison tests. Their proposed common core centres on programme theory, alternative causal hypotheses, and systematic evidence about the links in the causal chain. The TASO guidance covers small cohorts in higher education and profiles a range of counterfactual, theory-based, case-based, participatory, and modelling approaches (Fox et al., 2022). It also makes clear that question-to-method tables require judgement and should not be read as categorical rules.
These guides establish that small-n evaluation is not synonymous with qualitative research and that causal claims can draw on several forms of evidence. They also show why a flat list of methods is insufficient. The approaches differ in the claim they address and in the work performed by comparison, intervention, process evidence, stakeholder knowledge, or modelling. A classification that places these elements at one conceptual level makes method selection appear simpler than it is.
The remaining problem is to connect the causal claim, available evidence, and inferential operation without assuming that each evaluation question belongs to one method family. A mechanism study and an effect study can examine the same intervention without producing interchangeable conclusions. Diagnostic updating can assess evidence about several kinds of claim. Participation can shape outcomes and evidence across designs, while simulation produces results conditional on a model. Chapter 4 develops these distinctions.
The book builds on this guidance rather than replacing it. Experimental, quasi-experimental, theory-based, case-based, participatory, and modelling approaches remain useful descriptions of bodies of practice. They do not, however, answer the question of what a particular piece of evidence is expected to establish. The same label can cover designs with different units, contrasts, assumptions, and claim boundaries. The framework used here retains the methods’ disciplinary histories while making the causal work of each design explicit.

title: 2  Introduction
section: 2.3 From an evaluation question to an evidential warrant
text:
2.3 From an evaluation question to an evidential warrant
An evaluation question becomes a causal question only when it specifies the intervention or condition, the outcome, the unit, and the relevant period. “Did the programme work?” is not yet a question that a design can answer. It leaves open what changed, for whom, compared with what, and when. The same uncertainty arises when an evaluation asks how a programme worked but does not state the proposed process, the evidence that would support it, or the alternatives to be considered.
The framework asks evaluators to make these choices explicit before selecting a method. For an effect claim, they must identify a credible alternative treatment state and the design features that make the observed contrast informative. For a configurational claim, they must define the cases, conditions, outcome, and the basis for calibration. For a mechanism claim, they must identify the proposed process, observable implications, sources of evidence, and plausible rivals. Diagnostic, participatory, and simulation components require equally specific accounts of their role. The resulting design may be simple, but its causal warrant should be visible.
This is also a way to decide when not to make a causal claim. Some programmes have no usable comparison, no process evidence that can discriminate among explanations, and too little variation for a cross-case analysis. The evaluation can still describe delivery, document outcomes, identify concerns, or improve measurement for later inquiry. It should not report those activities as causal evidence. A defensible limitation is more useful to a commissioner than a claim that cannot survive scrutiny.

title: 2  Introduction
text:
2.4 Using the framework
The framework is intended for design, appraisal, and communication. At the design stage, it helps a team decide whether the available units, records, timing, and access to informants can support the intended claim. This may lead to a change in the evaluation question, additional measurement, a different sequence of methods, or a decision to postpone a causal study. These are design decisions, not failures of ambition.
During analysis, the framework provides a way to keep the conclusion aligned with the evidence. It asks whether a finding is an outcome description, an effect estimate, a configuration, a mechanism proposition, a diagnostic update, a participant-defined account, or a model result. Several may appear in the same evaluation. The report should state the role of each and avoid presenting their agreement as independent corroboration when they rely on the same sources or assumptions.
For commissioners and evidence users, the framework provides questions for appraisal. What causal claim was specified? What alternative explanation or intervention state was considered? Which observations bear on the claim? What was excluded or remained unobserved? What decision can the conclusion inform? These questions apply whether the evidence is numerical, documentary, participatory, or model-based. They do not require a reader to reproduce a technical analysis, but they make it possible to see where the causal warrant begins and ends.
The framework is not a decision tree that allocates a method automatically. A small number of sites does not decide whether process tracing, QCA, a single-case experiment, or another design is appropriate. The choice depends on the causal question, the nature of the intervention, the available variation, the evidence that can be collected, and the main risks to the conclusion. The decision framework in Chapter 14 develops this judgement in more detail.

title: 2  Introduction
text:
2.5 Contribution and scope
The book makes three contributions to this body of guidance. First, it organises causal reasoning around three forms of claim: effects or difference-making, causal configurations, and mechanisms or causal processes. It then distinguishes those claims from the inferential operations used to assess them and from the roles of participation and computational modelling. The purpose is not to introduce another list of methods, but to state what each component contributes to a causal argument.
Second, Part II examines six established method families through eight chapters. Chapter 6 covers single-case experimental designs, N-of-1 trials, and randomisation inference. Chapter 7 addresses qualitative comparative analysis and coincidence analysis. The generative family is developed separately through process tracing (Chapter 8), contribution analysis, which uses theory of change as a precursor (Chapter 9), and realist evaluation (Chapter 10). Chapter 11 considers Bayesian and other diagnostic approaches to evidence. Chapter 12 discusses most significant change and outcome harvesting as approaches to producing and interpreting evidence. Chapter 13 treats agent-based modelling and system dynamics as model-based tools that can support several causal claims.
Third, the book develops practical guidance for choosing, combining, and reporting methods. Method selection begins with the claim, unit of intervention, available variation, evidence quality, and main threats to inference. Integration requires each component to have a defined role and does not become credible merely because several methods agree. The later chapters extend these principles to commissioning, communication, and evaluation in constrained settings.
The book does not propose that small-n methods substitute for large-n designs whenever sample size is limited. A randomised or quasi-experimental design may remain feasible with few units, and a large-n study can investigate mechanisms, heterogeneity, or contextual variation. Nor are the six method families interchangeable or equal for the same claim. Their credibility depends on design conditions, measurement, execution, evidence provenance, and the assumptions needed for inference.
The framework is not a sequence in which every evaluation must progress from a counterfactual estimate to a mechanism account and then to a configuration. Programmes and decisions differ. An evaluator may begin with a process trace because the question concerns a contested implementation account. A repeated outcome series may be feasible while case diversity is not. A participatory process may be needed to define outcomes before any comparison is meaningful. The task is to justify the combination and order of methods used, not to reproduce all of them.
The book is grounded in development evaluation, where programmes often operate through institutions, places, or bounded populations that cannot be multiplied for research purposes. These are also common conditions in domestic public policy, health, education, and organisational change. The causal principles and methods are not specific to development. Examples are included only where the cited evaluation documents the claimed use. The book does not use constructed cases or invented numerical illustrations.

title: 2  Introduction
text:
2.6 Boundaries of the handbook
The book does not provide a universal rule for deciding whether an evaluation has a sufficiently small n. The relevant count is the one that constrains the claim: independent intervention units for an effect estimate, repeated observations for a temporal design, or diverse cases for a configurational analysis. Chapter 3 develops these distinctions. A study with many respondents may still face a small-n causal problem, while a study with few respondents may not.
Nor does the book treat methods as self-contained packages that can be applied once their terminology is learned. Good small-n evaluation depends on substantive knowledge of the programme, credible measurement, ethical access to people and records, and judgement about plausible alternatives. Statistical software, QCA software, evidence-test templates, participatory protocols, and simulation platforms can structure an analysis. None determines whether the intervention, outcome, cases, or sources have been defined appropriately.
The handbook therefore complements, but does not replace, detailed methodological guidance, domain expertise, and local knowledge. Its contribution is a common causal vocabulary for moving between them. It helps a team state whether it needs a contrast, a set relation, evidence about a process, an assessment of competing hypotheses, a participant-defined account, or a model-based scenario. It also gives reviewers and users a basis for asking whether the evidence meets the standard required by that choice.
Chapter 5 maps how publications mentioning selected method terms are distributed across disciplines, countries, and time. The search was used to map a literature and to identify records requiring full-text assessment. It did not establish method adoption, integration, evaluation quality, or a publication’s suitability as evidence for a causal claim. Its counts are therefore not used here to demonstrate the need for the framework or to estimate the prevalence of valid applications. Chapter 20 explains the further claim-level assessment required when literature is used for evidence synthesis.

title: 2  Introduction
text:
2.7 Structure of the book
Part I establishes the foundations. Chapter 3 explains what may be small in an evaluation and why the relevant count depends on the design. Chapter 4 then separates forms of causal claim, inferential operations, and approaches to producing evidence. Chapter 5 maps how the corresponding method terms appear in the indexed literature, as a point of reference for the disciplinary and geographic detail reported in each method chapter.
Part II covers the six method families introduced above. Part III turns to method selection, integration, and quality standards. Part IV situates the methods within the policy system: Chapter 17 describes the evidence-informed policymaking context in which evaluation evidence is produced and used, and the chapters that follow examine commissioning, communication with policy audiences, and adaptations in fragile, conflict-affected, or otherwise constrained settings. Part V considers how small-n findings can be synthesised without treating unlike claims and warrants as interchangeable (Chapter 21), before Chapter 22 draws together the implications and identifies questions for further methodological and empirical work.

title: 3  Defining Small-n
text:
3.1 What does n count?
There is no sample-size threshold at which an evaluation becomes small n. Ten observations may be adequate for one design and unusable for another. The relevant question is whether the available units, comparisons, or repeated observations can support the intended causal claim.
White & Phillips (2012) define small-n impact evaluation more narrowly as a setting with too few units of assignment to test differences between treatment and comparison groups. That definition captures a common problem in development evaluation, including national policy changes and capacity-building interventions in single organisations. It does not cover every constraint discussed in this book. An evaluation may have many observed individuals but few independently assigned districts, one treated unit but a substantial donor pool, or several cases that represent too few causal configurations for the proposed analysis.
This chapter uses small n to describe a binding inferential constraint, not a fixed number. The constraint must be stated in relation to the causal claim, the unit at which the intervention varies, and the evidence used for inference. This definition also separates sample size from evidence quality. One case may generate extensive records and observations, while a study with many participants may still have little independent variation relevant to the effect of the programme.
The unit counted by n follows from the claim and design. If a programme is assigned to districts, the number of surveyed residents does not increase the number of independently assigned units. The resident-level data may improve outcome measurement, but uncertainty about the district-level treatment effect still depends heavily on the number of districts and the assignment process. Treating participants as independent units would overstate the information supplied by the design.
The evaluation of biometric Smartcards in Andhra Pradesh illustrates the distinction. The programme operated across eight districts and affected approximately 19 million people, but rollout was randomised across 157 subdistricts (Muralidharan et al., 2016). Calling this an eight-unit or a 19-million-unit evaluation would misdescribe the experiment. For its main effect estimates, the relevant units were the subdistricts used in the randomised rollout.
The same issue arises when a programme reaches a bounded population. Observing all fifteen members of a training cohort removes sampling uncertainty about the measured outcomes of those participants. It does not create a comparison showing what would have happened without the training, nor does it establish that findings apply to later cohorts. Population coverage, causal identification, and generalisation are separate questions.
Several counts may therefore matter in one evaluation. These include the number of independently assigned or exposed units, the number of credible comparison units, repeated observations within units, and the number of cases representing different combinations of conditions. Reporting only the number of respondents conceals the constraint that governs inference.

title: 3  Defining Small-n
text:
3.2 Four binding constraints
Four constraints recur across small-n evaluations, and each limits a different form of causal claim. Few independent intervention units limit an effect estimate based on between-unit comparison. Weak support for a counterfactual comparison limits what any comparison, however constructed, can establish about an untreated alternative. Few or weakly informative repeated observations limit what a temporal design can support. Limited diversity across cases limits what a configurational analysis can identify. The constraints are described separately below and summarised together in Table 3.1.

3.2.1 Few independent intervention units
Some programmes vary across only one or a few units. A policy may be introduced nationally, or an institutional reform may affect one ministry. A clustered intervention may include many participants but only a few districts at the level where treatment varies. In these settings, conventional between-group estimation may be imprecise or impossible because there is little independent variation in exposure.
The number alone does not determine whether an effect can be estimated. Randomised timing, repeated introduction and withdrawal, or other design features may create informative contrasts within or across units. Their credibility depends on the assignment process, treatment stability, outcome measurement, spillovers, and the plausibility of the comparison.


3.2.2 Weak support for a counterfactual comparison
An evaluation can have many records and still lack a credible comparator. Untreated units may differ substantially from the treated unit, observations near an eligibility threshold may be sparse, or pre-intervention trends may not support a difference-in-differences design. The binding problem is then lack of overlap or relevant variation, not the raw sample count.
White & Phillips (2012) describe an evaluation of the Bangladesh Integrated Nutrition Project in which couples received nutritional counselling in only one of six project subdistricts. The effect of counselling couples could not be separated statistically from other features of that subdistrict. More observations within the same area would not resolve that confounding. The missing information concerned comparable variation in the form of counselling.


3.2.3 Few or weakly informative repeated observations
Within-unit designs require information over time. Three annual measurements and fifty daily measurements are not interchangeable, and the larger count is not necessarily better. Serial dependence, seasonality, outcome instability, changes in measurement, and the timing of programme introduction determine how much information the series contains.
Interrupted time-series analysis can examine one treated unit when a sufficiently stable pre-intervention series supports estimation of the expected trend (Bernal et al., 2017). No universal number of time points establishes that stability. Single-case experimental designs use repeated observations differently: controlled or randomised changes in treatment timing can provide design-based evidence even with one unit, provided the outcome is measured often enough across suitable phases (see Chapter 6).


3.2.4 Limited diversity across cases
Configurational methods require cases that display enough variation in outcomes and conditions to assess claims of necessity, sufficiency, or multiple causal pathways. The problem is not simply that the case count is low. Twenty nearly identical cases may contain less information about alternative configurations than ten deliberately selected cases with relevant variation.
The number of conditions matters alongside the number and diversity of cases. Adding conditions increases the number of logically possible configurations and can leave much of the truth table unobserved. Case selection, calibration, contradictory configurations, and limited diversity therefore determine what a configurational analysis can support (see Chapter 7).

title: 3  Defining Small-n
text:
3.3 Constraints can coexist
The four constraints are not mutually exclusive. A national reform may have one treated unit, no comparable untreated unit, a short and disrupted outcome series, and extensive process records. In that setting, the first two constraints limit an effect estimate, the third limits a temporal design, and the records may still be relevant to a mechanism inquiry. The evaluation should describe each condition separately. Calling the entire study small n does not say which conclusion is feasible.
The same point applies to a multi-site programme. Several sites may provide enough units for a limited comparison but too little variation in implementation to examine causal configurations. Repeated measurements may make changes over time visible while shared policy changes make it difficult to attribute those changes to the programme. An evaluation can use the information that is available, but it should not treat information relevant to one claim as a substitute for information required by another.
Constraints can also change during an evaluation. A comparison site may adopt a similar intervention, a planned outcome measure may become unavailable, a programme may be adapted differently across sites, or a data collection interruption may remove observations around the point of implementation. These events do not necessarily invalidate the evaluation. They require the team to revisit the causal claim, record the change, and explain how it affects the evidence. A design protocol that identifies the unit of inference, planned comparison, measurement schedule, and case universe makes this reassessment possible.
The interaction among constraints is one reason why simple thresholds are unhelpful. The same number of sites may be sufficient for an implementation study, inadequate for a cluster-level effect estimate, and useful for a deliberately bounded configurational analysis. The question is not whether a count has crossed a universal minimum. It is whether the design provides the variation, comparison, observations, or case diversity required for the stated claim.

title: 3  Defining Small-n
text:
3.4 Statistical consequences
Smaller samples commonly reduce precision and statistical power, but the consequences depend on the estimator and design. A null result from an underpowered study may be compatible with effects of policy relevance. Estimates can also be unstable because one observation or cluster has substantial influence. These problems should be shown through uncertainty intervals, design-specific power or sensitivity analysis, and examination of influential observations where appropriate.
Small samples do not make conventional p-values meaningless by definition. Exact randomisation inference may remain valid with few units when the assignment mechanism is known, although the set of possible assignments can limit attainable significance levels and power. Model-based analyses can also be used, but their results may depend strongly on distributional or functional-form assumptions that the data provide little scope to assess.
Three problems should not be collapsed into sample size. Identification concerns whether the design isolates the causal quantity of interest. Precision concerns how uncertain the estimate is. Generalisability concerns the cases, settings, or populations to which the result applies. A large dataset does not guarantee identification, and a carefully controlled small-n estimate may be precise for one unit while offering little evidence about other settings.
Small n also does not imply that the evidence is qualitative. Single-case experiments, randomisation inference, set-theoretic analysis, and formal simulation can all use quantitative data. Conversely, qualitative evidence may be collected in a large-n evaluation. The useful distinction is the role that each observation plays in the causal argument, not whether the dataset is labelled quantitative or qualitative.

title: 3  Defining Small-n
text:
3.5 Planning under a binding constraint
The relevant constraint should be identified before data collection whenever possible. A team planning an effect estimate needs to know the unit at which the intervention can vary, how many independent treatment changes or comparison units are feasible, and whether outcome measurement can detect the expected timing of change. A team planning a mechanism study needs to identify the proposed process, the records and observations that could distinguish it from alternatives, and the limits of access to those sources. A team planning a configurational analysis needs to define the case universe and determine whether the cases contain the required outcome and condition diversity.
These decisions also shape resource allocation. More respondent interviews may improve knowledge of implementation or experience, but they do not increase the number of independently assigned districts. More frequent measurement may strengthen a temporal design only if the outcome is measured consistently and the programme’s timing is known. Adding conditions to a configurational analysis can make a theory more detailed while leaving too few observed configurations to assess it. The value of additional data depends on the inferential problem it addresses.
Evaluation proposals should therefore state both the intended claim and the constraint that may limit it. This gives commissioners an opportunity to change the design while it is still possible: introduce a comparison, phase delivery, preserve a baseline, standardise an outcome measure, document implementation variation, or fund access to records. When these changes are not feasible, the proposal should state the narrower claim that will be pursued and what evidence would be needed for a stronger conclusion. This is more useful than promising impact evidence and redefining the claim after the data have been collected.
The same discipline applies at appraisal. A reviewer should ask whether the stated n corresponds to the unit of intervention and the claim, whether the design contains the comparison or observations it requires, and whether the conclusion extends beyond the cases and period examined. The reporting fields in Table 3.3 make these questions visible. They are not a checklist that certifies causal inference; they are the minimum information needed to assess it.

title: 3  Defining Small-n
text:
3.6 Data-rich boundary cases
Some methods study one treated unit while relying on substantial information elsewhere. They address a small number of treated units without necessarily operating under a generally data-poor design. The distinction prevents the unit of policy interest from being confused with the amount of evidence used for inference.
Synthetic control methods estimate a counterfactual for one or a few treated units from a weighted combination of untreated units (Abadie, 2021). Feasibility depends on the relevance of the donor pool, pre-intervention fit, the timing of treatment, and the absence of contamination. No fixed number of donor units is sufficient. The Basque Country study, for example, used other Spanish regions to construct a counterfactual trajectory for one treated region (Abadie & Gardeazabal, 2003).
Interrupted time-series designs may also examine a single unit, but they rely on repeated temporal observations and assumptions about the continuation of the pre-intervention process. Single-case experimental designs use repeated measurement with controlled treatment phases, while process tracing may examine one case using documents, interviews, and observed sequences. These designs share a small number of cases but draw their causal warrant from different sources.

title: 3  Defining Small-n
section: 3.7 Constraint, case selection, and intended use
text:
3.7 Constraint, case selection, and intended use
Small n sometimes results from programme structure. The intervention already covers one ministry, four districts, or a bounded group of participants. The evaluator cannot add independent units after implementation and must decide which claims the available variation and evidence can support. The appropriate conclusion may be that an effect cannot be estimated credibly, even though the programme can still be described or its implementation examined.
In other studies, evaluators select a small number of cases because they need detailed evidence about a mechanism or want to compare particular causal configurations. This is a decision about case selection and evidence, not proof that large-n designs cannot address mechanisms or heterogeneous effects. A mixed design may use a larger sample to estimate variation in effects and select cases for closer investigation.
Evaluation questions do not determine methods on their own. Method choice also depends on the unit and timing of intervention, available comparisons, outcome measurement, case diversity, access to process evidence, and the standard of credibility required for the decision. Before selecting a method, an evaluation should report the elements in Table 3.3.



Table 3.3: Information required to describe a small-n evaluation problem









Element
Question to answer




Causal claim
Is the evaluation estimating an effect, assessing a causal configuration, examining a mechanism, or combining these claims?


Unit of intervention
At what level is the programme assigned, introduced, or varied?


Independent variation
How many independent units or treatment changes bear on the claim?


Counterfactual support
Which observations represent the relevant alternative intervention state, and why are they comparable?


Temporal evidence
How many observations occur before and after intervention changes, at what interval, and with what missingness or dependence?


Case diversity
Which outcomes and configurations are observed, and which relevant combinations are absent?


Within-case evidence
Which records or observations bear on the proposed mechanism and its alternatives, and how independent are they?


Scope
Which units, period, population, and implementation form does the claim cover?






The term small n is therefore incomplete unless the evaluator states what is being counted and why the count constrains the claim. Chapter 4 builds on this definition by separating claims about effects, configurations, and mechanisms from the inferential operations and evidence used to assess them.

title: 4  Causal Reasoning in Small-n Evaluation
text:
4.1 Four traditions of causal reasoning
Identifying a binding constraint on n, as the previous chapter did, does not by itself tell an evaluator what kind of causal claim can still be made or which method fits it. That is a separate question, and answering it requires a vocabulary that does not yet exist in most guidance: one that distinguishes what is being claimed from how the claim is being supported. This chapter sets out that vocabulary. Chapter 3 identified four ways in which an evaluation can have a small n: the relevant constraint may concern independent intervention units, support for a counterfactual comparison, repeated observations over time, or diversity across cases. Those constraints affect the evidence available for a causal claim, but sample size does not determine the form of the claim or make one method appropriate by default.
Evaluation methods are often grouped by disciplinary tradition or by a qualitative–quantitative divide. Neither classification explains what the evidence is expected to establish. A single-case experiment, a process trace, and a participatory account may all examine one programme, but they make different uses of comparison, intervention, observation, and judgement. The framework used in this book therefore begins with the causal claim and the inferential work required to support it.
Three levels need to be kept separate. The first is the form of causal claim: an effect, a causal configuration, or a mechanism. The second is the inferential operation used to assess that claim: regularity, manipulation, or diagnostic updating. The third concerns how evidence and assumptions are produced, including participation and computational modelling. Comparison and process observation are design practices through which claims and operations are made concrete. Methods often combine elements from more than one level. Treating all of them as equivalent causal logics obscures those differences.
The book retains the term eight logics as a practical map of the reasoning that recurs in small-n evaluation. The map does not imply that all eight items have the same status. Three identify the claim at issue; three describe operations that can support a claim; and two concern the production and formalisation of evidence. Table Table 4.1 places them at their respective levels. The rest of the book uses this distinction to describe what a method contributes and what additional evidence it needs.
Figure 4.1 shows the same eight components arranged by level. Inferential operations supply the warrant for a causal claim; evidence production and formalisation, in turn, shape what the operations have to work with. The arrows indicate support, not sequence: an evaluation need not proceed level by level, and a single design often draws on more than one component within a level.
The vocabulary set out above did not appear from nowhere. It draws on a long philosophical argument about what it means for one thing to cause another, and four traditions in that argument shape how small-n evaluation reasons today. Each begins from a different question, and each privileges a different kind of evidence. Setting them side by side clarifies why the methods in Part II make the claims they do.
The first tradition is eliminative. John Stuart Mill’s methods of agreement, difference, and concomitant variation treat causal inference as the removal of candidate explanations by systematic comparison across observed cases (Mill, 1843). A condition present whenever the outcome occurs, and absent whenever it does not, becomes a candidate cause, while rival conditions are eliminated as the comparison widens. Mill’s logic requires little formal apparatus and applies naturally to a small number of closely examined cases, which is why it underlies both configurational analysis and the elimination of rivals in process tracing. Its weakness is that genuine causes can be missed when several conditions move together or when the relevant comparison is unavailable.
The second tradition treats causes as parts of packages rather than as isolated factors. John Mackie’s INUS account defines a cause as an insufficient but necessary part of a condition that is itself unnecessary but sufficient for the outcome (Mackie, 1965). An INUS cause is one ingredient in a combination that produces the effect, where other combinations could produce it too. The account captures two features that recur in development programmes: interventions rarely work alone, and the same outcome can be reached by more than one route. It provides the philosophical basis for configurational methods, which look for combinations of conditions rather than the average effect of a single one, and for the language of contributory causes used throughout this book (Cartwright, 2007).
The third tradition defines a cause through comparison with what would otherwise have happened. The potential-outcomes framework associated with Rubin treats the effect of an intervention on a unit as the difference between the outcome under treatment and the outcome under an alternative state, only one of which is ever observed (Holland, 1986; Rubin, 1974). Causation is a contrast between factual and counterfactual states, and the central problem is how the units came to be in one state rather than another. The framework makes the assumptions behind an effect estimate explicit, and it governs the counterfactual designs of Chapter 6. It says little on its own about the process connecting cause and outcome.
The fourth tradition represents causal systems as graphs. Judea Pearl’s structural causal models express assumptions as a directed acyclic graph and define an intervention as a change to that graph, using the do-calculus to determine when an effect can be identified from the available data (Pearl, 2009; Woodward, 2003). The formalism is the most explicit of the four about which assumptions permit a causal claim. At small n its value is usually representational rather than estimative: a graph can make the assumed structure and the threats to inference visible even when the data cannot support formal identification.
Table 4.2 compares the four traditions on how they define a cause, the place they give to mechanism, their degree of formalism, their data requirements, and their applicability at small n.
The traditions are not rivals to be chosen between so much as different starting points, each privileging a distinct evidential warrant. Eliminative reasoning asks which candidate survives comparison; the INUS account asks which combination is sufficient; the potential-outcomes framework asks what would have happened otherwise; the graphical approach asks whether the assumed structure permits a claim at all. These warrants map onto the components introduced above. Mill’s eliminative logic informs regularity and configurational reasoning, Mackie’s account underlies configurational methods, Rubin’s framework governs counterfactual designs, and Pearl’s models discipline the representation of assumptions that diagnostic reasoning then assesses. The historical line runs from Hume through Mill, Mackie, Rubin, and Pearl to the applied treatments of Pawson and Cartwright on which later chapters draw. Keeping the four warrants in view explains why no single method is sufficient at small n, and why the chapters that follow match each form of causal claim to the operation that can support it.

title: 4  Causal Reasoning in Small-n Evaluation
text:
4.2 Three forms of causal claim

4.2.1 Effects and difference-making
An effect claim states that an outcome would have differed if an intervention had been absent, introduced at another time, or implemented in another form. The potential-outcomes framework defines an effect through the contrast between outcomes under alternative treatment states (Holland, 1986; Neyman, 1990; Rubin, 1974). Structural causal models express a related intervention through changes to a specified causal system (Pearl, 2009). These frameworks do not require a large sample as a matter of definition. Sample size affects which comparisons can be estimated precisely and which assumptions can be examined with the available data.
At small n, an evaluator may estimate a difference through repeated observations within a unit, randomised intervention timing, or a comparison among a few units. The credibility of the estimate depends on the design. A change following programme introduction is not an effect estimate unless the design gives grounds for excluding maturation, secular change, measurement shifts, and other events at the same time.
Effect estimates do not by themselves explain how an intervention produced an outcome or whether the same result would occur elsewhere. Mediation, heterogeneity, and transportability can be studied within counterfactual frameworks, but they require additional data and assumptions. The limitation belongs to the particular design and evidence, not to counterfactual reasoning as a whole.


4.2.2 Causal configurations
Many programmes operate as one condition within a larger causal package. Mackie (1965) described an INUS condition as an insufficient but necessary part of a condition that is itself unnecessary but sufficient for the outcome. The formulation allows several combinations of conditions to produce the same result. It also allows a programme to contribute to an outcome without being sufficient on its own.
Configurational claims concern necessity, sufficiency, and equifinality within a defined set of cases and conditions. They may identify, for example, that effective local implementation occurs through more than one combination of staffing, authority, resources, and programme support. Such a result depends on how cases, outcomes, and conditions were selected and calibrated. It also depends on the observed diversity of configurations and on the treatment of contradictory or missing cases.
A set relation found across cases does not establish that changing one condition will produce the outcome. That intervention claim requires further assumptions about the causal interpretation of the conditions, their ordering, and the effect of changing one element while others remain in place. Configurational analysis can identify patterns consistent with causal packages, but its warrant is limited by the cases and evidence used to construct them.


4.2.3 Mechanisms and causal processes
A mechanism claim explains the process through which an intervention contributed to an outcome in a particular context. Generative accounts treat causal powers and mechanisms as features of the social world whose operation depends on surrounding conditions (Cartwright, 2007; Pawson & Tilley, 1997). Process-tracing approaches examine whether the observations expected under a proposed mechanism occur and whether competing explanations fit the evidence better (Beach & Pedersen, 2019).
Mechanism evidence can include the timing and sequence of events, administrative records, observed decisions, interviews, and traces left by implementation. The volume of evidence is less important than its relation to the hypotheses under consideration. Several interviews repeating the same account may add little if the informants rely on one source or share an interest in the conclusion.
A well-supported mechanism can explain an outcome without estimating an average treatment effect. It may also clarify why an estimated effect arose or why it varied across settings. Mechanism evidence remains vulnerable to incomplete records, post-hoc reconstruction, dependence among sources, and failure to consider plausible alternatives.



Table 4.3: Three forms of causal claim used in this book











Form of claim
Question addressed
Main basis for inference
Main boundary




Effect or difference-making
Would the outcome have differed under another intervention state?
A designed or justified comparison between observed and counterfactual outcomes
Does not explain the causal process without additional evidence


Causal configuration
Which conditions or combinations are necessary or sufficient in the cases studied?
Calibrated set relations and comparison across configurations
Does not by itself establish the effect of intervening on one condition


Mechanism or causal process
Through what process did the intervention contribute to the outcome in this context?
Evidence about sequences, activities, actors, and competing explanations
Does not by itself estimate the magnitude or prevalence of an effect






The three forms overlap. An evaluation may estimate an effect, investigate the mechanism that produced it, and examine the configurations under which that mechanism operated. They are separated here because each claim requires different evidence and can fail for different reasons. They should not be treated as exclusive questions assigned to separate professional traditions.

title: 4  Causal Reasoning in Small-n Evaluation
section: 4.3 Inferential operations and sources of evidence
text:
4.3 Inferential operations and sources of evidence
Regularity and manipulation contribute to causal inference without forming two additional types of causal claim. Regularity is an observed pattern: an outcome repeatedly follows an intervention, or two calibrated conditions occur together across cases. Such patterns may support any of the three claims, but association does not become causal merely because it is stable or survives adjustment for observed covariates. The design must still justify why confounding, selection, measurement error, and competing processes do not account for the pattern.
Manipulation concerns what can be learned by changing a putative cause. Woodward (2003) defines causal relationships through their response to interventions under specified conditions. In evaluation, deliberate assignment or controlled changes in intervention timing can strengthen an effect claim. Manipulation is therefore a feature of some designs, including some single-case experiments, rather than a separate answer to a different causal question.
Diagnostic updating is also an inferential operation. Evidence changes confidence in a causal hypothesis according to how probable the evidence would be if that hypothesis, or a rival, were true. The updating may be expressed numerically through Bayes’ theorem or qualitatively through the relative probative value of observations. Diagnostic reasoning can be applied to effect, configuration, and mechanism claims. Its credibility depends on the hypotheses considered, the assessment of the evidence under each hypothesis, dependencies among observations, and sensitivity to contested judgements.
Participation concerns who defines the outcome, provides knowledge, interprets evidence, and challenges the resulting account. Stakeholders can identify unrecorded changes, explain implementation decisions, and expose assumptions that an external team would miss. Their agreement does not validate a causal claim on its own. Participation can strengthen an evaluation when different positions are represented and claims are checked against other evidence; it can weaken one when authority, selection, or programme incentives suppress disagreement.
Simulation examines whether specified rules and parameter values generate an observed or anticipated pattern. Agent-based models and system-dynamics models can clarify programme theory, explore feedback, and compare scenarios that cannot be implemented in practice. The results remain conditional on the model. A simulation supports a claim about the real programme only to the extent that its structure, parameters, and outputs are justified against relevant evidence.
crumbs: 4  Causal Reasoning in Small-n Evaluation

title: 4  Causal Reasoning in Small-n Evaluation
section: 4.4 How the method families relate to causal claims
text:
4.4 How the method families relate to causal claims
Part II retains six method families because they correspond to recognisable bodies of practice. The families are not six self-contained theories of causation. Counterfactual, configurational, and generative methods are organised mainly around a form of causal claim. Diagnostic methods formalise the assessment of evidence. Participatory methods organise the production and interpretation of evidence. Simulation provides model-based analysis that can support several kinds of claim.



Table 4.4: Relationship between the six Part II method families and causal claims











Method family
Main contribution
Methods discussed in Part II
What the family does not establish on its own




Counterfactual (Chapter 6)
Estimates whether an outcome differed under alternative intervention states
Single-case experimental designs; N-of-1 trials; randomisation inference
The mechanism, transferability, or policy value of the estimated difference


Configurational (Chapter 7)
Examines necessary and sufficient conditions and multiple causal pathways
Qualitative comparative analysis; coincidence analysis
The effect of changing one condition while holding the causal package fixed


Generative (Chapter 8; Chapter 9; Chapter 10)
Tests explanations of how an intervention contributed to an outcome
Process tracing; contribution analysis; realist evaluation
An average effect or the prevalence of a mechanism beyond the cases studied


Diagnostic (Chapter 11)
Updates confidence in causal hypotheses using the probative value of evidence
Bayesian process tracing and related diagnostic approaches
Identification of an effect without a defensible design and hypothesis set


Participatory (Chapter 12)
Draws on affected actors to define outcomes, produce evidence, and interpret causal accounts
Most significant change; outcome harvesting
Causal validation through stakeholder agreement alone


Simulation (Chapter 13)
Explores the consequences of formal assumptions, feedback, and alternative scenarios
Agent-based modelling; system dynamics
A real-world causal effect without empirical calibration and validation






External scrutiny of the causal warrant is not evenly distributed across the six families. Participatory and diagnostic methods attract the most direct challenge to whether a causal claim has been established at all: participatory accounts rely on stakeholder attribution without a designed comparison, and diagnostic updating rests on sensitivity and false-positive values that are usually elicited rather than measured, together with an independence assumption across observations that is often violated in practice (Befani, 2020). Configurational analysis draws a comparable challenge from a different direction, since its determinism, its sensitivity to calibration choices, and its treatment of equifinality are recurring targets in the methodological literature (Schneider & Wagemann, 2012). Counterfactual and generative methods are challenged less often on whether their warrant is causal, because they sit closer to established causal-identification traditions; the disputes they attract concern scope, such as transferability or the prevalence of a mechanism, rather than the warrant itself.
The mapping is not exclusive. A single-case experiment combines a counterfactual contrast with intervention and repeated temporal observation. Bayesian process tracing combines mechanism evidence with diagnostic updating. A participatory process may improve the definition and measurement of outcomes used in a counterfactual or configurational analysis. Simulation may examine a proposed mechanism or generate scenarios whose implications are then tested against observed evidence.
These combinations do not automatically strengthen an evaluation. Two methods may rely on the same incomplete records, accessible informants, or assumptions about programme implementation. Their agreement then provides less corroboration than the number of methods suggests. Integration is useful when each component has a defined role, addresses a distinct threat to inference, and produces findings that can be compared without changing the claim midway. Chapter 15 develops those conditions.

title: 4  Causal Reasoning in Small-n Evaluation
text:
4.5 Avoiding category errors
The distinction among levels prevents several common errors. The first is to treat an inferential operation as if it determined the causal claim. Diagnostic updating can strengthen or weaken confidence in an effect, configuration, or mechanism proposition; it does not decide which of those propositions has been identified. Manipulation can strengthen an effect design, but a change in an intervention does not by itself establish that the outcome would have differed under a relevant alternative state. Regularity may describe an outcome pattern without determining whether the pattern is causal.
The second is to treat participation or simulation as substitutes for a causal warrant. Stakeholders may identify outcomes, correct an implementation account, and challenge the categories used by an external team. Those contributions can alter the question and evidence of an evaluation. They do not remove the need to assess alternative explanations for a causal conclusion. A simulation can make a causal theory explicit and reveal implications that are difficult to observe directly. It does not establish that the theory describes the programme unless its assumptions and outputs are tested against relevant evidence.
The third is to add methods without deciding how their findings relate. An evaluation may contain a repeated outcome series, interviews, a QCA, and a participatory workshop. The methods do not become a multi-logic design merely because they appear in the same report. The team needs to state which claim each component addresses, what threat it is intended to address, whether the evidence is independent, and how a disagreement will be interpreted. This is the basis for the integration designs developed in Chapter 15.
The framework therefore has two uses. It helps an evaluation team select a method family appropriate to a causal question. It also helps a reader audit a completed evaluation: identify the claim, locate the operation that supplies the warrant, and see where evidence production, assumptions, or unaddressed alternatives limit the conclusion.

title: 4  Causal Reasoning in Small-n Evaluation
section: 4.6 Theory of change and causal reasoning
text:
4.6 Theory of change and causal reasoning
A theory of change is often the starting point for small-n evaluation. It can describe how programme activities are expected to lead to intermediate changes and outcomes, identify assumptions about implementation and context, and make a mechanism proposition available for testing. It can also help a team decide which outcome needs measurement, which actors and records may provide evidence, and where a rival explanation could enter the process. These are useful functions in counterfactual, configurational, generative, diagnostic, participatory, and simulation work.
A theory of change is not, however, an additional method family or a causal warrant in its own right. A diagram of activities and expected outcomes does not establish that the programme produced the outcome, that a configuration was sufficient, or that the proposed mechanism operated. Those conclusions require evidence appropriate to the claim. Contribution analysis uses a theory of change to organise an account of contribution and to identify assumptions and alternative explanations; the theory becomes more credible only when those elements are examined against evidence , Chapter 9.
This distinction is important for commissioning. Terms of reference frequently require a theory of change, but they should also specify the claim the evaluation is expected to investigate and the evidence that could support it. A theory of change may reveal that an effect estimate is infeasible, that a process-tracing question is more appropriate, or that the programme operates through different configurations across sites. It does not settle that decision in advance.
crumbs: 4  Causal Reasoning in Small-n Evaluation

title: 4  Causal Reasoning in Small-n Evaluation
section: 4.7 From a causal question to a design
text:
4.7 From a causal question to a design
The framework can be used in a short sequence. First, define the intervention or causal condition, outcome, unit, period, and decision to which the conclusion will apply. Second, identify the form of causal claim: an effect, a configuration, a mechanism, or a deliberately specified combination. Third, identify the operation that could make the claim credible, such as a within-unit contrast, a calibrated cross-case comparison, a test of competing process explanations, or diagnostic assessment of evidence. Fourth, decide how evidence will be produced, recorded, checked, and interpreted, including the role of participation or simulation where relevant. Finally, state the alternative explanations, assumptions, and scope conditions that will remain in the report.
The sequence is not a mechanical decision rule. Feasibility may require the team to return to the question after examining records, access, ethical constraints, or programme timing. A planned effect study may become a study of implementation and mechanism because a comparison cannot be established. A theory of change may reveal that cases need to be defined differently for a configurational analysis. A participatory process may show that the outcome initially selected by a commissioner omits a change that participants regard as consequential. Revisions are legitimate when they are documented and when the final claim reflects the evidence that was actually obtained.
Chapter 14 provides a fuller decision framework for these choices. The purpose of the present chapter is narrower: to prevent the method label from deciding the question before the causal claim, inferential operation, and available evidence have been identified.
crumbs: 4  Causal Reasoning in Small-n Evaluation

title: 4  Causal Reasoning in Small-n Evaluation
section: 4.8 Choosing among methods at small n
text:
4.8 Choosing among methods at small n
No method family has general priority independently of the claim, design, and evidence. Random allocation can provide a strong basis for an effect estimate, including at small n, but it does not guarantee adequate measurement, implementation fidelity, or external relevance (Deaton & Cartwright, 2018). A detailed process account may explain how an outcome occurred, but it can remain unconvincing if the evidence was selected after the conclusion or plausible alternatives were not examined. A QCA solution may fit the observed cases and still be sensitive to calibration or limited diversity.
Method choice therefore requires more than matching a broad question to a named family. The evaluator must specify the intervention or exposure, outcome, units and period covered by the claim, relevant alternative states or explanations, available variation, and intended use. The design can then be assessed against the main threats to that claim. Shared standards such as transparency about assumptions, evidence provenance, rival explanations, and uncertainty remain applicable across methodological traditions (Brady & Collier, 2010).
Purpose matters because an evaluation intended to decide whether to continue a programme may require different evidence from one intended to revise implementation. Patton (2008) places intended use and users at the centre of evaluation design. Intended use does not remove the need to assess whether the available design can support the requested conclusion. A useful answer to a different question is not evidence for the original claim.
Part II examines the six families in turn, beginning with counterfactual designs at small n. The chapters retain their methodological identities while using the distinctions developed here: what causal claim is being made, what inferential work the method performs, what evidence it requires, and what remains unresolved.

title: 5  The Small-n Methods Literature: A Bibliometric Map
text:
5.1 Questions and units of analysis
The chapters that follow describe eight components of causal reasoning and the method families built on them. This chapter maps how the corresponding terms appear in the indexed research literature: how many publications name each method, where that literature concentrates by discipline and country, how it has changed over time, and how far the labelled families overlap. The map describes how named small-n methods appear in the indexed literature and helps identify publications for closer review in the method chapters. It does not treat the number of publications as a measure of methodological quality, evaluator capability, or adoption in evaluation practice.
The analysis distinguishes four records of evidence. The raw discovery archive contains every configured expression found in a title or abstract. The core-method corpus contains labels suitable for comparative bibliometric analysis. The supporting-simulation corpus covers agent-based modelling and system dynamics separately. The evaluation and development subsets contain records coded as applications after method relevance has been assessed. Theory of change remains in the discovery archive as a conceptual precursor; it is not counted as a method.
The raw archive supports retrieval and audit. The core-method corpus supports cautious description of named-method publication counts, disciplinary and venue distributions, authorship, institutional location, and co-mention between the core method families. Its principal unit is a unique OpenAlex work–method pair. A publication that names two methods contributes one pair to each method, while family totals deduplicate the work within each family.
The validated subset addresses two narrower questions: whether the intended method was used in an evaluation of an identifiable intervention, programme, policy, reform, service, or implementation effort; and whether that evaluation concerns international development. The unit remains the work–method pair because one publication may apply one named method while mentioning another only in discussion. A development application has either an LMIC setting or an explicit development purpose.

title: 5  The Small-n Methods Literature: A Bibliometric Map
text:
5.3 Corpus construction and validation
The automated filter retains articles, reviews, books, book chapters, reports, dissertations, and preprints. It does not exclude records on the basis of language or OpenAlex topic. Language is incomplete in some OpenAlex records, and a common topic exclusion would affect the method families unevenly. Computer-science classifications, for example, include relevant agent-based models, while agricultural and health classifications may contain development applications.
Records are deduplicated by OpenAlex work identifier within each method. Search variants such as British and American spellings therefore do not produce additional observations. The processed files preserve separate tables for works, work–method pairs, and author–institution–work relations. This structure allows method counts to use unique works while authorship analyses use stable identifiers and can apply fractional credit.
Keyword screening marked 28,687 possible evaluation applications; it did not determine final inclusion in the application subset. A reproducible sample of 1,242 records was drawn within each expression and separately for records with and without evaluation-related terms. A balanced first-stage sample of 273 records and a targeted second-stage review of 255 records, including 40 simulation records, have been coded by a reference reviewer. The screen records method relevance, evaluation application, and development application. Records marked as repeated or overlapping are held outside the denominator until their duplicate status is resolved.
The completed review shows why some exact phrases cannot be used as comparative method counts. Coincidence analysis also retrieves event-coincidence and detector procedures in climate science and physics. Contribution analysis retrieves engineering, source-apportionment, and economic decomposition methods. Most Significant Change often describes an outcome or ordinary comparative language rather than the participatory evaluation approach. These records remain useful for discovery, but the three labels are excluded from comparative surface counts. An intended-method record can still enter the evaluation or development subset after screening.
The workflow is described as an automated bibliometric filter with manual validation. It is not a PRISMA screening process or a systematic review of evaluation studies. A later systematic review could use the validated application subset as one source, but it would require additional databases, grey-literature searches, full-text eligibility assessment, and method-specific quality appraisal.

title: 5  The Small-n Methods Literature: A Bibliometric Map
text:
5.4 Analyses and claim boundaries
Publication trends and co-mentions use the comparative core-method records only. Labels with materially different technical meanings are excluded even when they are retained in the raw archive. Changes in counts may reflect publication volume, terminology, indexing coverage, or attention to a method. They do not establish how often evaluators use the method. Supporting simulation is reported separately, and theory of change is not reported as a method count.
Co-mention counts identify works whose title or abstract names methods from two families. The analysis reports both counts and a Jaccard coefficient because the family corpora differ greatly in size. Co-mention does not show that the methods were integrated in the same evaluation; the full text must be examined before making that claim.
Bayesian process tracing contains the phrase process tracing. This nested label is excluded from the family co-mention analysis so that one expression is not counted as evidence that diagnostic and generative methods appear together.
Disciplinary and venue analyses use the core-method surface corpus rather than an equal quota of highly cited publications. OpenAlex’s primary topic is reported as an algorithmic classification, not the publication’s definitive disciplinary location. Citation-selected subsets may still be used to identify prominent publications for reading, but they are not used to describe the structure of the field.
Authorship analyses aggregate by OpenAlex author identifier. Both full and fractional work counts are reported because large teams otherwise receive disproportionate weight. Institutional and geographic summaries use the affiliations attached to each authorship and retain missing affiliations. A high count means that an author appears frequently on publications in the corpus; it does not by itself establish a contribution to method development.
