Neither method controls for confounding on its own. Both can be combined with process evidence or another design where the evaluation requires a stronger causal claim. See Chapter 15 for combination protocols.
The principal strengths of participatory methods are their capacity to capture complexity, emergence, and unexpected outcomes. They centre participant voice and insider knowledge. They work at small n without requiring repeated measurement or pre-specified outcome indicators. They are less reliant on the evaluator’s prior theory about what the programme should produce.
The limitations are substantial. Both methods rely on participants’ recall, willingness to report, and relationship with the programme. Social desirability can lead people to over-attribute change. Neither method provides a formal way to rule out confounding. MSC selection reflects the values and power of the panels; outcome harvesting can cherry-pick favourable outcomes when substantiation is weak. Process tracing can investigate a mechanism behind a selected outcome, and configurational analysis can examine patterns across documented cases. These combinations do not automatically strengthen a claim: their roles and source dependence must be specified (Chapter 15).
crumbs: 12  Participatory Approaches to Evidence About Change

title: 12  Participatory Approaches to Evidence About Change
text:
12.8 Reporting and claim boundaries
The report should state the participation and verification process before presenting selected stories or outcomes. For MSC, it should identify the change domains, the number and source of stories, the composition of each selection panel, the criteria used, the selected and rejected stories, and the verification undertaken. For outcome harvesting, it should identify the outcome definition, the routes through which candidate outcomes were identified, who drafted and revised the outcome statements, the substantiators, the evidence reviewed, and outcomes that could not be substantiated. These details allow readers to assess the process that produced the findings.
The final claim should name the change, the actor or group concerned, the period, the evidence that supports occurrence, and the programme role that remains plausible after substantiation. It should also distinguish a verified outcome from a verified contribution. Evidence can establish that an organisation changed a practice without establishing why it did so. A contribution claim requires evidence about the programme’s activities, timing, proposed pathway, and relevant alternatives. A participatory evaluation should not turn a well-documented change into a causal conclusion merely because participants regard the programme as influential.
Quantification requires particular care. Counts of stories, selected stories, or harvested outcomes do not measure the size of a programme effect or the prevalence of a change. They may reflect the routes used to recruit participants, the number of people available to report, the ease of documenting certain outcomes, or a panel’s selection criteria. A report can give these counts as information about the process, but it should not treat them as outcome estimates without a design that supports such an interpretation.
crumbs: 12  Participatory Approaches to Evidence About Change

title: 12  Participatory Approaches to Evidence About Change
section: 12.9 Timing, resources, and reasons not to use the methods
text:
12.9 Timing, resources, and reasons not to use the methods
MSC is most useful when the programme can collect and discuss stories over time. Repeated cycles allow selection criteria to be challenged, domains of change to be revised, and emerging concerns to inform implementation. A single retrospective story-collection exercise can still identify participant accounts of change, but it lacks the monitoring role and may depend heavily on recall. Outcome harvesting is often used retrospectively, but it also benefits from early planning: contemporaneous records, clear dates, and access to people outside the programme make later substantiation more credible.
Neither method is appropriate when participants face material risk from disclosure and the evaluation cannot protect them, when there is no feasible way to substantiate the central claims, or when the decision requires an estimated treatment effect. They are also a poor fit where participation is being used ceremonially: when the programme has already determined the questions, interpretation, and findings, while asking participants only to supply favourable stories. A descriptive consultation may still be ethically valuable, but it should not be presented as participatory causal evaluation.
The necessary resources include facilitation, translation where required, safe data management, time for verification, and independent review. The work is often underestimated because stories and outcomes can be collected quickly. The more demanding part is documenting how they were selected, checking whether the reported change occurred, tracing the claimed contribution, and retaining material that challenges the preferred account. A design that funds collection but not substantiation has chosen testimony over evaluation.
crumbs: 12  Participatory Approaches to Evidence About Change

title: 12  Participatory Approaches to Evidence About Change
section: 12.10 Use in a wider evaluation design
text:
12.10 Use in a wider evaluation design
Participatory methods are particularly useful at the point where a programme theory is incomplete. They can reveal outcomes that were not anticipated by designers, identify groups for whom delivery differs, and expose assumptions that require later testing. This is a direct contribution to causal inquiry, even where the methods do not provide a counterfactual or a formal diagnostic update themselves. The next design step should follow from the uncertainty identified: a mechanism claim may require process tracing, an implementation pattern may require comparison across cases, and an outcome effect may require a counterfactual design.
The combination must preserve source independence. If participants, programme staff, and the substantiator all depend on the same programme records or organisational account, the appearance of triangulation can be misleading. The evaluation should identify where sources are connected and seek information from affected groups, independent records, or other actors when that is safe and relevant. Where it cannot, the conclusion should say that the contribution claim rests on dependent evidence.
crumbs: 12  Participatory Approaches to Evidence About Change

title: 12  Participatory Approaches to Evidence About Change
text:
12.11 Quality assurance during analysis
Quality assurance begins with the treatment of raw material. The team should preserve the original wording of narratives and outcome accounts, translations where used, the date and route of collection, and the changes made while an account is being condensed into a story or outcome statement. Editing is often necessary for clarity and confidentiality. It becomes a problem when it removes qualifications, alters agency, or makes the account fit the programme theory more closely than the source did. The record should show what was changed and why.
Interpretation should be separated from selection. A panel may select a story because it raises a difficult issue, is well substantiated, or reflects a valued change. These are different reasons, and they should not be collapsed into a claim that the selected story is typical or proves programme success. Outcome harvesters likewise need to distinguish an outcome that is important to stakeholders from an outcome for which the programme’s contribution is well supported. The process can report both judgements, provided it explains the basis for each.
Independent challenge is useful at three points: after the collection strategy is set, while candidate accounts are being substantiated, and before conclusions are approved. A reviewer can ask whose accounts are absent, whether an outcome statement includes more than the evidence supports, whether a named alternative has been investigated, and whether a sensitive account has been made safe to report. This is not a substitute for participant involvement. It protects participants and readers from a process in which involvement is used to shield a programme from scrutiny.
The final quality check should examine whether the chapter’s claim language matches the process followed. A story selected by a panel is a selected story. A story checked against one record is partly corroborated. An outcome reviewed by an informed but connected person has limited independent substantiation. A causal contribution may be plausible without being established. These distinctions should remain visible when evidence is summarised for decision-makers.
crumbs: 12  Participatory Approaches to Evidence About Change

title: 12  Participatory Approaches to Evidence About Change
text:
12.12 From findings to decisions
Participatory findings can support decisions when the decision matches the evidence. A verified account of an access barrier can justify investigation of a delivery problem. Repeated, substantiated reports of an unintended consequence can require an adaptation or safeguard. An outcome statement showing a change in organisational practice can identify a result worth tracing further. These uses do not require the evaluation to claim that the programme caused a population outcome.
The decision record should state the finding, the people affected, the evidence and its limitations, the action proposed, and the uncertainty that remains. This helps distinguish a response to credible participant evidence from a management decision made for other reasons. It also provides a basis for returning to the issue after implementation changes. Participatory evaluation has a learning function only if participants can see whether and how their accounts altered the programme’s response.
Feedback should be designed with the same care as collection. Returning selected stories or harvested outcomes to participants can correct factual errors, expose disagreement, and allow people to challenge an interpretation before it enters a formal report. It can also create risks if participants are asked to endorse a conclusion in front of those who control programme access or resources. The team should choose feedback routes that allow correction without making agreement a condition of participation.
The limits of the evidence should remain visible in public communication. A concise outcome story may be useful for a programme report, but it should not replace the record of selection, substantiation, dissent, and unresolved alternatives. Where a report uses a story to illustrate a broader finding, it should say that the story illustrates the finding rather than treating it as proof of prevalence. This is particularly important when stories are used to advocate for funding or scale-up.
crumbs: 12  Participatory Approaches to Evidence About Change

title: 12  Participatory Approaches to Evidence About Change
text:
12.13 Claim limits and transfer
Participatory evidence travels poorly when stripped from the conditions in which it was produced. An account of change may depend on the programme’s delivery model, the relationship between participants and implementers, local political conditions, or the participant group that was able to take part. Transfer to another setting requires an account of which of these features are relevant, and evidence that they are present or can be created elsewhere. A selected story or harvested outcome does not itself establish that recurrence.
The same restraint applies to negative findings. A report that participants did not identify a particular change may reflect the absence of change, the choice of participants, the way the question was framed, the risks of disclosure, or the timing of collection. The evaluation should investigate these possibilities before interpreting silence as a programme failure or success. This is one reason to retain a clear record of recruitment, non-participation, and the conditions of collection.
Participatory methods are a source of systematically collected, stakeholder-informed evidence about change and its possible explanation. They widen what an evaluation can observe and whose interpretation is considered. They do not remove the need to define claims, substantiate outcomes, investigate alternatives, or choose another design when the decision requires an estimate of effect.
The next chapter examines computational simulation, a supporting tool that formalises assumptions and explores their implications without collecting new empirical evidence.

title: 13  Computational Simulation as Complement to Small-n Designs
text:
13.1 Agent-based modelling
Agent-based modelling and system dynamics are not themselves small-n evaluation methods. Where Chapter 12 drew evidence from stakeholder accounts and verification, this chapter turns to computational tools that operate at any scale, from a handful of agents to millions. They can make a causal theory explicit, explore the implications of stated assumptions, and in limited circumstances supply probability inputs for diagnostic evaluation. They do not create an empirical counterfactual when a comparison is unavailable. The chapter concentrates on these supporting roles rather than on computational technique.
Three sources anchor the chapter without playing identical roles. Gilbert & Troitzsch (2005) provides a foundational account of agent-based social simulation, Sterman (2000) sets out system-dynamics modelling, including feedback structures and model testing, and Befani et al. (2021) shows a restricted diagnostic use of simulation: deriving likelihood inputs from a simplified model for a Bayesian update. These are foundations for building and interrogating models, not evidence that a modelled scenario estimates an intervention effect.
The bibliometric review provides a reason for restraint. Many records that name agent-based modelling or system dynamics describe a model, not an evaluation of an intervention. In the two-stage reviewed sample, 73 of 80 records used the intended modelling term and 24 were coded as applications; the purposive sample does not estimate the frequency of evaluation use in the wider literature. Supporting simulation is therefore kept separate from the book’s comparative method corpus (Chapter 23).
An agent-based model (ABM) represents a system as a collection of autonomous agents that follow behavioural rules. Each agent perceives its local environment, interacts with neighbouring agents, and updates its state accordingly. The aggregate behaviour of the system emerges from these micro-level interactions rather than from a set of top-down equations. This bottom-up architecture makes ABM well suited to modelling causal mechanisms, because the analyst must specify the rules that produce the outcome rather than merely estimating a relationship between variables.
Three features of ABM are relevant for small-n evaluation. First, ABM can generate probability inputs for diagnostic updating. Befani et al. (2021) set out how simulated evidence patterns can supply likelihood inputs where empirical frequencies are unavailable and expert elicitation is contested (Chapter 11). The estimates remain conditional on model structure and assumptions. Second, ABM can represent mechanism chains that process tracing investigates. A model can express a stated theory of change as agent rules and show what system patterns follow from them. If the model reproduces several observed patterns only under particular assumptions, it can narrow a set of plausible accounts; it cannot verify the assumptions that generated the fit. Third, an ABM can compare explicitly modelled scenarios, including a scenario without a programme rule. The difference is a model-based scenario contrast, not an empirical estimate of what would have happened without the intervention.
Validation is the central challenge. An ABM is only as credible as its rules, and the analyst must justify those rules with empirical evidence or well-established theory. Pattern-oriented modelling offers one approach: the analyst specifies multiple empirical patterns that the model must reproduce simultaneously, which constrains the parameter space and reduces the risk of overfitting to a single outcome. Even so, simulation results should be treated as structured thought experiments rather than as empirical findings. They sharpen causal reasoning; they do not replace empirical evidence.
crumbs: 13  Computational Simulation as Complement to Small-n Designs

title: 13  Computational Simulation as Complement to Small-n Designs
text:
ABM in brief. Autonomous agents follow local interaction rules; system behaviour emerges from the bottom up. Key platforms: NetLogo, Mesa (Python), Repast.








A modelling study is not automatically an evaluation



Simulation can inform policy design without supplying evidence that a policy caused an observed outcome. A model becomes part of an evaluation only when it is built around an identifiable intervention, is confronted with relevant empirical evidence, and is used to assess a stated causal claim or policy choice. These conditions need to be specified in the evaluation, not inferred from the use of simulation software or from the model’s policy relevance.








ABM supporting intervention refinement: ChildObesity180



Hennessy et al. (2016) developed an agent-based model to aid the evaluation and refinement of ChildObesity180 interventions for school-aged children in the United States. The model drew on two obesity-prevention initiatives and public data, and was intended to explore intervention design, data gaps, and alternative implementation scenarios. The authors state that the modelling effort stopped short of testing explanatory or predictive power. This is a useful boundary case: it was developed within an intervention and evaluation context, but its output was model-based support for refinement, not an empirical estimate of programme impact (Hennessy et al., 2016).








Development-context example: model-based evaluation of malaria interventions



Griffin et al. (2010) used a simulation model of Plasmodium falciparum transmission to evaluate strategies for reducing malaria across settings in sub-Saharan Africa. The model represented human and mosquito infection dynamics and projected how combinations of long-lasting insecticidal nets, indoor residual spraying, and treatment might reduce transmission at different baseline intensities, and where elimination was plausible. Its output is a set of model-based scenario contrasts, conditional on the assumed transmission structure and parameters, rather than an empirical estimate of any single programme’s effect. The case illustrates simulation in a development context: a way of comparing intervention scenarios and identifying where empirical evaluation and investment might focus, used alongside field data rather than in place of it.
crumbs: 13  Computational Simulation as Complement to Small-n Designs

title: 13  Computational Simulation as Complement to Small-n Designs
text:
13.2 System dynamics


SD in brief. Stocks (accumulations) + flows (rates of change) + feedback loops = dynamic system behaviour over time. Key platforms: Vensim, Stella, AnyLogic.
System dynamics (SD) models represent a system as a set of stocks (accumulations), flows (rates of change), and feedback loops. A causal loop diagram maps the qualitative structure: which variables reinforce each other (positive feedback) and which counteract each other (negative feedback). A quantified SD model translates this diagram into differential equations that can be simulated over time.
SD supports small-n evaluation by providing a formal way to examine a theory of change in a feedback-rich system. An SD model makes proposed feedback structures explicit and allows the team to examine their implications under stated parameter values. It can identify assumptions that need empirical scrutiny; it cannot establish that a feedback loop operated as specified.
Second, SD enables scenario analysis that can inform contribution analysis (Chapter 9). A model can compare scenarios with and without a specified programme component. The difference between their trajectories is an implication of the model, conditional on the stock–flow structure, parameters, and assumptions about other influences. It can expose whether a contribution story depends on an implausible feedback structure or parameter value. It cannot demonstrate that the programme made the corresponding difference in the observed world. Sterman (2000) provides the foundational treatment of SD modelling, including calibration, sensitivity testing, and validation procedures.






Using system dynamics within an evaluation



A system-dynamics model can be used to test the internal coherence of a theory of change, identify feedback processes that monitoring may miss, and compare explicitly modelled scenarios. The result remains conditional on the stock–flow structure, parameter values and validation evidence. It is not an estimated programme effect. This is why system dynamics can sharpen a contribution analysis but cannot settle its causal claim on its own.








System-dynamics evaluation: public-health reporting in New York State



Merrill et al. (2013) used system-dynamics techniques within a case-study evaluation of electronic health-information exchange for public-health reporting at the New York State Department of Health. The team collected project documentation and qualitative evidence from seven experts over eight months, then developed causal-loop diagrams iteratively from reference modes and accounts of implementation. The model clarified interacting implementation factors and possible leverage points. It did not estimate the effect of health-information exchange on public-health outcomes; it supported an implementation evaluation of a complex technology programme (Merrill et al., 2013).
crumbs: 13  Computational Simulation as Complement to Small-n Designs

title: 13  Computational Simulation as Complement to Small-n Designs
text:
13.3 Integration with small-n methods
The value of simulation for small-n evaluation lies in its integration with the methods covered in earlier chapters. Table 13.1 summarises three concrete pairings.



Table 13.1: Integration protocols for simulation and small-n methods











Pairing
Simulation role
Practical protocol
Cross-reference




ABM + Bayesian process tracing
Generate likelihood distributions under stated hypotheses
Build ABM of the causal mechanism; run Monte Carlo simulations under the focal and rival hypotheses; use the output distributions to inform likelihood inputs for updating
Chapter 11


SD + contribution analysis
Construct and test the contribution story
Translate the theory of change into an SD model; simulate with-programme and without-programme scenarios; compare trajectories
Chapter 9


ABM + QCA
Explore the implications of a configurational account
Translate a proposed QCA solution into agent rules; examine which model assumptions generate or disrupt it; compare the implications with observed cases
Chapter 7








The ABM + Bayesian pairing has the clearest methodological formulation of these three protocols. Befani et al. (2021) show how simulation-derived probabilities can be used where subjective elicitation would otherwise supply the diagnostic inputs.
The first pairing is the most developed methodologically. Befani et al. (2021) show how simulated probabilities can address the probability-estimation problem discussed in Chapter 11. The second is a way of testing the coherence of a contribution story, not a formal integration protocol. The third is more speculative still. An ABM can explore the implications of a configurational account, but synthetic configurations cannot test whether a QCA solution is robust in the empirical population. They can show which model assumptions would reproduce or disrupt a proposed solution.
crumbs: 13  Computational Simulation as Complement to Small-n Designs

title: 13  Computational Simulation as Complement to Small-n Designs
text:
13.4 Model construction, calibration, and validation
A simulation should begin with a bounded decision problem and an explicit account of what the model is intended to represent. The team needs to specify the system boundary, the actors or stocks included, the processes that connect them, the time horizon, and the outcome to be examined. Every omitted process is an assumption about irrelevance or about the model’s intended scope. These choices should be documented before scenario results are discussed.
Calibration aligns model parameters with available evidence; validation asks whether the model can reproduce relevant observed patterns without relying on the same information in every step. Neither task is a ceremonial check. A model can fit an observed pattern through several incompatible parameter combinations, and a good fit does not verify the causal mechanism embedded in the code. Evaluators should report the data sources, parameters estimated or fixed from outside evidence, calibration procedure, fit diagnostics, and the observed patterns used for comparison (Sterman, 2000).
Sensitivity analysis is the minimum safeguard for policy scenarios. It should show which conclusions persist when uncertain assumptions, parameters, initial conditions, or structural relations are varied within a defensible range. A result that changes materially under a plausible alteration is itself a finding about uncertainty. Scenario output should therefore be reported as conditional model behaviour, with the assumptions that drive it, rather than as a prediction of what an intervention will achieve.
crumbs: 13  Computational Simulation as Complement to Small-n Designs

title: 13  Computational Simulation as Complement to Small-n Designs
text:
13.5 Governance, participation, and transparency
Model building involves substantive judgement. Programme staff, participants, decision-makers, and technical modellers may each know different parts of the system. Their involvement can expose missing feedbacks, unrealistic behavioural rules, inaccessible data, and implementation constraints. It can also create pressure to include assumptions that favour an existing programme decision. The evaluation should record who contributed to the model, which assumptions were contested, and how disagreements were resolved or retained.
Transparency requires more than a diagram of the model. A report should identify the model purpose; entities, states, rules, and interactions; equations or code; input data and their provenance; parameter values; calibration procedure; validation tests; scenarios; random seeds where relevant; and all sensitivity analyses. Reproducible code and shareable data should be provided where confidentiality permits. Where they cannot be shared, the report should explain what cannot be inspected and how that limits independent review.
Participatory model building can improve a programme theory without validating it. Stakeholders may agree that a feedback loop is plausible because it reflects their experience. That agreement is useful for specifying the model and identifying evidence to collect. It does not establish that the feedback operated in the cases studied. The evaluation should keep the distinction between a jointly developed causal hypothesis and an empirically supported mechanism.
crumbs: 13  Computational Simulation as Complement to Small-n Designs

title: 13  Computational Simulation as Complement to Small-n Designs
text:
13.6 Scenario interpretation and decision use
A scenario asks what the model produces after specified assumptions are changed. Its result can support a decision when the decision concerns the consequences of those assumptions within the modelled system. It is most useful for comparing options, identifying threshold effects, locating assumptions that drive divergence, and deciding what empirical information would reduce uncertainty. It is not evidence that the corresponding policy will produce the modelled outcome in the world.
Commissioners should specify this role in advance. They should state whether the model is intended to clarify a theory of change, support implementation planning, identify information needs, generate diagnostic probability inputs, or explore conditional scenarios. They should not ask a simulation to settle an empirical effect question when no observational or experimental evidence is available. The relevant response may be to redesign the empirical evaluation, not to increase the complexity of the model.
Scenario results should report ranges and conditions, including cases in which the model gives a different answer. A single preferred trajectory hides the uncertainty that matters for use. Where a decision is sensitive to one unverified behavioural rule or parameter, the report should identify that dependency and set out what observation could test it. This turns simulation into a tool for disciplined learning rather than an authority that closes a disputed causal question.
crumbs: 13  Computational Simulation as Complement to Small-n Designs

title: 13  Computational Simulation as Complement to Small-n Designs
text:
13.7 When simulation is not appropriate
Simulation is a poor choice when the intervention, outcome, and system boundary cannot be specified with enough precision to construct defensible rules or stocks and flows. It is also unsuitable when available evidence cannot inform the assumptions that drive the decision, when the model cannot be reviewed by people with relevant technical and substantive expertise, or when the timetable allows only an untested model to be presented as a result.
The resource requirements are material. An adequate simulation requires modelling expertise, access to relevant evidence, time for iterative checking, computing resources where needed, and a process for version control and review. A visually persuasive model built quickly from uncertain inputs can be more damaging than a simple qualitative theory because it gives assumptions an appearance of numerical authority. The appropriate conclusion in such circumstances is often that the causal theory needs empirical investigation before it can be modelled for decision support.
crumbs: 13  Computational Simulation as Complement to Small-n Designs

title: 13  Computational Simulation as Complement to Small-n Designs
text:
13.8 Reporting, review, and reuse
The report should state the model’s role at the outset: theory development, implementation planning, conditional scenario exploration, or the estimation of probability inputs for diagnostic updating. It should identify the decision question, model boundary, causal assumptions, input data and their provenance, calibration and validation results, scenarios, sensitivity analysis, and the version of the code that generated each result. Graphs must identify whether a series is simulated or observed. Earlier specifications should be retained when the model changes during an evaluation, together with the evidence or judgement that prompted the change.
Independent review needs both modelling and substantive expertise. Technical review can assess computational reproducibility and the implementation of the stated model. Substantive review can assess whether the boundary, rules, data sources, and scenarios represent the intervention and setting. The handover package should include executable code, input data or instructions for obtaining them, a parameter register, scripts that reproduce reported outputs, scenario definitions, software versions, and a changelog. Before a model is reused, the team should assess whether the intervention, population, causal theory, and decision question remain within its original boundary.
crumbs: 13  Computational Simulation as Complement to Small-n Designs

title: 13  Computational Simulation as Complement to Small-n Designs
section: 13.9 Claim boundaries and combination with empirical designs
text:
13.9 Claim boundaries and combination with empirical designs
Simulation can sharpen an empirical evaluation by identifying observations that would distinguish competing model structures, estimating the implications of measurement error, or testing whether an interpretation is sensitive to a stated assumption. Process tracing can assess whether the modelled sequence occurred in an observed case. Configurational analysis can identify cross-case patterns that a model must be able to accommodate. Counterfactual designs can estimate an intervention contrast against which a model’s assumptions or longer-run scenarios can be assessed. These are complementary tasks, not interchangeable forms of evidence.
The contribution of a model is strongest when it is confronted with evidence capable of challenging it. A model that only repeats its own assumptions can be internally coherent and still irrelevant to the programme under evaluation. Conversely, disagreement between a model and empirical evidence need not mean that the data are wrong. It may reveal an omitted process, a mis-specified behavioural rule, a measurement problem, or a boundary that was drawn too narrowly. The evaluation should treat disagreement as an opportunity to revise the causal account.
Simulation supplies conditional consequences of a formalised theory. It can make assumptions inspectable, help select empirical tests, and clarify the decisions supported by available knowledge. It cannot establish that a programme caused an outcome without empirical evidence about the programme, its implementation, and relevant alternatives.
crumbs: 13  Computational Simulation as Complement to Small-n Designs

title: 13  Computational Simulation as Complement to Small-n Designs
text:
13.10 Strengths, limitations, and applicability
Simulation handles complexity, non-linearity, and emergence in ways that verbal theories of change cannot. An ABM can reveal unintended consequences that arise from agent interactions. An SD model can identify tipping points and feedback traps. Both force the evaluator to make causal assumptions explicit, which disciplines the reasoning process even when the model itself is imperfect.
The limitations are equally clear. Model validity is always contestable. Every simulation rests on assumptions about agent rules (ABM) or functional forms (SD), and different assumptions can produce different conclusions. The risk of confirmation bias applies: an analyst who believes in the programme’s effectiveness may unconsciously calibrate the model to confirm that belief. Computational expertise is a practical barrier. Building and validating a simulation model requires skills that most evaluation teams do not possess, and the cost of acquiring those skills may not be justified for every evaluation. Simulation results can be data-informed through calibration and validation, but they remain model-based: their implications depend on the model structure, parameters, and scenarios. They complement empirical evidence; they do not substitute for it.



Table 13.2: Applicability of simulation approaches in small-n evaluation










Criterion
Agent-based modelling
System dynamics




Primary role
Generate probabilities; model mechanisms; virtual counterfactuals
Map feedback structures; scenario analysis; dynamic contribution stories


Minimum data
Qualitative evidence on agent rules; quantitative calibration data for validation
Causal loop diagram; stock/flow estimates; time-series data for calibration


Expertise required
Programming (Python, NetLogo, or similar); simulation methodology
SD software (Vensim, Stella, or similar); differential equations


Causal claim
Supports claims from other logics; does not generate independent causal evidence
Supports claims from other logics; does not generate independent causal evidence


Main limitation
Model assumptions drive results; validation is difficult with few empirical cases
Assumes continuous variables and homogeneous populations; feedback structure must be known


Best combined with
Bayesian process tracing; QCA
Contribution analysis; process tracing












The case against and for computational simulation



Three criticisms recur. First, simulation models can produce any result by adjusting their assumptions. A model is only as good as its rules, and with enough degrees of freedom, the analyst can fit any narrative. Second, simulation adds a layer of abstraction that distances the evaluation from the empirical evidence. Stakeholders may distrust findings that rest on “what-if” scenarios rather than on observed data. Third, the expertise and time required to build credible simulations may not be proportionate to the evaluation budget, especially in resource-constrained settings.
The response is not that formal models remove these problems. Pattern-oriented modelling and sensitivity analysis can expose the implications of choices about parameters and structure; they do not validate those choices. A documented simulation may be more open to inspection than an implicit verbal theory, but its results remain conditional. The required expertise and time should be judged against the uncertainty the model is expected to reduce.


Simulation is a supporting modelling tradition, not an additional route to causal inference. The next chapters address the practical choices that follow: how to select and combine the book’s method families, and how to assess the resulting design.

title: 14  A Decision Framework for Method Selection
text:
14.1 Existing selection tools
Part II distinguishes three forms of causal claim–effects, configurations, and mechanisms–and the operations that can support them. The practical question is how to select and combine those operations for a particular evaluation. Without an explicit selection procedure, the evaluator’s training can determine the method before the causal question has been specified. A transparent procedure also lets commissioners examine the basis for a design choice rather than accept professional convention (Sempé et al., 2025).
Two existing frameworks offer partial guidance. Fox et al. (2022) organises methods into two families: “effects of causes” (counterfactual designs) and “causes of effects” (theory-based approaches). This distinction is useful as a first cut, but it groups different forms of causal claim under the same heading. Process tracing, contribution analysis, and QCA all fall under “causes of effects,” yet they use different forms of evidence and answer different questions. White & Phillips (2012) takes a different approach, distinguishing quantitative approaches adaptable to small samples from qualitative and theory-based approaches. The 3ie framework also maps sources of bias and proposes common steps for causal analysis. Both tools advance the field. Neither links the full range of evaluation questions to the distinctions used in this book.
We start from the evaluation question rather than from the method. The analyst specifies whether the claim concerns an effect, configurations, or a mechanism; identifies the unit or units in which it can be observed; and examines the variation, evidence, and plausible alternatives available. Those choices produce a shortlist of methods and evidential operations. They do not produce an automatic answer.
crumbs: 14  A Decision Framework for Method Selection

title: 14  A Decision Framework for Method Selection
text:
14.2 A claim-based decision matrix
Table 14.1 maps six types of evaluation question against four programme attributes. Each cell identifies methods and supporting operations that may be suitable. The matrix is not prescriptive. Case number is one consideration, but method choice also depends on the claim, the available variation, the quality and timing of evidence, the plausibility of alternatives, and the decision to be informed. Many evaluations involve more than one question type, and the next chapter discusses how to combine their evidential roles within a single design.



Table 14.1: Decision matrix: evaluation questions, programme attributes, and candidate methods












Evaluation question

One or a few cases with limited evidence

Effect: did it cause the outcome?
Synthetic control only where a defensible donor pool exists; otherwise assess whether a counterfactual is possible

Comparative designs or replicated SCEDs where their assumptions hold
SCED, including reversal or multiple-baseline designs, where phase structure and measurement support them


Contribution or mechanism: did it contribute, and through what process?
Contribution analysis; process tracing; diagnostic updating where tests are specified
Contribution analysis with a stated theory of change; targeted process evidence
Contribution analysis across sites; realist evaluation where CMO propositions can be examined

Configuration: which condition combinations produce the outcome?

Usually insufficient variation
QCA or CNA only if the cases and condition measurement permit a truth-table analysis
Temporal QCA only where the time structure and independence assumptions are defensible

Most significantchange
Outcome harvestingacross sites

Feedback or non-linearity: what does a formalised causal theory imply?
Model a bounded theory of change alongside an empirical method
Develop a qualitative causal-loop account before deciding whether simulation is warranted
Model heterogeneity only where agent rules and evidence justify it
Calibrate dynamic relations where suitable time-series evidence exist








The matrix is not prescriptive. Most evaluations require more than one question and therefore more than one component. See Chapter 15 for protocols on combining components within a single design. A concise version for commissioning and inception work is in the method-selection aid.
Three features of the matrix need emphasis. First, counterfactual designs are not limited to large samples. SCEDs and randomisation inference can be useful with few units, but only when the design provides a credible contrast: repeated measurement, a comparator, or a known assignment process. Case number alone does not supply that contrast. Second, configurational analysis has an evidential lower bound. QCA and CNA require variation in both conditions and outcomes. A sparse truth table does not become informative because it has been coded carefully.


Configurational evidence. There is no universal minimum number of cases. The relevant question is whether the available cases can distinguish the proposed configurations, retain meaningful diversity after calibration, and support an analysis that can be challenged by contradictory cases. A small-n configurational design should make that judgment explicit.
Third, simulation appears in the bottom row as a supporting tool rather than a causal warrant. It enters the matrix when the question involves feedback or non-linearity, and it operates alongside an empirical method.

title: 14  A Decision Framework for Method Selection
text:
14.3 Worked examples
Three published evaluations illustrate how the matrix maps real evaluation problems to logics and methods.
Example A: Gender-responsive budgeting in Kabale District, Uganda. Bamanyaki & Holvoet (2016) evaluated a civil society initiative that advocated for gender-responsive budgeting to improve maternal health service delivery in a single Ugandan district.


Bamanyaki & Holvoet (2016) combines contribution analysis with process tracing and Bayesian tests in a single-district governance evaluation.
There was one treated unit (the district), rich qualitative data (advocacy records, budget documents, key informant interviews with local officials and health workers), and a complex causal chain from civil society advocacy through budget allocation to service delivery. The evaluation question spanned contribution and mechanism. Entering the matrix at “contribution, few units, rich data” points to contribution analysis and process tracing. Entering at “mechanism, few units, rich data” points to process tracing with Bayesian updating. The evaluators used exactly this combination: they mapped the programme theory linking advocacy to maternal health outcomes, identified the causal mechanism, derived observable predictions, and tested the evidence using Bayesian logic (hoop and smoking-gun tests). The evaluation design combined three logics: generative (contribution analysis mapped the theory of change), diagnostic (Bayesian tests assessed the strength of evidence for each mechanism step), and the process-tracing method bridged both. Persson et al. (2013), analysing anti-corruption reforms as a collective action problem, illustrate the same structural challenge: complex governance interventions with a single treated unit that demand theory-based causal reasoning rather than cross-case comparison.
Example B: NHS modernisation in London. Greenhalgh et al. (2009) evaluated the NHS Modernisation Agency’s “whole-scale transformation” programme across four health care organisations and three clinical areas. The questions concerned mechanism and contextual variation: how did the programme operate, and why did its operation differ across settings? The evaluation developed initial context–mechanism–outcome propositions, examined them against evidence from each site, and refined them iteratively. This is a realist design for examining mechanisms across heterogeneous settings. It does not itself establish set-theoretic sufficiency; a configurational question would require a separate assessment of case and condition variation. Blackman et al. (2011) illustrates a related systems-oriented approach to public-health evaluation across English local authorities.
Example C: Writing intervention for struggling first-graders in Spain. Arrimada et al. (2018) followed 179 first-grade pupils with twice-weekly writing probes during 120 days of classroom instruction. The authors selected twelve pupils with low composition performance and poor handwriting for a further 72 days of parent-supervised Tier 2 tasks. Ten pupils improved in composition quality, and eight performed within the normal range relative to peers at the end of the intervention. The study illustrates the value of repeated measurement and of examining a maturational explanation through a comparison group and a non-verbal measure. It was not a standard staggered multiple-baseline design: the Tier 2 phase began as a common change for the selected pupils. The matrix therefore identifies the evidence that would be needed for a stronger counterfactual claim, rather than assigning the study to a design it did not use. Horner et al. (2005) set out the methodological standards that a multiple-baseline design would need to meet in an educational setting.

title: 14  A Decision Framework for Method Selection
text:
14.4 Making and recording the selection
The matrix is best used as a sequence of design decisions, not as a lookup table. A request for an impact evaluation does not establish that an effect can be estimated. The evaluator first states the proposed causal claim in a form that could be wrong: for example, that a programme changed a named outcome for a defined population over a stated period. The next question is what contrast could distinguish that claim from plausible alternatives. Where neither a comparison nor a repeated outcome series is available, the appropriate design may be contribution or mechanism-focused rather than a claim about net effect.
The unit of analysis also changes the feasible design. A programme may operate in one district but leave repeated observations of schools, facilities, households, or decisions. That structure can make a within-unit design possible. It does not automatically create independent cases. Conversely, a multi-site programme can have many sites yet little useful variation if implementation was uniform, outcome measures are not comparable, or the sites share the same shock. The design note should state which units provide the evidential leverage and why they can be compared.
Evidence is often available at different points in the causal chain. Administrative records may show delivery and timing; interviews and documents may illuminate decisions and mechanisms; outcome measurement may be sparse or delayed. Those differences should determine the questions that receive the strongest treatment. A contribution analysis can use implementation records and stakeholder accounts to examine whether a proposed pathway is credible. Process tracing can test a disputed step where records, interviews, and timing allow rival accounts to be separated. Neither procedure turns missing outcome evidence into an estimate of net effect.
The same discipline applies to simulation. A causal-loop diagram may help identify feedback, delays, or unintended consequences before a programme is implemented. It cannot establish that the programme produced an observed outcome unless its empirical assumptions are supported independently. When a model is included, the design should identify which empirical logic will test its assumptions or use its results, and what decision the model will inform (Hennessy et al., 2016; Sterman, 2000).

14.4.1 A short design record
Before fieldwork, the evaluator and commissioner should be able to agree a short written record of the selection. It does not replace a protocol. It records the decisions that otherwise tend to be made informally as data arrive.







Design question
Record before data collection




Claim
The outcome, population, period, and causal claim that the study will and will not make


Decision
The decision, user, and time by which findings are needed


Unit and variation
The unit of analysis; treated and comparison units or phases; relevant heterogeneity; possible interference


Evidence
Outcome measures, records, documents, observations, and interviews; their timing, access, and likely quality


Alternatives
The main rival explanations and the observations that would weaken each one


Method and evidential role
The proposed method or combination of methods, with a reason tied to the preceding rows


Boundaries
Claims that the design cannot support, foreseeable ethical constraints, and conditions that would require redesign



This record makes disagreement visible early. A commissioner may require an answer about effect when implementation is already complete and there is no outcome series or credible comparator. The appropriate response is to identify the resulting limit, not to relabel a theory-based inquiry as an impact estimate. Alternatively, the evaluation may be able to collect a series prospectively, introduce an intervention in phases, or retain a comparison group. Those are programme and commissioning decisions, not analytic adjustments made after the evidence has been collected.


14.4.2 Choosing between plausible approaches
Several approaches can be defensible for the same programme. The choice should follow the claim that carries the decision. A district-wide reform may justify process tracing if the issue is whether a particular administrative decision unlocked implementation. It may justify realist evaluation if the concern is how delivery differed across organisations. It may require both if the decision concerns a disputed pathway and the conditions under which that pathway operates. Combining methods is useful when each has a distinct evidential job; it is not useful when several methods repeat the same unexamined assumptions.
Method selection also has resource implications. Process tracing requires time to reconstruct chronology, identify alternatives, and obtain records that can discriminate between them. Realist evaluation requires sufficient access across contexts to refine rather than merely list context–mechanism–outcome propositions. Participatory approaches require time, safeguards, and a clear account of who has authority to interpret or contest findings. These requirements should be costed at commissioning. A design that cannot support its own evidence collection should be narrowed before fieldwork rather than repaired through a more elaborate analysis.
An independent review should test the selection against the initial claim. It should ask whether the proposed method has an appropriate unit of analysis; whether its contrast, process observations, or configurations can address the stated alternatives; and whether the intended conclusion exceeds the evidence. This is particularly useful when a familiar method has been specified before the evaluation question. It protects evaluators who need to say that the available evidence supports a narrower but still useful claim.

title: 14  A Decision Framework for Method Selection
section: 14.5 Feasibility is part of the design
text:
14.5 Feasibility is part of the design
Feasibility should be assessed before a method is chosen, not treated as a later operational problem. Access to sites, records, and participants determines what observations can be made and who can contest their interpretation. A plan for process tracing that depends on confidential correspondence may fail if access is not negotiated before key actors leave. A QCA that treats sites as comparable may fail if administrative indicators were assembled under different rules. A participatory approach may be inappropriate if participants cannot safely discuss the programme or if the organisation has not agreed how disagreement will be handled. These are design constraints because they alter the evidence available for a causal claim.
Timing is equally consequential. Some claims require evidence while a programme is being introduced: the sequence of decisions, implementation choices, and early adaptations may no longer be recoverable later. Other claims require time for an outcome to occur. A commission that asks for attribution immediately after delivery may be able to examine implementation and early mechanisms, but not a final outcome that has not had time to change. The selection record should distinguish the decision deadline from the time required for the proposed outcome and causal process to become observable.
Ethics and safeguarding also influence method choice. A withdrawal design may be unacceptable where a service is believed to reduce harm. Randomising an implementation sequence can be reasonable only when the sequence is administratively possible and does not unfairly delay access. Interviews about contested decisions can expose staff or community members to professional or political risk. The protocol should identify these conditions and specify how they will affect the evidence strategy. Ethical constraints do not make causal reasoning optional; they identify which contrasts and observations are unavailable.

14.5.1 Pre-specification and adaptation
The principal causal claim, unit of analysis, outcome definition, and basis for comparison should be recorded before results are examined. This matters in small-n work because there are often many reasonable analytical choices and little redundancy to reveal a discretionary change. Pre-specification is not a demand that fieldwork proceed mechanically. It distinguishes a justified response to new information from a change that follows an apparent result.
An adaptive design should therefore keep an amendment record. It should state what changed, when it changed, why the original plan was no longer suitable, and which conclusions are affected. Suppose interviews identify a mechanism that was absent from the initial theory of change. It may be appropriate to add evidence collection and to treat the mechanism as a revised proposition. It is not appropriate to present that proposition as though it had been the original test. The distinction gives readers a basis for judging what the evidence can bear.
The same applies to calibration and coding choices. A QCA needs transparent membership thresholds and a reason for the conditions included. Process tracing needs a stated account of the observations that would raise or lower confidence in a mechanism. Contribution analysis needs a theory of change that identifies rival explanations rather than merely restating programme activities. Changes to these choices should be explained in the report, with the consequences for interpretation. The aim is not to freeze inquiry; it is to make the development of the inquiry inspectable.


14.5.2 Sensitivity and negative findings
The selection framework should lead directly to a sensitivity plan. For counterfactual designs, the plan may specify alternative outcome windows, the treatment of missing observations, placebo or falsification checks, and the consequences of spillover. For process tracing, it may identify the evidence that would weaken the preferred mechanism and the sources most likely to produce it. For configurational work, it should test whether reasonable calibration choices or case thresholds change the identified configurations. These checks are part of the evidential warrant, not a technical appendix added after a positive finding.
Negative and inconclusive findings also need a place in the design. No observed outcome change may reflect an ineffective intervention, an outcome measured too early, an implementation failure, or a measure unable to register the expected change. A well-chosen logic helps separate these possibilities. Where the evidence cannot separate them, the report should say so. An evaluation is more useful when it identifies the unresolved alternative than when it converts uncertainty into a statement that nothing happened.
crumbs: 14  A Decision Framework for Method Selection

title: 14  A Decision Framework for Method Selection
text:
14.6 A review sequence for commissioners
Commissioners often receive a proposed method before they receive a fully specified claim. The following sequence can be used to review a brief or inception report.

What decision will use the findings, and what needs to be known for that decision?
What causal claim is proposed, for whom, over what period, and at which level of analysis?
What observations could distinguish the claim from the most plausible alternatives?
Which observations are genuinely available within the time, access, and ethical constraints?
Which method addresses those observations, and what conclusion does it permit?
What would make the proposed design infeasible or require it to be amended?

The sequence may result in a narrower question than the commissioning brief originally anticipated. That is often preferable to commissioning a method that cannot address the brief and reporting a stronger conclusion than the evidence supports. It may also reveal an opportunity to improve the programme’s information system or rollout plan so that a later evaluation can answer a question that is currently out of reach.
crumbs: 14  A Decision Framework for Method Selection

title: 14  A Decision Framework for Method Selection
text:
14.7 Common selection errors
The first error is to choose a method because it is familiar. A team trained in experimental methods may treat every question as a search for a comparator, even when the central uncertainty concerns implementation or a disputed mechanism. A team trained in theory-based evaluation may reconstruct a credible pathway without asking whether a feasible design could estimate an effect. Familiarity is not disqualifying, but it is not a design justification. The proposed method should be compared with the causal claim and the evidence it requires.
The second error is to treat a theory of change as evidence. A theory of change is necessary for contribution analysis, realist evaluation, and much process tracing because it makes the proposed causal sequence explicit. It does not show that the sequence occurred. The design must specify observations that would distinguish programme activity from the mechanism through which it was expected to matter, and from alternative explanations for the observed outcome.
The third is to use a label in place of an evidential strategy. Calling a study mixed methods does not explain how its sources will bear on the same claim. Calling it participatory does not establish how accounts will be substantiated or how unequal authority will be handled. Calling it a systems approach does not identify a feedback structure that can be examined. The selection record should name the observations, comparison, or test that makes the label consequential.
Finally, evaluators sometimes respond to a constrained commission by adding methods until the proposal appears comprehensive. A design with interviews, workshops, a survey, and a model can still leave the causal question unanswered if the sources are not connected to alternatives or if the work cannot be completed to an adequate standard. A smaller design with a stated claim, a credible source of leverage, and explicit limits is usually easier to scrutinise and more useful to the decision-maker.
crumbs: 14  A Decision Framework for Method Selection

title: 14  A Decision Framework for Method Selection
text:
14.8 When to combine methods
The worked examples illustrate a recurring pattern. Most realistic evaluations involve more than one question, and no single method answers all of them. The decision matrix helps identify the methods and operations required; it does not specify how to combine them. The integration plan should state the order in which each component will be used, which finding will be carried from one component to another, and how disagreement between components will be interpreted. A contribution analysis may identify the steps that process tracing will test; repeated outcome evidence may identify an unexpected change that requires a mechanism-focused inquiry; participatory accounts may identify outcomes that require independent substantiation. Sequential, concurrent, and nested designs have different coordination requirements. The next chapter addresses these protocols directly.

title: 15  Integrating Methods and Causal Claims
text:
15.1 Patterns of integration in the literature
Part II distinguishes causal claims about effects, configurations, and mechanisms, and the methods that can support them. Chapter 14 considered how to select those methods; this chapter considers how they can be combined without blurring their claims. A counterfactual design addresses a causal contrast. Process tracing investigates a proposed mechanism. QCA examines configurations of conditions. Commissioners commonly need more than one of these answers (Creswell & Plano Clark, 2018; Teddlie & Tashakkori, 2009). The issue is whether each component has a defined evidential job and whether the resulting findings can be interpreted together.
The bibliometric corpus can show whether core method families use a shared vocabulary. It cannot show, without reading the publications, whether those methods were used together in one evaluation. Figure 15.1 therefore reports title-and-abstract co-mention rather than integration. The analysis covers 18,520 unique works and 18,687 method–work pairs in the comparative core-method corpus. Theory of change and computational simulation are reported separately because they are, respectively, a contextual precursor and supporting modelling literature. Labels with materially different technical meanings are retained for discovery but excluded from this comparison. The Methods appendix describes the retrieval and filtering rules.
Explicit overlap is uncommon. The largest pair is configurational with generative and mechanistic approaches: 101 works name a method from both families, or 0.62 per cent of the works naming either family. This group includes the established combination of QCA and process tracing, where cross-case results inform within-case analysis (Rohlfing & Schneider, 2018). Generative and participatory approaches co-occur in two works (0.02 per cent). No other pairing occurs. These counts describe the terminology visible in titles and abstracts. They do not establish that the named methods were applied, much less integrated.
Counterfactual methods have no cross-family co-mentions in this corpus. That is a result about visible terminology, not proof that evaluators never combine them with process tracing, QCA, or participatory methods. A second method may be named only in the full text; ambiguous method names may also create false matches. The absence of a co-mention can still guide the literature review: proposed combinations such as SCED with process tracing or randomisation inference with QCA cannot yet draw on a sizeable, readily identifiable body of publications. Their methodological case has to be made from the inferential tasks each component performs.
crumbs: 15  Integrating Methods and Causal Claims

title: 15  Integrating Methods and Causal Claims
text:
Figure 15.1: Title-and-abstract co-mention between core method families, 2000–2025. Cells report the Jaccard coefficient: the number of works naming both families divided by the number naming either family. Data: OpenAlex, retrieved 2 August 2026.






Lieberman (2005) formalised the nested analysis strategy, combining large-n statistical analysis with small-n case studies selected on the basis of the statistical results. Schneider & Rohlfing (2013) extend this to QCA, proposing formal protocols for combining set-theoretic analysis with process tracing.
crumbs: 15  Integrating Methods and Causal Claims

title: 15  Integrating Methods and Causal Claims
text:
15.2 Integration designs
Three design types structure the combination of methods within a single evaluation. The mixed-methods literature distinguishes sequential, concurrent, and embedded (or nested) designs (Creswell & Plano Clark, 2018; Greene, 2007). The terminology below adapts these forms to causal inquiry.

15.2.1 Sequential integration
In a sequential design, one component precedes and informs the other. Schneider & Rohlfing (2013) set out protocols for combining QCA and process tracing. A configurational analysis can identify cases that are typical of a proposed pathway, deviant cases, or cases that discriminate between rival configurations; process tracing then investigates whether the proposed within-case mechanism occurred. The order matters because the cross-case analysis supplies a reason for selecting the cases, while the within-case inquiry examines a different claim. The reverse sequence is also possible. Process tracing can develop or revise propositions before a configurational analysis examines whether the relevant conditions distinguish outcomes across a defined case set. In either direction, the protocol should specify how the first component will affect case selection, theory development, or analysis in the second.


15.2.2 Concurrent integration
In a concurrent design, two or more components operate in parallel during the same evaluation period. The protocol needs to identify the distinct question for each component, the evidence each will collect, and the point at which their findings will be compared. A counterfactual component might assess whether a defined outcome changed, while participatory evidence identifies outcomes or implementation consequences that the pre-specified measure did not capture. Agreement does not make one source a validation of the other, because the components may address different claims. Divergence should prompt a review of the outcome definition, the causal pathway, the quality of the measures, and the limits of the participating evidence.


15.2.3 Nested integration
In a nested design, one component is embedded within another. Befani & Mayne (2014) show how contribution analysis and process tracing can be combined: the contribution story identifies the pathway and assumptions requiring scrutiny, while process-tracing tests assess selected links and alternatives. The two components do not have the same job. Contribution analysis keeps the inquiry connected to the full theory of change; process tracing provides a more demanding evidential assessment for particular claims. Simulation can also be nested as a supporting tool where it clarifies a theory of change, explores a feedback process, or tests the implications of stated assumptions. It does not generate empirical evidence for a causal mechanism simply by producing an output (Chapter 13).


Befani & Mayne (2014) demonstrate how process tracing and contribution analysis can be formally combined in a nested design, with diagnostic tests providing the evidential foundation for key links within the contribution story.
Table 15.1 summarises the three types.



Table 15.1: Three integration designs for multi-method evaluation

Coordination challenge
