title: 15  Integrating Methods and Causal Claims
text:
15.3 Building an integration protocol
Integration should be designed before the separate components begin. The first task is to separate the claims. An evaluation may ask whether an intervention changed an outcome, whether a proposed mechanism operated, which contextual combinations were associated with success, and whether participants experienced changes not captured in the outcome measure. These are related questions, but they are not interchangeable. The protocol should identify the claim, evidence, method, and expected contribution of each component.









Component
Claim addressed
Evidence and unit
How it informs the wider design




Counterfactual component





Mechanism component





Configurational component





Participatory component





Simulation component, if used






The table is deliberately blank. It prevents a familiar failure of mixed-method design: collecting several forms of evidence and deciding only at the reporting stage what each was intended to establish. A component without a distinct claim may be unnecessary. A claim with no component may require the evaluation question to be narrowed or the design to be changed.
The second task is to define the handover between components. In a sequential design, the handover may be a case-selection rule, a set of hypotheses, or a revised theory of change. In a concurrent design, it may be a jointly agreed outcome definition, a shared chronology, or a scheduled comparison of interim findings. In a nested design, it may be the set of causal links selected for diagnostic testing. The protocol should specify who makes the handover decision, what evidence will be available at that point, and what happens if the first component produces a result that does not support the planned second component.
The third task is to keep analytical independence where it is needed. Evidence used to formulate a mechanism should not automatically be treated as independent confirmation of that mechanism. Researchers who collect participatory accounts should be clear about whether those accounts are evidence of experienced change, sources of hypotheses, or evidence for a causal link. Where the same document or informant contributes to several components, the report should say so. Apparent convergence is weaker when every component relies on the same underlying source.

15.3.1 Shared concepts, separate inference
Combined designs need common definitions of the programme, outcome, period, and relevant context. Without them, one component may examine a change in service delivery while another examines a later population outcome, and their findings will appear to conflict although they concern different events. A shared chronology is often the simplest safeguard. It records implementation decisions, exposure, other relevant events, and the points at which each evidence source was collected. It also makes clear when an alleged mechanism preceded an outcome and when it did not.
Common definitions do not require identical inference. A process trace may conclude that a mechanism is well supported in one case. A QCA may find that the corresponding condition is not necessary across the case set. These conclusions can coexist: a mechanism may operate in one pathway without being the only route to the outcome. The report should preserve this distinction instead of converting a within-case finding into a cross-case generalisation.
Counterfactual and theory-based components require particular care. An estimated effect does not identify the mechanism that produced it. A credible contribution story does not estimate the size of an effect. Where both are present, the integration claim may be that the observed effect is consistent with a specified pathway and that the pathway has been examined against alternatives. It should not state that the mechanism has been proved solely because an effect and a plausible story are both present.


15.3.2 Planning for disagreement
Disagreement between components should be anticipated in the protocol. The team should state whether a discrepancy will trigger further evidence collection, re-examination of an assumption, a revision of the theory of change, or a qualified conclusion. This avoids treating findings from a preferred method as decisive by default.
Disagreement can arise for substantive reasons. Outcomes may improve through a pathway not included in the original theory. An intervention may work in some contexts while failing in others. Participants may value changes that the primary outcome does not measure. It can also arise from measurement error, differences in time horizon, selective participation, or dependence between sources. These possibilities need to be considered before the final synthesis; otherwise the discussion of divergence becomes a post hoc explanation for an inconvenient result.
The final synthesis should therefore have three parts. It should report the conclusion from each component at the level it can support. It should identify where those conclusions reinforce, qualify, or contradict one another. It should then state the integrated conclusion and the remaining uncertainty. This order protects against a smooth narrative that conceals a weak component or an unresolved contradiction.
crumbs: 15  Integrating Methods and Causal Claims

title: 15  Integrating Methods and Causal Claims
text:
15.4 Resourcing and governance
Multi-method designs take more than the sum of their individual methods. The additional work includes agreeing definitions, maintaining a common chronology, coordinating fieldwork, and reviewing interim findings without allowing one component to shape the evidence collected by another. The budget should provide for these tasks. If it covers only separate data-collection streams, integration will be postponed until reporting, when it is difficult to revisit a missing observation or a poorly defined comparison.
Responsibilities also need to be clear. A technical lead may be responsible for the counterfactual analysis, another investigator for process tracing, and community partners for participatory work. Someone must nevertheless be responsible for the integrated claim: maintaining the protocol, identifying dependencies between sources, recording amendments, and ensuring that no component is described as evidence for a question it did not address. That role requires enough authority to challenge the preferred interpretation of any one component.
Data governance can limit integration. Administrative data may be available only in an aggregated form, while interviews contain identifiable accounts of the decisions that produced the observed pattern. The integration plan should identify what can be linked, who can access linked information, and what must remain separate. Protecting confidentiality may prevent some desirable cross-checks. The report should describe the resulting limitation rather than implying that all evidence was examined together.

15.4.1 Reporting an integrated design
Readers should be able to reconstruct the design without inferring it from a sequence of method sections. A report can begin with the causal questions and a diagram or table showing the role of each component. It should then describe the components separately, including their units, evidence, assumptions, and limitations. The synthesis section should cite the results from those components rather than introducing a new conclusion with no visible evidential route.
The report should distinguish three forms of statement. A component-level finding states what a particular analysis found. An integration finding states how two or more component findings relate. A programme conclusion states what those findings permit the evaluation to say for the decision at hand. This distinction is especially important where the components operate at different levels: an individual-level SCED cannot by itself establish a district-wide effect, and a district-level process trace cannot by itself establish the experience of all participants.
Visual displays can help, but only when they preserve those distinctions. An integration table may show the causal question, component, evidence, finding, and implication for each conclusion. A common chronology can show whether the proposed mechanism preceded the outcome. Neither should turn a provisional mechanism into a confirmed pathway through layout alone.
crumbs: 15  Integrating Methods and Causal Claims

title: 15  Integrating Methods and Causal Claims
text:
15.5 When not to integrate
Combining logics is not always warranted. The evaluation may have one narrow decision question that a well-specified design can answer without a second component. It may have insufficient time or access to conduct the components adequately. The proposed methods may make incompatible claims about the same evidence without a credible way to reconcile them. In these circumstances, a focused design with explicit limits is preferable to a nominally integrated study.
Integration is also inappropriate when it obscures a disagreement that the evaluation cannot resolve. If administrative data point in one direction and participant accounts in another, the responsible conclusion may be that the evidence is inconsistent and that a further decision requires new information. A combined narrative that selects the more convenient finding is not integration. It is a reporting choice that hides the uncertainty the evaluation was commissioned to assess.
crumbs: 15  Integrating Methods and Causal Claims

title: 15  Integrating Methods and Causal Claims
text:
15.6 Quality criteria for integration
Three criteria distinguish rigorous integration from ad hoc method mixing.
The first criterion is coherence. The components must rest on compatible assumptions. Contribution analysis and diagnostic process tracing can be combined because a contribution story identifies links and alternatives for which diagnostic tests are then specified. QCA and process tracing can also be combined: QCA identifies cross-case patterns, while process tracing examines a proposed mechanism within selected cases. Some pairings require particular care. Set-theoretic necessity claims and Bayesian probability updates answer different questions. An evaluation that uses both must not treat one as a translation of the other.
Coherence also requires a compatible level of inference. A case-level account can explain an outcome in that case; it cannot establish that the same mechanism was necessary across a population. A set-theoretic finding can describe a configuration in the observed case set; it does not identify the size of an intervention effect. The integration protocol should state where each component’s conclusion begins and ends, and the final synthesis should not extend a conclusion beyond the component with the relevant warrant.
The second criterion is transparency. The integration rationale must be reported explicitly. A multi-method evaluation report should state which question each component addresses, why it was chosen, and how findings from different components are brought together. Without that account, a report is a collection of findings rather than an integrated causal account.
Transparency includes the points at which the design changed. If an early component altered the cases selected for later investigation, the report should give the selection rule and the result of applying it. If field evidence required a theory of change to be revised, the earlier and revised propositions should be distinguishable. If data access prevented a planned comparison, the final claim should be revised accordingly. These details permit a reader to assess whether integration followed the protocol or whether the protocol was reconstructed after the findings were known.
The third criterion is the treatment of divergence. When components disagree, the disagreement may be informative. A process trace may support a mechanism that a QCA does not find to be necessary; the mechanism may operate in one pathway without being the only route to the outcome. A SCED may show no effect while an MSC story reports meaningful change. The outcome measure may not capture what participants describe, or the reported change may not be attributable to the intervention. The evaluator should report the disagreement and assess these alternatives rather than suppress it.
Divergence should not automatically be treated as a substantive discovery. It can also reflect different populations, observation periods, definitions, or sources of bias. The evaluator should first establish whether the components actually address the same claim. Where they do, the report should set out the alternative explanations for the discrepancy and the evidence bearing on each. Where they do not, the report should explain the different conclusions without forcing a single verdict.

title: 15  Integrating Methods and Causal Claims
text:
15.7 Looking ahead
This chapter and the preceding one have addressed method selection and method combination. The next chapter turns to a different dimension of quality: biases, transparency, and reporting standards that apply across all small-n methods.

title: 16  Bias, Transparency, and Quality Standards
text:
16.1 Sources of bias at small n
Every evaluation method is vulnerable to bias. Chapter 15 considered how multiple logics can be combined; this chapter examines the safeguards that apply to each logic and to their integration. Larger samples can reduce random error. They do not correct a systematically biased measure, selective case access, or an unsupported causal assumption. In small-n evaluation, a limited number of cases and evidence sources often leaves less redundancy with which to detect those problems. The task is to identify the threat, show how it was investigated, and state what remains unresolved.
White & Phillips (2012) identified three families of bias that affect small-n impact evaluations. Each operates differently depending on the logic being used, but all three are present across methods.
Respondent biases arise when the people providing evidence distort it, whether deliberately or unconsciously. Social desirability bias can lead respondents to report what they think the evaluator wants to hear. Recall bias can affect accounts of past events, especially when participants are asked to reconstruct causal sequences after the fact. Stakeholders may also attribute observed changes to the programme because it is salient or because they have an interest in its continuation. These risks are particularly relevant where stakeholder testimony is a substantial part of the evidence base, including participatory approaches (Chapter 12) and process-tracing inquiries that depend on key informant interviews.
Evaluator biases arise from the analyst’s own reasoning processes. Confirmation bias can lead evaluators to seek and weight evidence that supports prior beliefs about a programme. In Bayesian process tracing (Chapter 11), prior probabilities and assessments of evidence can make those judgements visible, but they can also expose disagreement about them (Befani, 2020). Anchoring can give early evidence undue influence as new information is assessed. Vivid or recent evidence can receive more weight than systematic but less memorable data. These risks require particular attention whenever evaluative judgement is central to the route from evidence to conclusion.
Selection bias arises from the choice of cases, sites, or units. At small n, case selection is an analytical decision rather than a sampling procedure, and it can shape the finding. Selecting on the dependent variable, for example by choosing only cases where a programme appeared to succeed, can inflate the apparent effectiveness of the intervention. Convenience sampling can introduce systematic differences between the studied cases and the population of interest. In configurational methods (Chapter 7), the choice of cases determines the truth table and can affect which solutions the analysis identifies.
crumbs: 16  Bias, Transparency, and Quality Standards

title: 16  Bias, Transparency, and Quality Standards
text: Three bias families. Respondent bias concerns accounts provided by informants. Evaluator bias concerns analysis and judgement. Selection bias concerns the cases or observations included. Their consequences depend on the design and the available opportunities for corroboration.
crumbs: 16  Bias, Transparency, and Quality Standards

title: 16  Bias, Transparency, and Quality Standards
text:
16.2 Mitigation strategies
Four strategies can reduce the risk of bias in small-n evaluations. Their value depends on the causal claim and on whether they change the evidence available to assess it.
Structured protocols constrain the evaluator’s discretion at each step. A pre-specified causal claim and theory of change, where relevant, identify the mechanisms to be investigated and the evidence that could support or weaken them. Coding rubrics specify how evidence is classified. Checklists require the evaluator to consider rival explanations systematically rather than selectively.
Pre-specification of causal claims applies beyond experimental designs.


Pre-specification. A time-stamped protocol or inception report can record causal claims, evidence plans, analytical decisions, and the conditions under which they may be amended. The point is an auditable record, not a particular platform.
Before collecting data, the evaluator states the causal claims to be examined and the observations that would support or weaken each one. Pre-specification does not prevent bias. It allows a reader to distinguish planned analysis from an amendment made after findings emerged.
Blinding can separate evidence collection from causal assessment where feasible. In Bayesian process tracing, for example, different team members may gather and code evidence and assess priors or evidence tests. This does not remove judgement, but it can make some decisions less dependent on one person’s preferred conclusion. Blinding is more difficult in participatory methods, where the evaluator is often directly involved in facilitating the evidence-generation process.
Sensitivity analysis varies the analyst’s assumptions and reports whether the conclusions change. The specific form of sensitivity analysis depends on the logic being used, and each method family has developed its own protocols.
In QCA, sensitivity analysis involves testing whether the solution holds when cases are added or removed, when calibration thresholds are shifted (particularly the crossover point), or when conditions are recoded.


QCA calibration and robustness procedures are introduced in Chapter 7. The sensitivity guidance here extends them to a formal quality assurance protocol.
Schneider & Wagemann (2012) stress that calibration choices require substantive justification and transparent robustness assessment. The evaluator should report plausible alternative thresholds, whether they change truth-table membership or solution terms, and the cases responsible for any change. Where a single calibration decision changes the solution, the conclusion depends on a choice that requires explicit defence.
In Bayesian process tracing, sensitivity analysis can vary the prior probability and the sensitivity and false-positive rate estimates for each test, then assess whether the posterior odds support the same conclusion. The analysis should make the alternative inputs visible and report whether reasonable changes alter the conclusion (Befani, 2020). If they do, the causal claim is sensitive to probability judgements that require explicit defence.
In contribution analysis, sensitivity analysis involves considering alternative contribution stories and assessing whether the evidence distinguishes between them. Each causal link in the theory of change should be tested against the most plausible rival explanation for that link, not just the overall alternative hypothesis. If the contribution story rests on a single causal link for which the evidence is ambiguous, the evaluation should report that link as a point of fragility.
In SCED analysis, sensitivity analysis can examine whether the conclusion changes when different appropriate analytical approaches are used, when influential observations are treated according to a stated rule, or when a justified alternative phase specification is considered. The report should state which analytical choices were planned, which were amended, and whether the main conclusion changes (Kratochwill et al., 2013).
If the conclusion is sensitive to reasonable alternative assumptions under any of these protocols, the evaluator should report that fragility rather than suppress it.
crumbs: 16  Bias, Transparency, and Quality Standards

title: 16  Bias, Transparency, and Quality Standards
text:
16.3 Evidence records and independent challenge
Small-n evaluations benefit from an evidence record that links claims to their sources. The record need not be elaborate. For each substantive causal claim, it should identify the source, when the observation was made, the relevant unit, the method through which it was obtained, and the alternative explanation it bears on. A document may establish the date of a decision but say little about how that decision was implemented. An interview may describe a mechanism but be affected by recall, position, or interest. Recording these distinctions prevents a source from carrying more weight than it can support.
An audit trail should also record coding decisions, excluded cases or observations, amendments to the protocol, and unsuccessful attempts to obtain evidence. These are not administrative details. A missing record can itself affect the causal account, particularly where the absence is related to organisational incentives or political sensitivity. The report need not disclose confidential material, but it should explain what evidence could not be inspected and the implication for the conclusion.
Independent challenge is useful when an evaluation depends heavily on expert judgement. A reviewer can inspect whether the initial theory of change contains genuine alternatives, whether process-tracing tests distinguish them, whether QCA calibration follows the stated substantive anchors, or whether phase changes in a SCED were fixed before outcomes were examined. The reviewer need not repeat every analysis. The purpose is to test the route from evidence to conclusion and to identify discretionary decisions that deserve fuller reporting.

16.3.1 Quality assurance during fieldwork
Quality assurance should occur while evidence can still be improved. Teams can review the shared chronology, check whether the planned sources remain accessible, compare coding across a small subset of material, and identify whether the implementation record contains the events needed to assess the theory of change. These checks should be documented separately from substantive interpretation. Otherwise a fieldwork review can become an opportunity to adapt the evidence plan to an emerging preferred conclusion.
The response to a shortfall depends on its nature. If an outcome measure is missing, an effect claim may need to be narrowed. If the original mechanism is not observable, the evaluation may still document implementation but should not claim to have tested that mechanism. If one case becomes inaccessible, the implications for comparison, configurational diversity, or transfer should be assessed before replacing it with a more convenient case. Explicit decisions at this stage are more credible than a later account that treats the final evidence base as though it had been planned from the outset.
crumbs: 16  Bias, Transparency, and Quality Standards

title: 16  Bias, Transparency, and Quality Standards
section: 16.4 Logic-specific checks within a common standard
text:
16.4 Logic-specific checks within a common standard
The common safeguards do not remove the need for method-specific quality criteria. Counterfactual designs require an account of the comparison, the assignment or phase structure, outcome measurement, interference, and any concurrent events that could explain a change. A result should not be described as an effect merely because it follows an intervention in time. The report must show why the observed contrast warrants that interpretation.
Configurational analysis requires a transparent case universe, a defensible calibration strategy, and close attention to limited diversity and contradictory configurations. Researchers should report the cases retained in the analysis, the condition definitions, truth-table decisions, and the robustness of the solution. A minimally sufficient solution is not a general account of causation. It describes a relationship within the cases, measures, and calibration choices examined.
Generative approaches require clear propositions about the mechanism, conditions, and expected observations. Realist evaluation should distinguish proposed CMO configurations from configurations supported by the evidence. Contribution analysis should identify alternative explanations for the main links in the theory of change. Process tracing should state why a particular observation is expected under one explanation and not another. In each case, a detailed narrative is not enough: the reader needs to see how the evidence changes confidence in the claim.
Participatory approaches require additional attention to voice, authority, and risk. The report should identify who took part, who did not, how accounts were selected or substantiated, and how disagreement was handled. Participation can improve the relevance of questions and identify changes otherwise missed by administrative data. It does not give stakeholder accounts privileged access to causal attribution. That conclusion still depends on the evidence and reasoning set out in the design.
Simulation requires a record of model purpose, structure, parameterisation, calibration where relevant, validation exercises, and uncertainty. A model may be useful for examining the consequences of stated assumptions even when it cannot estimate an intervention effect. Reports should not use a plausible model output as confirmation that the programme caused an observed outcome. The empirical evidence for the causal links and the modelling evidence should be described separately before they are interpreted together.
crumbs: 16  Bias, Transparency, and Quality Standards

title: 16  Bias, Transparency, and Quality Standards
text:
16.5 Reporting standards
Several method-specific reporting standards exist. SCRIBE (Single-Case Reporting guideline In BEhavioural interventions) provides a structured checklist for SCED studies (Tate et al., 2016). The CONSORT extension for N-of-1 trials (CENT) adapts the familiar clinical trial reporting framework to single-case designs (Shamseer et al., 2015). RAMESES (Realist And Meta-narrative Evidence Syntheses: Evolving Standards) covers realist evaluation and realist synthesis (Wong et al., 2013). Transparency standards for QCA specify how to report calibration decisions, truth table analyses, and solution terms (Schneider & Wagemann, 2010).
These standards share common elements: they require the evaluator to report design decisions, describe data sources, justify analytical choices, and acknowledge limitations.


Method-specific standards. SCRIBE for SCEDs (Tate et al., 2016). CENT for N-of-1 trials (Shamseer et al., 2015). RAMESES for realist evaluation (Wong et al., 2013). Schneider & Wagemann transparency standards for QCA (Schneider & Wagemann, 2010).
They differ in what they emphasise, reflecting the different logics on which each method rests. A multi-logic evaluation therefore needs to show both how each component met its own standards and how their findings were related in the overall causal account.
Table 16.1 proposes a unified reporting checklist for small-n impact evaluations. The items are organised by evaluation phase and apply regardless of which logic or combination of logics the evaluation uses.



Table 16.1: Proposed reporting checklist for small-n impact evaluations









Phase
Reporting item




Design
State the evaluation questions and the logic(s) selected to address each one



Justify the choice of logic(s) with reference to programme attributes and data availability



Describe the case/unit selection procedure and the criteria used



Report pre-specified causal claims and analytical protocols, together with any amendments


Data
Describe each data source and its relationship to the causal claim



Report potential biases for each data source (respondent, evaluator, selection)



Describe the steps taken to mitigate each identified bias


Analysis
Report the analytical procedure for each logic used



Describe calibration, coding, or classification decisions and their justification



Report sensitivity analyses and their results


Interpretation
State the causal claim(s) and the evidential warrant for each



Report convergence or divergence across logics, if a multi-logic design was used



Identify limitations that the mitigation strategies did not address



Distinguish between findings that are well-supported and findings that are tentative






The checklist is not a replacement for method-specific standards. Evaluators using SCEDs should follow SCRIBE in addition to this checklist. Evaluators using realist evaluation should follow RAMESES. The checklist provides a common framework for evaluations that combine methods and helps readers assess the quality of a small-n evaluation across traditions.

16.5.1 Using the checklist
The checklist is useful at inception, during fieldwork, and at reporting. At inception, it can expose a gap between the intended claim and the evidence that will be collected. During fieldwork, it can be used to record changes in access, measurement, or case selection before those changes become invisible in the final report. At reporting, it gives reviewers a way to distinguish an evidence limitation from a limitation that has not been considered.
Completing every item does not make a causal claim credible. The checklist cannot create a comparator where none exists, recover an unobserved mechanism, or resolve a politically constrained evidence base. Its role is narrower: it requires evaluators to show their design decisions, the sources that support their claims, and the threats that remain. A report that identifies a limit clearly can still be useful to a commissioner. A report that conceals the limit cannot be assessed.
The standard should also be proportionate. A short formative inquiry does not require the same documentation as a multi-year, multi-site evaluation. It should nevertheless state its question, evidence base, and claim boundary. Conversely, an evaluation making an effect or attribution claim should provide enough information for another researcher or reviewer to inspect the design, reproduce the main analytical steps where possible, and understand why competing explanations were discounted.
From an EIPM perspective, structured reporting standards can support the institutional conditions for appraising evidence (Sempé et al., 2025). Transparency about the claim, evidence, assumptions, and remaining limits gives users and intermediaries a basis for deciding how much weight to give a finding. The checklist above provides one instrument for reviewing these features across a multi-logic evaluation. It does not show that a reporting format will produce evidence use or policy change.
The final part of the book shifts from methodology to the policy ecosystem, examining how small-n evaluations are commissioned (Chapter 18), how their findings are translated for policy audiences (Chapter 19), and how methods adapt in constrained settings (Chapter 20).

title: 17  Small-n Methods and Evidence-Informed Policymaking
text:
17.1 The EIPM ecosystem
Evaluation methods affect what evidence can be produced, but they are only one part of the evidence-to-policy system. The questions commissioners ask, the data and access available to evaluators, institutional incentives, relationships between researchers and policymakers, and the political setting all shape what is studied and whether the findings are used. A broader methodological repertoire cannot remove these constraints, although it can widen the range of programmes for which evaluators can make and assess causal claims.
This chapter locates the book within a conceptual framework for evidence-informed policymaking (EIPM) developed for the FCDO Research Commissioning Centre (Sempé et al., 2025). The framework distinguishes actors, pathways of change, outcome domains, and moderating factors. It helps clarify where a methods guide might contribute and what such a guide cannot be expected to change on its own.
The framework identifies three broad categories of actors. Evidence producers generate research and evaluation findings. Evidence intermediaries synthesise, translate, or broker knowledge. Evidence users draw on evidence when making or implementing decisions (Court & Young, 2003; Nutley et al., 2007). These roles often overlap. A government evaluation office may commission a study, help produce it, and use its findings; an evaluation team may generate evidence and translate it for a policy audience.
The actors operate through four pathways of change. Capabilities concern the knowledge, skills, and resources needed to produce, appraise, and use evidence. Relationships and networks connect actors across professional and institutional boundaries. Structures and processes include the rules, incentives, routines, and arrangements through which evidence is commissioned and considered. Evidence culture concerns the norms and expectations that shape the place of evidence within an organisation or policy system.
The framework also distinguishes four outcome domains. Conceptual outcomes concern how actors understand a problem. Attitudinal outcomes concern their disposition towards evidence and its use. Procedural outcomes concern changes in how decisions are made. Content outcomes concern changes to the substance of a policy or programme. These domains are analytically distinct, but evidence need not move through them in a fixed order. A study may alter how a problem is understood without changing policy content, or it may influence a procedure only after being taken up through an established network.
Political conditions, resources, institutional capacity, socio-cultural norms, and the wider governance environment moderate these relationships (Cairney, 2016; Parkhurst, 2017). They affect which questions can be asked, which evidence can be produced, whose knowledge is considered credible, and whether findings enter a decision process. Figure 17.1 therefore presents the framework as an ecosystem rather than a sequence of steps.
The distinction between pathways and outcomes is particularly relevant to evaluation methods. A methodological guide may contribute to a capability by giving an evaluator or commissioner a clearer way to define a causal claim. It may contribute to a procedure if an organisation changes how it commissions or reviews evaluations. Neither change demonstrates that a programme has been altered or that a policy decision was improved. Those are content outcomes that depend on the evidence, the decision process, and the conditions in which the decision is made.

title: 17  Small-n Methods and Evidence-Informed Policymaking
text:
17.2 Where methodology enters
Methodological capability matters because an evaluation team must be able to identify a defensible claim, select a design suited to it, and explain the limits of the resulting inference, and small-n settings can make this harder when familiar large-sample designs are poorly matched to the programme. This does not make methods the principal constraint on evidence production: a suitable design may exist while access, data quality, time, ethics, or political conditions make it unusable, and commissioners may favour a familiar design even where another would serve the question better.
The possible contribution of small-n methods is clearest in the capabilities pathway. Producers may be better able to formulate and investigate causal claims when they can draw on a wider set of inferential operations; commissioners and intermediaries may be better able to appraise an evaluation when its assumptions and evidential requirements are stated explicitly. Structures and processes also matter: terms of reference, procurement rules, access agreements, reporting standards, and review procedures can enable or restrict the use of an appropriate method. Relationships and evidence culture are not downstream effects of better methods; they influence the questions that reach evaluators, the forms of knowledge admitted into an evaluation, and whether methodological capability is used at all.

title: 17  Small-n Methods and Evidence-Informed Policymaking
text:
17.3 How this book may contribute
The book’s most direct contribution is to methodological capability. The causal reasoning framework in Chapter 4 gives producers, commissioners, and intermediaries a vocabulary for distinguishing the claim being made, the inferential operation used to examine it, and the evidence on which the inference depends. The method chapters then show how different designs perform those operations under small-n conditions. This may improve design and appraisal, but whether it changes evaluation practice is an empirical question.
The guidance on method selection, integration, and reporting may also contribute to structures and processes. It could, for example, support more explicit terms of reference, make design choices easier to scrutinise, or provide a basis for reviewing claims that do not rely on conventional statistical metrics. These effects depend on commissioners and evaluation organisations adopting the guidance and adapting it to their procedures. They do not follow from publication of the book itself.
Any contribution to EIPM outcomes is less direct still. Clearer causal reasoning may change how an actor understands a programme, and a well-designed evaluation may eventually inform a policy decision, but between those points lie interpretation, contestation, institutional routines, and competing forms of knowledge that lie outside the book’s scope.
Table Table 17.1 summarises the mapping. The table is not a results chain. It identifies where the book can plausibly contribute and where additional conditions are required.

title: 17  Small-n Methods and Evidence-Informed Policymaking
text:
17.4 Limits of the EIPM mapping
The mapping should not be read as a claim that more rigorous evaluation always produces more useful evidence. Rigour concerns the relationship between a claim and its warrant. Usefulness also depends on the question asked, the timing of the evidence, the decision under consideration, and the interests at stake. An impeccably designed study may arrive after a decision has been taken or address an outcome that matters little to those responsible for implementation. A less conclusive account may still identify a problem that requires attention. The two considerations should be discussed together, but they are not the same.
Nor can an EIPM framework decide whose objectives an evaluation should serve. Commissioners may define a question around a programme’s intended outcome, while participants identify a different consequence as more important. Government records may permit comparison on one outcome and omit another. The response is not to assume that one source is neutral or that all perspectives provide the same warrant for every claim. It is to state how outcomes were selected, whose evidence is used, and what each source can establish. Participatory approaches in Chapter 12 take up this issue directly; the point applies to all methods.
There is also a risk in treating policy use as the only indication that evaluation has mattered. Evidence may inform a decision without appearing in a formal policy document. It may prevent an unsupported claim from being used to justify expansion. It may clarify that an effect has not been established and prompt further data collection. Conversely, a finding may be cited in a policy decision while its limitations are ignored. The EIPM outcome domains help distinguish these possibilities, but they do not supply a simple measure of appropriate use.
For this reason, the book uses the EIPM framework as a contextual map, not as a causal theory of the handbook’s influence. The later chapters can identify how methods may be commissioned, conducted, translated, and synthesised more responsibly. They cannot show, by virtue of that guidance, that an organisation will adopt it or that policy will improve. Those claims would require evidence on organisational practice and decision-making.
The remaining chapters in this part turn from the methodological framework to practice. Chapter 18 examines how evaluations are commissioned, Chapter 19 how their findings are communicated to policy audiences, and Chapter 20 how designs are adapted in fragile, conflict-affected, or otherwise constrained settings.

title: 18  Commissioning Small-n Evaluations
text:
18.1 The commissioning problem
The preceding chapters addressed method selection and integration from the evaluator’s perspective. This chapter considers the decisions made by commissioners before data collection begins. Terms of reference, timing, access arrangements, and the definition of an acceptable conclusion all affect what the evaluation can establish.
The EIPM framework positions commissioning at the intersection of the structures and processes pathway and the capabilities pathway (Sempé et al., 2025). Commissioning processes determine which programmes receive evaluation, which causal questions are asked, and which methods are treated as acceptable. If they are calibrated only to large-n designs, small-scale programmes can be excluded or assessed through designs that cannot support the claims requested. The issue is institutional as well as procedural.
Terms of reference can make four choices before an evaluation team has assessed feasibility. They can frame the question as an effect question, prescribe a named design, define quality through statistical metrics alone, or require one primary numerical finding. Each choice can be appropriate for a programme with a clear intervention contrast, sufficient independent units, and outcome data suited to the design. They become a problem when the requested claim, unit structure, available comparison, and outcome timing have not been examined together.
Small-n settings make this problem visible. A programme may have too few independently treated units, no credible untreated comparator, limited temporal observations, or insufficient diversity across cases. An RCT or difference-in-differences estimator may then be infeasible, or it may answer a different question from the one the commissioner needs answered. Statistical precision is one form of rigour. It does not replace the requirements of configurational, diagnostic, generative, participatory, or simulation-supported inquiry. A commission should specify the claim required and the evidence available before it asks for a particular estimator (OECD-DAC Network on Development Evaluation, 2019; United Nations Evaluation Group, 2018).

title: 18  Commissioning Small-n Evaluations
section: 18.2 From method prescription to logic specification
text:
18.2 From method prescription to logic specification
The decision matrix in Chapter 14 provides the foundation for a different approach to commissioning. Instead of prescribing a method, the commissioner specifies the causal question and the programme attributes, and the ToR identifies the appropriate causal logic or logics. The evaluator then proposes methods that implement those logics, given the available data.
This shift has three operational implications. First, the ToR should state the evaluation question in terms that map onto the causal tasks in the decision framework: a net effect, contribution, a mechanism, pathway diversity, emergent outcomes, feedback and dynamics, or diagnostic assessment of a disputed claim. A request for “impact” is insufficient until it specifies the outcome, population, time period, and causal claim.
Second, the ToR should characterise evaluability constraints rather than assume a design. The relevant constraints are the four dimensions of small n defined in Chapter 3: independent intervention units, support for a counterfactual comparison, repeated observations over time, and diversity across cases. It should also state access to records and sites, the timing of programme delivery and outcomes, known sources of interference, and ethical limits on the comparison or evidence strategy. This information permits evaluators to judge which logic is feasible.
Third, the ToR should define quality criteria that match the logic, not the tradition. For a counterfactual SCED, quality criteria include the number of phase replications, the stability of the baseline, and the results of randomisation inference. For a QCA, quality criteria include calibration transparency, truth table completeness, and robustness to case exclusion. For a contribution analysis, quality criteria include the specificity of the theory of change, the independence of evidence sources for each mechanism step, and the treatment of rival explanations. The reporting checklist in Chapter 16 provides a starting point for logic-specific quality criteria.

title: 18  Commissioning Small-n Evaluations
text:
18.3 Commissioning risks
The following risks arise when a commission is designed before the causal question and available evidence have been assessed together.
The first is method displacement: a ToR specifies an estimator before the evaluation question, units, comparison structure, and timing have been assessed. The resulting study can be formally compliant while unable to support the claim requested. Reviews of impact-evaluation approaches argue for selecting designs in relation to the evaluation question and conditions rather than treating one design family as universally appropriate (Bamberger et al., 2012; Stern et al., 2012). Befani & O’Donnell (2016) provides a practical tool for matching questions to feasible methods.


Method displacement. The issue is a mismatch between a prescribed method and the claim, units, evidence, and timing available to the evaluation. Befani & O’Donnell (2016) provides a method-selection tool that begins with those features.
The second is evaluation exclusion. A programme may be treated as unsuitable for evaluation when it cannot support the design expected in an organisation’s guidance. Guidance on broadening impact-evaluation designs was developed partly to address the limits of treating experimental and quasi-experimental approaches as the only credible options (Department for International Development, 2012). A commissioning portfolio that applies this restriction will contain evidence about the programmes that meet it and less structured learning about those that do not. The absence of an effect estimate is not evidence that a smaller programme has no effects or mechanisms.
The third is logic mismatch. A commissioner may ask how a change occurred while specifying a counterfactual design, or ask for a net-effect conclusion while commissioning only a contribution account. The first design may assess whether an outcome changed without explaining the mechanism. The second may examine a plausible pathway without estimating an effect. The decision matrix provides a way to identify these mismatches before contracting.

title: 18  Commissioning Small-n Evaluations
text:
18.4 A commissioning protocol
The following protocol translates the book’s framework into a commissioning workflow. It does not replace institutional procedures but provides a structured overlay for small-n evaluation design.
The first step is question specification. The commissioner, evaluation team, and relevant programme stakeholders formulate questions that correspond to the causal tasks in the decision framework. Each question should name its expected evidential product: for example, an effect estimate, a contribution account, a tested mechanism proposition, a configuration analysis, a substantiated outcome account, or a model used to examine a stated dynamic.
The second step is constraint mapping. The commissioner documents the four dimensions of small n for the programme: independent intervention units, support for a counterfactual comparison, repeated observations over time, and diversity across cases. The commissioner also records data availability and quality constraints that will affect method feasibility.
The third step is logic identification. Using the decision matrix, the commissioner and evaluation team identify which causal logics are feasible given the evaluation questions and programme constraints. Where multiple logics apply, the team determines whether a sequential, concurrent, or nested integration design is appropriate, drawing on the protocols in Chapter 15.


Step 3 draws directly on the decision matrix in Chapter 14. Step 4 draws on the reporting checklist in Chapter 16. The protocol links commissioning practice to the analytical tools in Parts II and III.
The fourth step is quality framework specification. For each selected logic, the ToR specifies quality criteria drawn from the reporting standards in Chapter 16. The quality criteria replace generic statistical metrics with logic-appropriate indicators of rigour.
The fifth step is evaluator selection. The commissioning organisation assesses whether candidate evaluators have the capabilities to implement the specified logics. Experience in RCTs does not demonstrate competence in Bayesian process tracing or fuzzy-set QCA. Capability assessment is part of the EIPM capabilities pathway: organisations that broaden the pool of evaluators with small-n expertise enlarge the evidence they can commission over time (Patton, 2008).

18.4.1 What the terms of reference should specify
The ToR should make the commissioning decisions available for scrutiny without pre-empting justified methodological judgement by the evaluation team. Table Table 18.1 provides a blank specification. It can be completed at inception and revised through the amendment process when access, implementation, or measurement differs from what was expected. The table does not require the commissioner to decide the final method before procurement. It requires the commissioner to state the causal task and the information on which feasibility will depend.



Table 18.1: Blank specification for terms of reference for a small-n evaluation









ToR element
Information to specify




Decision and users
The decision, timing, and users for whom the evaluation is commissioned


Causal claim
The effect, configuration, mechanism, diagnostic, participatory, or simulation question to be addressed


Intervention, outcome, unit, and period
The condition or programme component, outcome definition, unit to which the claim applies, and period covered


Binding constraints
Independent intervention units, counterfactual support, repeated observations, case diversity, and any access or ethical limits

The proposed method family or families and the inferential role of each component


Quality and review

Amendment and reporting

18.4.2 Adaptive commissioning
The ToR should allow a design to be revised without making revision costless or invisible. An inception phase can test whether the proposed comparison exists, whether outcome records cover the required period, whether implementation has varied as expected, and whether the sources needed for a mechanism inquiry can be accessed independently. The team should report the result of that assessment before moving to the main analysis. If the original claim is no longer feasible, the commissioner can decide whether to alter the claim, invest in additional data, defer the evaluation, or proceed with a narrower purpose.
A documented change is preferable to preserving the original label while changing the design underneath it. For example, a commission initially described as an impact evaluation may end with an implementation account and a tested mechanism proposition if no credible effect comparison can be established. That result may still be useful. The final report should describe the evidence that was obtained, explain why the planned claim changed, and state what the revised design does and does not establish.
Adaptive commissioning also requires a clear division of responsibilities. Commissioners are responsible for access, permissions, decision timing, and the conditions under which the evaluation is undertaken. Evaluators are responsible for explaining how those conditions affect the claim and for proposing defensible amendments. Participants and programme staff may need to be involved where outcome definitions, source access, or interpretation affect the design. The contract should make these roles explicit so that later disagreement about evidence or conclusions is not managed through informal pressure on the evaluation team.

title: 18  Commissioning Small-n Evaluations
text:
18.5 Contracting for an evaluable design
The contract should protect the design decisions made at inception. It should state the expected access to programme records, sites, and relevant participants; the timetable for permissions and data transfer; the independence of the evaluation team; and the process for approving amendments. A method can be feasible in a proposal and become infeasible when access to the relevant unit, outcome record, or implementation chronology is withheld. That change should trigger a documented review of the claim, not an unreported substitution of a weaker design.
Commissioners should also distinguish between deliverables that document work and deliverables that make claims. An inception report should set out the question, theory of change where relevant, evidence plan, case or unit structure, and claim boundaries. An interim product may report implementation evidence or emerging descriptive patterns without treating them as final causal findings. The final report should explain what was collected, what changed from the inception plan, and which claims the evidence supports. This sequence gives commissioners opportunities to resolve access and scope problems while they remain actionable.
Independence requires more than a statement in the ToR. Commissioners may need access to confidential programme material and may also have a legitimate interest in the findings. The contract should specify who can comment on factual accuracy, who can request clarification, and who has responsibility for the evaluators’ conclusions. It should prevent a factual review from becoming an unrecorded negotiation over interpretation. Where independence cannot be assured, the report should say how that constraint affected the evidence and review process.

18.5.1 Budget and timing
Small-n evaluation is not necessarily inexpensive. Process tracing requires time to reconstruct sequence and examine alternatives. Participatory work requires engagement, safeguarding, and procedures for substantiation. QCA requires careful definition and calibration of conditions. A short commission can be appropriate for a focused question, but it should not promise a broad attribution claim when the time does not permit the required observations.
The commissioning timetable should be aligned with programme decisions and outcome timing. If findings are required before an outcome can reasonably change, the commission may focus on implementation, early mechanisms, or the evidence needed for a later outcome study. If a phased roll-out or an information system is still being designed, the commissioner may be able to preserve a comparison, repeated measurement, or a clear implementation record. These choices are most useful before delivery begins.
Figure 18.1 summarises the five steps as a sequential workflow with feedback loops. The arrows between steps are not strictly linear: constraint mapping may prompt revision of the evaluation questions, and logic identification may reveal that the original question framing is infeasible. The protocol is iterative by design.

title: 18  Commissioning Small-n Evaluations
text:
18.6 Institutional implications
Logic-based commissioning may require changes beyond individual terms of reference. Organisational guidance, review arrangements, and management systems can make it easier or harder to commission designs that do not fit a conventional treatment–comparison template (OECD-DAC Network on Development Evaluation, 2019; United Nations Evaluation Group, 2018). Review panels need expertise appropriate to the methods that an organisation expects to commission. Management systems can record the causal claim and method family used, alongside broad labels such as “qualitative” and “quantitative.” Leeuw & Furubo (2008) describe such arrangements as evaluation systems and emphasise that an organisation’s epistemological orientation shapes the evidence it commissions.
An organisation that recognises only counterfactual estimates as credible impact evidence will be unable to commission some mechanism, configurational, participatory, or simulation-supported questions as causal inquiry. Broadening the repertoire does not require treating all claims as equivalent. It requires matching the standard of appraisal to the claim and method. Commissioner–evaluator interaction during design is associated with later evaluation use in reviews of the utilisation literature (Johnson et al., 2009). That association supports early discussion of the causal question and feasible design; it does not show that a particular ToR format will produce policy use.
These institutional changes address the structures and processes pathway in the EIPM framework. They are slower to achieve than reforming individual ToR documents, but without them, reformed ToR remain anomalies within an institutional environment that defaults to large-n conventions. The next chapter turns from how evaluations are commissioned to how their findings are communicated: the translation challenge that arises when small-n evidence enters policy processes calibrated to statistical summaries.

title: 19  Translating Small-n Evidence for Policy
text:
19.1 Evidential products by logic
An evaluation produces findings that require interpretation before they can inform a decision. Chapter 18 addressed how evaluations are specified and procured; this chapter turns to what happens after findings are produced. Translation is particularly demanding when an evaluation produces a set relation, a mechanism proposition, a diagnostic assessment, a participant-defined outcome account, or a model scenario rather than a conventional effect estimate (Greenhalgh & Wieringa, 2011; Lavis et al., 2003). The communication product must make the finding intelligible without changing its causal claim or evidential warrant.
This chapter addresses the translation challenge. It relates the evidential product of each method family to the EIPM outcome domains and proposes communication strategies that preserve the inferential integrity of each claim while making findings accessible to non-specialist audiences (Sempé et al., 2025).
Each method family produces a distinctive type of claim. The differences are not merely stylistic: they concern the causal question, evidence, assumptions, and limits. Treating these products as interchangeable, or as substitutes for a statistical effect estimate, misrepresents what the evaluation has established. Policy evidence is interpreted in deliberative settings as well as through technical appraisal; the form of a finding therefore affects what readers can understand and challenge (Majone, 1989).
Counterfactual methods, including SCEDs and randomisation inference, can produce within-unit effect estimates: the measured difference between intervention and baseline phases for each unit. Where the design permits randomisation inference, a p-value can be derived from the assignment or timing mechanism rather than an asymptotic distribution. The claim is that the intervention changed the outcome for this unit, under the assumptions required by the design. The evidential product is often expressed as an effect estimate, but it describes the units and comparison examined rather than a population average by default.
Configurational methods (QCA, CNA) produce set-theoretic statements about conditions or combinations of conditions that are necessary or sufficient for an outcome within the analysed case set. They do not estimate a probability of success or the size of an effect. The policy product should retain the case universe, outcome definition, and calibration decisions on which the configuration depends.
Generative methods (process tracing, contribution analysis, realist evaluation) produce accounts of a proposed causal pathway. Their conclusions should identify which links are supported, which alternatives were examined, and which parts of the pathway remain uncertain. The claim concerns causal process, not the magnitude of an effect at each step.
Diagnostic methods, including Bayesian process tracing, assess how evidence changes confidence in a causal hypothesis. Where numerical updating is used, a posterior probability is conditional on the prior and on the diagnostic properties assigned to each test. A policy brief should state that condition and link to the underlying analysis.
Participatory methods (MSC and Outcome Harvesting) produce accounts of change identified by participants or programme actors and examined through stated substantiation procedures. The product should identify whose accounts were included, what corroboration was obtained, and the boundary between reported change and causal attribution.
Simulation methods (ABM and system dynamics) can produce model-based scenarios of how a system behaves under stated assumptions. The resulting claim is conditional on model structure, inputs, calibration where relevant, and the scenario definition. It is not an empirical estimate of programme effect without independent empirical support.

title: 19  Translating Small-n Evidence for Policy
text: Six evidential products. (1) Within-unit effect estimate. (2) Set-theoretic statement. (3) Mechanism narrative. (4) Posterior probability. (5) Stakeholder-validated outcome. (6) Model-generated trajectory. Each rests on a different causal logic.

title: 19  Translating Small-n Evidence for Policy
section: 19.2 Mapping evidential products to EIPM outcomes
text:
19.2 Mapping evidential products to EIPM outcomes
The EIPM outcome domains describe possible routes through which evidence enters policy; they do not permit a fixed ranking of method outputs. The relevant question is which decision a finding can inform and what the decision-maker would need to know to use it.


The four EIPM outcome domains — conceptual, attitudinal, procedural, content — are defined in Chapter 17. Each domain represents a different pathway through which evidence changes policy and practice.
An evidence product should state the finding, the causal claim it supports, the decision to which it is relevant, and the limits on use. A counterfactual finding may bear on whether to continue an intervention for the studied unit. A configurational finding may inform conditions to examine before adapting implementation. A mechanism account may identify an assumption requiring attention. These are possible uses, not a hierarchy of evidence products.
Communication can affect whether a reader understands an unfamiliar logic and can assess its relevance to a decision (Bowen & Zwi, 2005; Nutley et al., 2007; Weiss, 1979). It cannot make a weak claim strong. The translation strategies below therefore begin with the evidential boundary rather than the preferred policy message.
crumbs: Small-n Evidence in Policy and Development Practice
19  Translating Small-n Evidence for Policy

title: 19  Translating Small-n Evidence for Policy
text:
19.3 Translation strategies
Four strategies help evaluators and intermediaries communicate small-n findings without distorting their inferential content.
Strategy 1: Name the causal logic explicitly. Every evidence product should state which logic produced it and what kind of claim it supports. A diagnostic brief should identify the hypothesis, the observations assessed, and whether numerical updating was used. This alerts the reader that the finding is not a statistical effect estimate and provides a vocabulary for appraising it on its own terms. The eight-logics framework in Chapter 4 supplies this vocabulary.
Strategy 2: Translate the finding into a policy-relevant claim. A technical statement should be accompanied by a plain-language account of what it permits a decision-maker to consider. The translation must retain the type of claim: a sufficiency claim remains a sufficiency claim, and a conditional model result remains conditional.
Alamos-Concha et al. (2026) provide a documented example in an evaluation of training transfer in Flemish small and medium-sized enterprises. Their sequential QCA–process-tracing design separated two questions: the configurations associated with training transfer and the causal processes operating within selected cases. For a commissioner or policy user, the useful translation is therefore not a single statement that the training worked. It is an account of the configurations examined, the within-case mechanism evidence, and the settings to which that account may plausibly travel. The case also shows why a brief should link to its technical analysis: the basis for selecting cases for process tracing is part of the claim.


Translation rule. A QCA or CNA conclusion should retain its condition set, outcome definition, case universe, and calibration basis. A sufficiency claim must not be restated as a probability or effect size.
The translation must preserve the logical structure (Cartwright & Hardie, 2012). A sufficiency claim should not be restated as a probability or an effect size. A mechanism narrative should not be reduced to a single “bottom line.”
Strategy 3: Report the evidential boundaries. Every small-n finding has boundaries that the communication should make explicit. A SCED effect estimate applies to the units studied, not to a population. A QCA solution applies to the cases analysed and is conditional on the calibration decisions. A posterior probability is conditional on the prior and the probability estimates for each test. Reporting these boundaries is not a weakness disclosure; it is a specification of what the finding does and does not establish. Policymakers who understand the boundaries can use the finding appropriately rather than either over-generalising or dismissing it.
Strategy 4: Match the communication format to the audience. Different actors may need different levels of detail and different routes to the underlying analysis (Oliver et al., 2014; Patton, 2008). Intermediaries can help tailor evidence products for specific audiences (Lomas, 2007; Ward et al., 2009). A two-page evidence brief for a senior policymaker can lead with the policy-relevant claim and the logic that supports it, with technical detail in an annex. A technical appendix for evaluation specialists should report the full analytical procedure, including sensitivity analysis and robustness checks. A presentation to a programme management committee may use a phase-comparison graph, a display of cases covered by a configuration, or a diagram separating a proposed pathway from the evidence bearing on it.

19.3.1 The structure of a policy brief
A brief should begin with the decision to which the evidence is relevant, followed by the finding in plain language. The next sentence should name the causal logic and the evidence that warrants the claim. A short limitation statement belongs in the main text, not only in technical documentation. Readers need to know whether the conclusion concerns a particular unit, a defined case set, a proposed mechanism, participant-reported change, or a modelled scenario before they decide how much weight to give it.
The brief should distinguish a finding from a recommendation. An evaluation may establish that an outcome changed under a specified design, that a mechanism is supported by particular evidence, or that a configuration was associated with an outcome in the analysed cases. A recommendation additionally requires a judgment about costs, feasibility, equity, political authority, and acceptable risk. Those judgments may draw on the evaluation, but they are not produced by the causal method. Separating them prevents an evidence brief from presenting a policy preference as an empirical conclusion.
Technical material should remain accessible. A brief can link to an appendix that reports case selection, measurement, calibration, diagnostic tests, sensitivity analysis, source limitations, and amendments to the protocol. The link does not absolve the brief of explaining the central warrant. It allows the audience that needs to inspect the analysis to do so without turning the main product into a methods report.


19.3.2 Translation as a two-way process
Translation is not completed when a report is simplified. Programme managers, policy staff, intermediaries, and affected groups may identify a decision constraint, alternative explanation, or implementation detail that the evaluation did not address. These responses can improve the interpretation of findings if they are recorded and assessed rather than treated as confirmation. They can also identify a subsequent question for evaluation.
Engagement with users may clarify the decision context and identify missing evidence. It should not permit a preferred interpretation to displace the evaluation’s stated claim boundary. Where users disagree with a conclusion, the evidence brief should show the basis for the conclusion and the uncertainty that remains.






Reporting a Bayesian diagnostic finding



The report should identify the causal hypothesis, the diagnostic tests, the assumptions used to assess each test, and the resulting uncertainty. It should distinguish the evidence that supports implementation, the evidence that bears on a mechanism, and the evidence that rules out alternatives.
Technical report: State the prior, the diagnostic properties assigned to each test, the sequence of updating, and sensitivity analyses. Link the conclusion to the source material and explain any dependence among tests.
Evidence brief: State the conclusion in plain language, name the main evidence types, and identify the assumptions or alternatives that qualify the claim. Link to the technical report for the full assessment.
Verbal briefing: State the conclusion, the reason for confidence, and the main limit in one short sequence. Avoid converting a conditional diagnostic conclusion into an unconditional statement of fact.

19  Translating Small-n Evidence for Policy

title: 19  Translating Small-n Evidence for Policy
text:
19.4 Using findings in decisions
Small-n findings commonly inform three different decisions. A continuation decision asks whether a programme or component should be retained under conditions similar to those studied. An adaptation decision asks what needs to change in delivery, context, or monitoring. A learning decision asks what uncertainty should shape the next design or evaluation. The evidence brief should name the decision type. This stops a mechanism account from being used as if it were an effect estimate and stops an effect estimate from being used as if it explained how implementation should change.
The decision may require information beyond the evaluation. A conclusion that a pathway was supported does not establish that it is affordable to retain or scale. A configuration associated with success may identify conditions that are administratively or politically impossible to reproduce. An outcome account may identify a change valued by participants while leaving its distributional consequences unresolved. The brief should identify these additional judgments so that the evaluation is used as evidence within a decision, rather than as a substitute for the decision.
Translation products should locate uncertainty in terms that matter for action. They can identify whether uncertainty concerns the causal claim, transfer to another setting, the feasibility of an adaptation, or the values at stake in a recommendation. Each may require a different response: further evidence collection, a bounded pilot, an implementation review, or an explicit policy judgment. A generic recommendation to obtain more evidence is insufficient when the source of uncertainty has not been identified.

19.4.1 Recording use without overstating influence
Evaluation teams and commissioners may record whether findings were discussed, incorporated into a decision process, or used to change an information system, implementation plan, or subsequent question. These are observations about use. They do not demonstrate that the evaluation caused the decision, since policy choices are also shaped by authority, resources, timing, and competing evidence. A use record should therefore describe the event, the evidence product considered, and the role attributed to it by the relevant decision-makers.
This record can improve later commissioning. It shows whether a brief reached the relevant users in time, whether its claim and limitations were understood, and whether additional evidence would have changed the decision. It also prevents a familiar retrospective claim: that an evaluation was influential because a later policy moved in the same direction as its recommendation.

title: 19  Translating Small-n Evidence for Policy
text:
19.5 Numbers, visualisation, and uncertainty
Numbers can make a finding appear more settled than it is. A posterior probability, consistency score, effect-size estimate, or model projection is useful only with an explanation of what it measures and the assumptions required to interpret it. A policy brief should not place a number in a headline if the rest of the brief does not explain the unit, comparison, calibration, prior, or model scenario on which it depends. The numerical result may be retained in a chart or summary box, with a direct link to the technical account.
Visualisation can clarify the causal structure when it shows evidence rather than decoration. A phase graph can show the timing of an intervention and outcome observations. A theory-of-change diagram can distinguish a proposed pathway from links supported by evidence. A configuration display can show which cases are covered by a solution and which are contradictory or deviant. A model diagram can identify feedback assumptions. Each visual should have a caption that says what it represents and what it does not establish.
Uncertainty should be located, not merely acknowledged. An evidence brief can state whether uncertainty arises because an outcome was measured imprecisely, a rival explanation remains plausible, a mechanism link is poorly observed, a calibration choice changes the result, or the study covers a limited set of cases. These are different limitations. They call for different responses and should not be collapsed into a general caveat at the end of a document.
The form of the recommendation should follow this assessment. A finding with a credible within-unit effect and a known implementation context may support continued delivery while further evidence is collected on transfer. A finding that depends on a disputed mechanism may support a targeted implementation review. A simulation result may support testing a scenario or monitoring a feedback process. The brief should name the action that the evidence can justify, and the action it cannot yet justify.

title: 19  Translating Small-n Evidence for Policy
text:
19.6 Audiences, authority, and release
Different audiences may have legitimate reasons to read the same evaluation differently. Programme managers need information they can use to adjust delivery. Senior decision-makers may need the claim boundary, the main uncertainty, and the implications for a pending choice. Technical reviewers need the design, data, and analytical record. Participants and affected organisations need an account that is intelligible, does not disclose sensitive information, and does not overstate what their accounts show. These audiences cannot be served by replacing the technical report with a short brief. They require connected products with a consistent claim.
The evaluation team should agree a release protocol before findings are circulated. The protocol can set out factual review procedures, protection of confidential sources, the treatment of sensitive annexes, and the distinction between comments on accuracy and disagreement with interpretation. This is particularly important where a process trace draws on internal documents or where participatory evidence could identify respondents indirectly. A delay or restriction may be necessary to protect people; it should not be used to remove qualified conclusions that a commissioner finds inconvenient.
Authority should be visible in the communication product. A report may identify the evaluation team’s conclusion, the decision that lies with a commissioner, and the perspectives provided by participants or external reviewers. Combining these voices under an anonymous institutional conclusion can obscure disagreement and turn an evaluative judgment into apparent consensus. Where there is disagreement, the brief should identify its source and explain whether it concerns facts, causal interpretation, feasibility, or values.

19.6.1 Transfer and scale
Decisions about adaptation or scale raise the question of whether a finding can apply elsewhere. Small-n evidence can inform that question, but it rarely answers it directly. The relevant transfer question is whether the causal conditions, population, implementation capacity, and decision context of the new setting are sufficiently similar to the setting studied. A mechanism account can identify conditions that need to travel. A configurational analysis can identify combinations worth examining. A within-unit effect can establish a result for the unit studied. None of these warrants a general claim that the intervention will have the same effect in a new population.
An evidence brief should therefore replace general scale claims with a transfer assessment. It can state which conditions were observed, which have not been examined elsewhere, what monitoring would be needed during adaptation, and what result would lead the organisation to stop or revise implementation. This reframes scale as a sequence of evidence-informed decisions, not as a conclusion appended to a successful case.
