19  Translating Small-n Evidence for Policy

title: 19  Translating Small-n Evidence for Policy
text:
19.7 What translation should not do
Translation should not remove the distinction between observation and inference. A brief may report that records show an activity occurred, that interviewees described a mechanism, or that a model generated a scenario. It should not silently convert any of these into proof that an intervention caused an outcome. The technical route from observation to conclusion may be shortened for a non-specialist reader, but it should remain visible.
Translation should not use uncertainty selectively. A brief that foregrounds favourable findings while moving limitations to a footnote changes the practical meaning of the evaluation. The same applies when a report gives extensive attention to uncertainty around a negative result but treats a positive result as self-explanatory. The relevant uncertainty should be reported for the claim that matters to the decision, regardless of whether the result is welcome.
Finally, translation should not create false agreement. An evaluation can be useful when it identifies a disputed mechanism, a configuration that does not travel, or an outcome measure that does not capture a change participants regard as material. Those findings may complicate a decision. They are still evidence. A policy-facing product earns trust by making that complication intelligible, not by removing it from view.

title: 19  Translating Small-n Evidence for Policy
text:
19.8 The “hierarchy of evidence” problem


Petticrew & Roberts (2006) critiqued the transfer of clinical evidence hierarchies to social policy. Stern et al. (2012) proposed that rigour is logic-specific rather than design-ranked, the position adopted throughout this book.
A hierarchy that ranks all methods by design type is not sufficient for the range of causal questions addressed in this book (Guyatt et al., 2008; Petticrew & Roberts, 2006). Clinical evidence hierarchies were developed principally for questions about the average effect of a defined treatment, where randomisation addresses a specific threat of confounding. Development and public-policy evaluations may also ask about mechanisms, configurations, contribution, or emergent outcomes, often for interventions that are not standardised and populations that cannot be treated as interchangeable. A hierarchy used as a universal default can dismiss those questions before the evidence required to answer them has been assessed (Cairney, 2016; Parkhurst, 2017).
The eight-logics framework provides an alternative. Instead of ranking methods by design type, it asks whether the method is appropriate for the causal question being posed and whether it is implemented with the rigour that its own logic demands (Stern et al., 2012). A process trace may be the relevant source of evidence for an explanatory question, while a quasi-experiment may be required for an effect question. Neither conclusion follows from the method label alone. Rigour is a property of the match between question, logic, method, and implementation, not a property of the method alone.
This argument does not claim that all methods are equal or that rigour is relative. It claims that rigour is logic-specific. Chapter 16 sets out the corresponding quality checks, and Chapter 18 places them in the design process. The translation strategies in this chapter show how the resulting evidence can be communicated without changing the claim it supports.

The next chapter turns to fragile and conflict-affected states and other constrained environments, where the moderating factors identified by the EIPM framework interact with the methodological constraints of small-n evaluation.

title: 20  Small-n Evidence in Constrained Settings
text:
20.1 The compounding gap
The preceding chapters set out the conditions under which a causal claim can be designed, examined, and reported. In some settings, access to those conditions is limited. Fragile and conflict-affected settings (FCAS), institutional reform programmes in low-capacity environments, and emergency response evaluations may combine small-n constraints with political instability, resource scarcity, weak institutional capacity, limited data infrastructure, and restricted physical access (Sempé et al., 2025). The OECD has noted that evaluating peacebuilding and state-building interventions requires designs that accommodate instability, attribution ambiguity, and limited baselines (OECD, 2012).
This chapter examines how these moderating factors affect the six method families and the reasoning components set out in Chapter 4. It identifies threats to valid application, the adaptations that remain defensible, and the conditions under which the intended claim should be narrowed or the evaluation should not proceed.
The FCAS evidence gap map reviewed 5,327 empirical studies and found specialised small-n methods in fewer than 2 per cent of records (Sempé, 2026). This is a literature-mapping finding, not an estimate of the prevalence of valid small-n evaluation. It nevertheless identifies a limited verified application base for methods that could be relevant where programme units, comparisons, records, or access are constrained. Reviews of impact evaluation and measurement in humanitarian settings also describe the difficulty of applying conventional designs under instability and limited data (Brück et al., 2016; Puri et al., 2017).
The relevant question is whether the proposed method can be implemented without changing the claim beyond recognition. A method may be appropriate in principle but infeasible because the setting does not support its measurement, access, comparison, or safety requirements. Adaptation should identify what remains possible, what is lost, and whether the intended conclusion must be narrowed (Garbarino & Holland, 2009; White, 2014).

title: 20  Small-n Evidence in Constrained Settings
text:
20.2 Constraints by logic

20.2.1 Counterfactual logic
SCEDs and randomisation inference require repeated measurement of the outcome across baseline and intervention phases. Three constraints can threaten this requirement in FCAS and other constrained settings. First, physical access may be intermittent. If data collectors cannot visit a programme site on a regular schedule, the temporal density required for a SCED is compromised. Gaps in the measurement series weaken the assessment of baseline stability and can limit randomisation tests. Second, an outcome measure may not capture the relevant construct in the setting where it is used. Third, phase-reversal designs may be ethically unacceptable if withdrawal exposes participants to harm.
Adaptations. Remote data collection, including mobile surveys, satellite imagery, or electronically transmitted records, may reduce gaps in a measurement series, but it does not establish that the remote measure captures the outcome validly. Multiple-baseline designs can avoid withdrawal where staggered introduction is administratively and ethically possible. Where gaps prevent the planned comparison, visual analysis can describe the observed pattern, but it does not restore the counterfactual warrant that the missing observations have weakened (Kratochwill et al., 2013).


Remote measurement. Remote sources may maintain an outcome series when physical access is restricted. Their validity, missingness, and relation to the causal claim still require assessment.


20.2.2 Configurational logic
QCA and CNA require defensible calibration of condition sets across the cases included. Reliable data on contextual conditions may be absent or based on proxies of uncertain validity; a change in one condition can alter the truth table and its solution. Very small case sets also limit the diversity available to distinguish configurations. There is no universal numerical threshold that resolves this problem. The evaluator must show whether the available cases, condition definitions, and outcome variation can support the proposed analysis.
Adaptations. Qualitative anchors and structured expert assessment can supplement uncertain indicators only when their rationale, disagreement, and relation to cases are reported. Neither QCA nor CNA is justified by a very small number of cases alone. Sensitivity analysis should show whether plausible calibration choices change the solution and identify conditions dependent on a single source.


20.2.3 Generative logic
Process tracing, contribution analysis, and realist evaluation can require access to people and records that describe how a programme operated, what changed, and why. Institutional memory may be disrupted, records may be inaccessible, and informants with direct knowledge may no longer be available. Respondents may also face security risks from providing candid accounts of programme operations, particularly in governance, justice, or security-sector reform programmes (Bush & Duggan, 2014). A theory of change may be incomplete when a programme was designed and adapted under emergency conditions.
Adaptations. Contribution analysis can begin from a theory of change reconstructed from programme documents and available interviews, provided the report is explicit about the evidence available for each step. Process tracing can draw on documentary evidence when informant access is limited, though the range of mechanism tests may narrow. Where respondent safety is a concern, data-collection protocols should be reviewed against “do no harm” principles before fieldwork begins. A realist inquiry may need to narrow its CMO propositions and report where evidence cannot distinguish the proposed mechanism from alternatives.


20.2.4 Diagnostic logic
Bayesian process tracing requires the evaluator to estimate the sensitivity and false-positive rate of each diagnostic test. These probability estimates are already challenging in data-rich settings, as Befani (2020) has documented. In constrained settings, two additional problems arise. First, the evidence base for estimating test probabilities is thinner. If the evaluator has fewer documents, fewer informants, and less contextual knowledge, the basis for judging whether a test result is a true positive or a false positive is weaker. Second, the prior probability itself may be harder to establish when the evaluation is operating in a context with little precedent and few comparable programmes.
Adaptations. Structured elicitation may make uncertainty in diagnostic assumptions explicit, but it does not supply an empirical basis for a probability estimate. Befani et al. (2021) is a proof of concept for simulation-assisted diagnostic reasoning, not an evaluation application. Sensitivity analysis should report how plausible assumptions affect the conclusion. Where evidence is too thin for formal updating, qualitative diagnostic tests can organise the assessment of alternatives, provided the report does not convert their labels into numerical confidence.


20.2.5 Participatory logic
Most Significant Change and Outcome Harvesting depend on the willingness and ability of programme participants and stakeholders to provide candid accounts of change. Power dynamics may silence some voices, and people may not feel safe discussing changes that implicate armed actors or government officials. Access constraints can limit the diversity of participants reached. Translation and cultural mediation add further layers of interpretation to the accounts collected.
Adaptations. Remote collection may extend reach beyond physically accessible areas, but digital access can itself be uneven. Local facilitators may improve communication where they have appropriate language skills, independence, and safeguarding arrangements. MSC selection panels can include affected participants alongside programme staff and external evaluators. Outcome Harvesting should document its substantiation process and the sources unavailable for it. These measures may reduce particular risks; they do not make accounts representative of groups that could not participate safely.


20.2.6 Simulation logic
Agent-based models and system dynamics models require parameter values derived from empirical data, expert judgement, or both. In constrained settings, the primary threat is that the models are calibrated to data of uncertain quality, producing trajectories that are precise but inaccurate. A secondary threat is that the complexity of the modelling environment creates a black box that commissioners and policy users cannot interrogate.
Adaptations. Participatory model-building can make local assumptions and disagreement visible when quantitative calibration data are scarce. It does not validate the resulting model. The model should be presented as a structured exploration of stated scenarios, with explicit documentation of which inputs are data-driven and which are assumption-driven. Sensitivity analysis should show how plausible changes in assumptions alter outputs.

title: 20  Small-n Evidence in Constrained Settings
text:
20.3 Cross-cutting adaptation principles
Three principles apply across the method families discussed in this chapter.
First, transparency about constraint adaptation should be built into the evaluation report. When a method is adapted for a constrained setting, the adaptation should be documented, the inferential consequences should be stated, and the reader should be able to judge whether the adaptation preserved the logic’s core warrant or compromised it. An evaluation that reports its constraints openly is more credible than one that applies a full-strength method claim to data that do not support it.
Second, integration is not a remedy for missing evidence. A second logic is useful when it has a distinct evidential job and access to a different source or unit. It cannot compensate for a gap shared by every component. A process trace using incomplete records and a configurational analysis calibrated from the same incomplete records may reproduce the same limitation. A counterfactual component with a damaged outcome series and a participatory component may answer different questions, but the latter does not repair the comparison. The integration protocol should state what each component adds and which uncertainties remain shared.
Third, the “do no harm” principle governs all adaptation decisions.


ALNAP (2016) provides the standard framework for evaluation ethics in humanitarian settings. The “do no harm” principle overrides all methodological considerations.
No methodological gain justifies exposing participants, informants, or data collectors to harm. When data collection in a conflict-affected setting would require access to areas controlled by armed groups, the evaluator must weigh the evidential value against the physical risk. When the publication of findings could endanger programme beneficiaries, the evaluation report must be designed to protect identities and sensitive information. These are not methodological constraints in the usual sense. They are ethical constraints that override methodological considerations and that any responsible commissioning protocol must address before the evaluation begins (ALNAP, 2016).

title: 20  Small-n Evidence in Constrained Settings
section: 20.4 Triage, claim reduction, and stopping rules
text:
20.4 Triage, claim reduction, and stopping rules
Constrained settings require an explicit decision about whether the proposed evaluation is feasible before resources are committed. The decision should not be based on whether some data can be collected. It should be based on whether the available observations can support the claim requested without creating unacceptable risk. A short feasibility assessment can identify the intended outcome or mechanism, the accessible unit or units, the evidence that could distinguish the main alternative explanation, the security and ethical constraints, and the decision that would use the findings.
Where the assessment finds a gap, the claim should be narrowed before fieldwork. An evaluation may be able to document implementation when it cannot estimate an effect; it may be able to reconstruct selected decisions when it cannot test a complete mechanism; it may be able to record participant-identified outcomes when it cannot establish their distribution or attribution. These are useful products if they are described accurately. They become misleading when a report keeps the original impact language after the evidential basis has changed.
Stopping rules should be agreed in advance. They may include loss of safe access to a site, a security incident affecting participants or data collectors, loss of a critical outcome series, an inability to protect confidentiality, or a level of missingness that prevents the planned comparison. The rule should specify who decides whether to pause, revise, or stop the work, and how the decision will be recorded. It should not leave field teams to choose between safety and an unexamined contractual requirement.

20.4.1 Building evidence during delivery
Some constraints can be reduced through programme design. A programme can retain dated implementation records, define a small number of outcomes that can be measured safely, record changes in delivery and exposure, and agree procedures for secure data storage. These measures do not turn an emergency response into a trial. They preserve the chronology and observations needed for later contribution, mechanism, or descriptive inquiry.
Commissioners should distinguish this prospective evidence work from a retrospective evaluation commissioned after delivery. Where access is likely to be intermittent, a modest routine record may be more valuable than an ambitious endline survey that cannot be repeated. Where a programme changes rapidly, a dated record of decisions and adaptations can be necessary to interpret any later outcome pattern. The choice of what to preserve should follow the programme’s causal questions and risks, not a generic monitoring template.
crumbs: Small-n Evidence in Policy and Development Practice
20  Small-n Evidence in Constrained Settings

title: 20  Small-n Evidence in Constrained Settings
text:
20.5 Reporting constrained evidence
The report should state the constraints in its methods and interpretation, not only in a limitations section. It should identify which planned sources were available, which were not, how access or safety changed the design, and what conclusion follows from the revised evidence base. It should also distinguish evidence that could not be collected from evidence that was collected but is unreliable or contested. These situations have different implications for use.
A constrained setting does not justify lower standards of disclosure. It may justify a narrower claim, a delayed release, aggregation of sensitive information, or an internal technical annex with protected detail. The public product should still allow readers to understand the causal question, the sources used, the adaptations made, and the remaining uncertainty. This is the basis on which a commissioner can decide whether the evaluation informs immediate action, programme learning, or a later and more complete study.

20.5.1 Data responsibility and local authority
Data protection is part of causal quality in constrained settings. If identifiers, locations, or detailed event records cannot be stored or released safely, that may limit replication, audit, and independent challenge. The appropriate response is not to ignore the limitation or to publish sensitive material in the name of transparency. It is to establish access controls, preserve a secure record where possible, and explain which parts of the evidential route can be reviewed and by whom.
Local authority also affects interpretation. Local researchers, service providers, and participants may identify a security risk, an institutional practice, or a meaning of an outcome that external evaluators cannot infer from a remote record. Their role should be specified in the protocol, including how disagreement is handled and how their contribution is acknowledged. Involvement does not remove the need to examine alternative explanations. It can improve the definition of the causal question and reveal evidence that would otherwise be missed.


20.5.2 A proportionate conclusion
The conclusion should match the design that remained feasible, not the design initially intended. It may state that an implementation record is consistent with a proposed pathway; that a mechanism claim is supported only for selected steps; that a model clarifies a scenario under stated assumptions; or that the available evidence cannot support the effect claim requested. Such conclusions can inform programme management and the design of subsequent evidence collection. They should not be presented as second-best versions of an impact evaluation.
The discipline required in constrained settings is therefore not methodological improvisation. It is clear specification of the claim, protection of people and data, careful preservation of the available evidence, and a report that does not conceal what the setting prevented the evaluation from knowing.

section: 20.6 Recovering an evidence strategy after disruption
text:
20.6 Recovering an evidence strategy after disruption
Disruption does not always require the evaluation to end. It may require the team to separate evidence that was collected before the disruption from evidence collected afterwards, revise the period covered by the causal claim, or postpone an outcome assessment until access and measurement are restored. The amendment should explain whether the disruption is itself part of the causal context. A conflict escalation, population movement, or sudden change in programme delivery can affect both the intervention and the outcome; treating it only as missing data may conceal a central alternative explanation.
Recovery should be staged. The first task is to establish safety and data protection. The second is to reconstruct a dated record of what changed in access, implementation, and measurement. The third is to decide whether the original claim remains testable, should be narrowed, or should be deferred. This sequence prevents pressure to resume data collection from determining the inference before the evidence structure has been reconsidered.
The final report can then distinguish an interrupted evaluation from a failed one. An interrupted study may still contribute a documented implementation chronology, evidence on conditions under which delivery became impossible, or a revised theory of change for future work. Its value lies in what those records establish, not in an attempt to recreate the original design through assertion.
The next chapter considers how small-n findings can be synthesised across studies without flattening their different warrants. Chapter 22 then draws together the book’s argument, the method repertoire, and the EIPM perspective developed in this part.

title: 21  Evidence Synthesis of Small-n Studies
text:
21.1 Start with the causal claim
Evidence synthesis is often presented as the final step of an evaluation sequence: identify studies, assess quality, and combine findings. That sequence is insufficient for small-n evidence. Studies may use the same method label while addressing different causal questions, defining outcomes differently, or relying on different warrants. A pooled estimate, a realist proposition, a configuration, and a set of substantiated outcome accounts are not interchangeable summaries of the same evidence.
This chapter examines how small-n findings can be compared and combined without flattening those distinctions. It covers two related tasks. The first is synthesis across separate studies. The second is synthesis within a programme that has several sites, cases, or implementation episodes. The tasks share questions about comparability and claim boundaries, but they differ in their units, access to data, and opportunities for prospective design.
The unit of synthesis is not the publication. It is a causal claim with an identifiable outcome, unit, intervention or condition, period, and evidential warrant. A study may contain more than one claim. A single-case design may support a within-unit contrast. Its implementation record may bear on fidelity. Interviews may provide evidence on a mechanism. Treating the article as one homogeneous item obscures those distinctions and can give weak evidence the appearance of support because it appears beside a stronger result under the same study label.
Before combining findings, the reviewer should therefore construct a claim record. The record identifies the causal question, the logic used, the unit and case population, the outcome definition, the intervention or causal condition, the evidence used, the assumptions, the conclusion, and the limits stated by the original authors. It should also record what the study did not establish. This permits later synthesis to distinguish a reported change from an estimated effect, a mechanism proposition from a verified mechanism, and an outcome account from an attribution claim.
The record is an analytical device, not a generic extraction form. It forces the synthesis to retain the relationship between a conclusion and the evidence that warranted it. It also makes it possible to compare studies from different fields without pretending that their methods supply the same type of causal knowledge.

title: 21  Evidence Synthesis of Small-n Studies
text:
21.2 Comparability before combination
Evidence can be combined only after the reviewer has determined what is comparable. Four questions determine that decision. Do the studies address the same causal question? Do they define the intervention, causal condition, and outcome in a sufficiently similar way? Do their units and settings permit a shared claim? Do the studies rely on warrants that can be assessed together?
Similarity of topic is not enough. Two programmes described as teacher training may differ in their active components, delivery, population, and outcome timing. Two process traces may examine the same policy but test different mechanisms. Two QCA studies may use the same condition label with different calibration anchors. These differences do not make comparison impossible. They determine whether the appropriate synthesis is a pooled estimate, a comparison of propositions, a configuration analysis, or a structured account of divergence.
The reviewer should also distinguish direct from systematic replication. Direct replication holds the intervention and outcome definition as close as possible to the original study. Systematic replication changes a setting, population, delivery feature, or condition in order to examine the boundary of the claim. The latter can be more informative for policy, but it does not justify treating all results as estimates of one common effect. The synthesis should report what was held constant, what varied, and what conclusion the variation permits (Barlow et al., 2009; Smith, 2012).
crumbs: 21  Evidence Synthesis of Small-n Studies

title: 21  Evidence Synthesis of Small-n Studies
text:
21.3 Synthesis across separate studies

21.3.1 Counterfactual claims
Single-case experimental studies can sometimes be synthesised through standardised effect sizes, hierarchical models, or structured visual comparison. The decision to pool should follow the design and outcome record. Phase structure, baseline trend, outcome direction, measurement scale, intervention fidelity, randomisation, and selective reporting affect whether effect estimates are comparable. Smith (2012) review the design, measurement, and analytic standards that make this assessment possible.
Pooling is not the default. A set of studies may support a conclusion about replicated within-unit contrasts while remaining too heterogeneous for one average effect. In that case, a synthesis can report the pattern of replications and the conditions under which the contrast appeared, did not appear, or could not be assessed. Chapter 6 provides the relevant effect-size and replication concepts.


21.3.2 Generative and diagnostic claims
Mechanism-focused synthesis begins with propositions, not effect sizes. Realist synthesis provides one established approach: it compares how a programme was expected to operate with evidence from different contexts, refining context–mechanism–outcome propositions as the review proceeds (Wong et al., 2013). Its appraisal is claim-specific. A trial may be relevant to an outcome contrast; a case study may be relevant to a decision process; an administrative record may bear on implementation. Their contribution depends on relevance to the proposition and the rigour of the particular evidence, not on an undifferentiated ranking of entire documents.
Process-tracing and contribution claims require an additional precaution. The same documentary source may be cited across several publications, and several reports may repeat a programme’s preferred explanation. A synthesis should identify such dependence rather than counting each publication as independent support. Contrary cases and alternative mechanisms are part of the synthesis, because they identify the conditions under which a proposition does not hold.


21.3.3 Configurational claims
Configurational findings can be compared when conditions and outcomes have compatible substantive definitions and calibration anchors. A synthesis should not combine solution terms merely because they use the same labels. The reviewer needs to inspect the case universe, the calibration rules, treatment of limited diversity, and the cases covered by each solution. Where these differ, the useful result may be a map of proposed configurations and their boundaries rather than a new truth table.
QCA can itself be used within a systematic review when primary studies can be treated as cases and their features coded consistently. That is a distinct research design, not a mechanical way to aggregate QCA publications. It requires an explicit theory of the conditions, transparent coding of the review evidence, and adequate diversity across the included studies. The resulting configuration explains a pattern among studies; it does not validate every causal conclusion reported in them.
Kahwati et al. (2016) provide a worked example. They applied QCA to studies from a completed review of interventions to improve medication adherence after heterogeneity had prevented quantitative pooling. The studies became cases; behaviour-change techniques and implementation features became conditions. Their experience identifies a practical limit for this chapter’s claim record: standard review abstractions did not contain enough intervention detail to support calibration. The team returned to the primary reports to clarify and supplement the extracted information. The QCA did not replace the completed review’s findings. It supplied a configurational question about combinations of features across the eligible studies. A synthesis protocol should make this additional coding and its source trail visible from the start.


21.3.4 Participatory and simulation-supported claims
Participatory evidence can be synthesised when the review preserves who identified an outcome, how it was substantiated, and whose accounts were not available. The aim is not to count stories as observations of one effect. It is to compare outcome descriptions, the values used in their selection, and the evidence offered for their accuracy or contribution. A synthesis may identify recurring changes, disagreements between groups, or outcomes that were not included in standard measures. It should not turn stakeholder agreement into causal attribution without further warrant.
Blundo-Canto et al. (2017) describe a learning system that adapted Outcome Harvesting across three collections of outcomes in agricultural research for development. For synthesis, its organisational implication is clear: repeated harvests can support comparison and learning when outcome statements, guiding questions, substantiation, and interpretation are documented consistently. They do not create a common effect measure. A cross-site participatory synthesis should report the range of outcomes, selection and substantiation procedures, and differences in who was able to contribute.
Simulation evidence requires a separate record of model purpose, structure, inputs, calibration, validation, and scenario definition. Two models may address the same policy issue while representing different causal processes. Their outputs should not be averaged unless their structure and uncertainty assessment justify that operation. More commonly, the synthesis compares assumptions, identifies where model results converge or diverge, and examines which empirical observations bear on the disputed parts of the models. Simulation can support a synthesis by clarifying a dynamic hypothesis; it cannot compensate for missing evidence on whether an intervention produced an observed outcome.
crumbs: 21  Evidence Synthesis of Small-n Studies

title: 21  Evidence Synthesis of Small-n Studies
text:
21.4 Synthesis within a programme
A programme may operate through several schools, districts, organisations, cohorts, or implementation episodes. Its evaluation can plan synthesis prospectively because the units, records, outcome definitions, and timing are partly under the programme’s control. This does not make the task equivalent to pooling separate studies. Sites may share staff, funding, policy shocks, reporting systems, or an intervention label that conceals meaningful differences in delivery.
The evaluation should begin by deciding what is to be compared across sites. A counterfactual component may examine repeated outcome series within each site. A configurational component may compare implementation and context across sites. Process tracing may investigate selected typical, deviant, or informative sites. Participatory work may identify outcomes or concerns not captured in the common measurement plan. Each component needs a specified role in the cross-site conclusion.
Alamos-Concha et al. (2026) illustrate a sequential design in which QCA identified configurations associated with training transfer in Flemish small and medium-sized enterprises and process tracing examined mechanisms in selected cases. The policy value of this arrangement was not a pooled estimate. QCA supplied a basis for cross-case comparison and case selection; process tracing supplied within-case evidence on how the proposed processes operated. The resulting conclusion remained conditional on the coded cases, the configuration definitions, and the selected process traces.

21.4.1 A protocol for within-programme synthesis
Before analysis, the evaluation team should record the common and site-specific elements of the programme, outcome measures, measurement schedule, available records, planned case selection, and likely sources of interference. A shared chronology is particularly important. It identifies whether sites received the same intervention at the same time, whether local adaptations occurred, and whether common events could explain an outcome pattern across all sites.
The protocol should then state how evidence moves between components. A configurational analysis may identify sites for process tracing. A process trace may identify a condition that needs to be measured across sites. A repeated outcome series may identify a change requiring an implementation review. The final synthesis should preserve the order of these decisions and distinguish a planned handover from an adaptation prompted by the data.
crumbs: 21  Evidence Synthesis of Small-n Studies

title: 21  Evidence Synthesis of Small-n Studies
text:
21.5 A protocol for synthesis
The protocol should be written before the reviewer begins to compare results. It need not require a conventional systematic-review question or a commitment to pooled analysis. It should state the causal question, eligible claim types, units and settings, sources to be searched, the evidence that will be extracted, and the conditions under which claims will be compared, combined, or retained separately. These choices can be amended when the literature reveals an unforeseen problem, but the amendment should state what changed and why.
The first stage is eligibility. A report is eligible only when it can contribute evidence to the stated claim. A paper that uses a method label without applying the method to a causal question is not an application. A study may be eligible for one claim and not another. A realist evaluation may contribute evidence on a mechanism while not providing an effect comparison. A SCED may be eligible for an effect synthesis but not for a review of system-level implementation. The protocol should record these decisions at the claim level.
The second stage is extraction and appraisal. Reviewers should work from the claim record and retain a link to the underlying passage, table, figure, or dataset. They should record whether evidence is independent, whether another report uses the same cases or records, and whether the conclusion was pre-specified or developed after results were known. A structured second review of a subset of claims can identify disagreements in interpretation, especially where calibration, mechanism tests, or outcome substantiation require judgement.
The third stage is a comparability decision. Claims may be placed in one of four categories:

Directly comparable: the causal question, contrast or condition, outcome, and warrant are sufficiently aligned for formal synthesis.
Comparable for patterned synthesis: the claims share a causal question but vary in context, implementation, or measurement; the synthesis examines replication, configurations, or proposition boundaries.
Comparable for explanation: the claims address related mechanisms or outcomes but require a theory-led account of why they differ.
Not comparable: the studies can be mapped together but should not be combined into one causal conclusion.

These categories are not a hierarchy. They are an account of what the available evidence permits. A review with no directly comparable claims can still be valuable if it identifies the mechanisms, conditions, and measurement differences that prevent a general conclusion. This result may be more useful for commissioning future work than an average constructed from non-equivalent studies.
The final stage is synthesis and challenge. The initial synthesis should be tested against contrary cases, alternative mechanisms, changes in calibration or inclusion decisions, and source dependence. The reviewer should ask what evidence would weaken the preferred conclusion and whether that evidence has been sought. A synthesis becomes less credible when every difference is interpreted as confirmation of a sufficiently flexible theory.
crumbs: 21  Evidence Synthesis of Small-n Studies

title: 21  Evidence Synthesis of Small-n Studies
text:
21.6 Reporting a synthesis
A synthesis report should make three decisions visible. First, it should show which claims were eligible for comparison and which were not, with reasons. Second, it should describe the evidence that supports each synthesis conclusion and any dependence among sources. Third, it should state the level of the final claim: a replicated within-unit contrast, a refined programme theory, a configuration applicable to a defined case universe, a set of substantiated outcomes, or a conditional model scenario.







Reporting question
What the synthesis should show




What was compared?
The claim record, case or study universe, and exclusions


Why was combination appropriate?
Definitions, units, outcome timing, warrant, and relevant variation


How were sources appraised?
Claim-specific relevance and rigour, including source dependence


What did the synthesis find?
The conclusion, contradictory evidence, and the cases or studies to which it applies


What remains uncertain?
Alternative explanations, transport limits, measurement gaps, and claims not supported


What follows for action?
Whether the finding informs continuation, adaptation, monitoring, a further study, or no causal decision



This structure prevents a familiar error: presenting a synthesis as stronger because it includes more studies while leaving the relationship among their claims unexplained. More documents can provide more evidence, but they can also repeat the same source, the same implementation account, or the same measurement problem. The quality of a synthesis depends on the comparison it makes, not on the length of its reference list.

21.6.1 Negative cases and quality appraisal
Contrary findings are not a residual category. They may identify a different configuration, a failed mechanism link, an outcome measured under different conditions, or a limit in the original claim. The synthesis should retain them as cases requiring explanation. Excluding them because their design or result differs from the majority can produce an account that describes only the conditions under which a programme appeared to work.
Appraisal should be tied to the purpose for which a source is used. A source may provide credible information on the date of a decision but weak evidence on the decision’s consequences. A single-case study may offer a strong within-unit contrast but limited information on transfer. An outcome account may establish that a participant-reported change was substantiated without establishing a population effect. Assigning a single quality score to an entire report can conceal these differences. The claim record should instead state what each source can and cannot contribute to the synthesis proposition.
The same discipline applies to grey literature and programme documents. Such material can be indispensable for reconstructing implementation, exposure, or a decision chronology. It may have been produced by an interested organisation and may omit contrary evidence. A synthesis should record provenance, access, and potential dependence before using the material as corroboration. Transparency does not require excluding grey literature. It requires explaining its evidential role.
crumbs: 21  Evidence Synthesis of Small-n Studies

title: 21  Evidence Synthesis of Small-n Studies
text:
21.7 The role of bibliometric mapping
The bibliometric appendix maps a literature. It identifies publications, method labels, co-mentions, and the extent to which records appear relevant to evaluation. That information can help a reviewer locate a field, identify ambiguous method names, and plan a search strategy. It does not establish that a method was applied correctly, that a publication contains a causal claim, or that the findings are comparable. The appendix should therefore be used as a discovery and scoping resource, not as an evidence synthesis.
The distinction is practical. A bibliometric record may name process tracing, contribution analysis, or simulation in a title or abstract while using the term in another technical sense or without applying it to an evaluation. A synthesis requires full-text eligibility assessment, extraction of the causal claim, method-specific appraisal, and a decision about comparability. The validated application subset can make this work more efficient. It cannot replace it.
Bibliometric mapping can also reveal a substantive absence. If few verified applications connect a method with a particular policy domain, the reviewer should not treat a large number of keyword matches as evidence of a mature synthesis base. The appropriate conclusion may be that the evidence base is too thin or too heterogeneous for synthesis. That finding can guide commissioning, primary research, and the next iteration of the literature map.
crumbs: 21  Evidence Synthesis of Small-n Studies

title: 21  Evidence Synthesis of Small-n Studies
text:
21.8 Planning for later synthesis
Commissioners can make later synthesis more useful by deciding early which elements of an intervention need to be comparable across sites or studies. This may include an outcome definition, a dated implementation record, core descriptors of the population and setting, and a way to record adaptations. It does not require uniform delivery in every context. It preserves enough information to distinguish a meaningful adaptation from an intervention that no longer has the same causal condition.
The decision should follow the intended claim. A programme seeking evidence on a repeated within-unit contrast needs measurement timing and phase information. A programme seeking to compare mechanisms needs a shared theory of change and a record of the observations used to assess its links. A programme seeking configurational learning needs consistent, substantively defensible condition definitions across its sites. A participatory programme needs a transparent approach to outcome selection and substantiation. These are commissioning choices as much as analytic ones.
Prospective planning also protects against selective synthesis. If evaluators specify the claims, core measures, and source records before results are known, later reviewers can see which sites or outcomes were not included and why. This does not prevent adaptation. It makes adaptation visible, and it allows a synthesis to distinguish a deliberate design change from a decision that followed a favourable or unfavourable result.
crumbs: 21  Evidence Synthesis of Small-n Studies

title: 21  Evidence Synthesis of Small-n Studies
section: 21.9 Limits and role in the handbook
text:
21.9 Limits and role in the handbook
Evidence synthesis does not create a common currency for all small-n methods. It makes their differences inspectable and identifies the narrower conclusions that a set of studies can support together. The appropriate result may be an effect estimate, a pattern of replications, a refined mechanism proposition, a bounded configuration, a map of participant-identified outcomes, or a decision that evidence should not yet be combined.
The chapter therefore connects the method chapters to commissioning and translation. Commissioners can preserve common measures, records, and decision points when a programme is expected to generate evidence across sites. Evaluators can specify how claims will be compared before results are known. Evidence users can see whether a synthesis supports a continuation decision, an adaptation, a further test, or only a more precise account of uncertainty. Chapter 21 returns to the wider argument: small-n causal inquiry requires a repertoire of logics, and synthesis must respect the warrant each logic provides.

title: 22  Small-n Evaluation as Causal Inquiry
text:
22.1 What the framework establishes
Small-n evaluation begins with a constraint, not with a method. There may be one national reform, a small number of service sites, no credible comparison unit, too few observations before implementation, or too little diversity across cases. The constraint determines which causal questions can be examined and what evidence is needed to answer them. It does not make every non-experimental account causal, and it does not make a qualitative method the default.
This book has argued that the first task is to specify the claim. An effect claim asks whether an outcome would have differed under another intervention state. A configurational claim asks which conditions or combinations are necessary or sufficient within a defined set of cases. A mechanism claim asks how an intervention contributed to an outcome in a particular context. These claims can concern the same programme, but their evidence and limits differ. A single evaluation may address more than one of them, provided that it does not move from one claim to another without making the additional inferential work visible.
The distinction matters because small-n evaluations are often asked to carry more than their evidence permits. A change in an outcome after implementation is not, on its own, evidence of an effect. A coherent account of implementation does not establish an effect in the absence of a comparison. A set-theoretic association does not show what would happen if one condition were changed. A stakeholder account can establish that an outcome was experienced and recognised without establishing its population prevalence or attribution. A simulated result remains conditional on the model. These are not defects of the methods. They are boundaries on the conclusions that each can support.
The framework in Chapter 4 separates forms of causal claim from inferential operations and from ways of producing evidence. Regularity and manipulation can support several kinds of inquiry; they are not additional types of causal claim. Diagnostic updating assesses the probative value of evidence for competing hypotheses. Participation affects who defines outcomes, contributes evidence, and interprets findings. Simulation makes assumptions about processes explicit and explores their implications. The six method families in Part II draw on these elements in different ways: counterfactual designs, configurational approaches, generative approaches, diagnostic approaches, participatory approaches, and computational simulation.
This organisation is intended to prevent two recurrent errors. The first is choosing a method from a label such as qualitative, theory-based, or small-n before identifying the question and evidence. The second is treating different methods as interchangeable routes to a single generic conclusion. Method choice should start with the intervention or causal condition, outcome, unit, period, available variation, and plausible alternative explanations. Chapter 14 translates those questions into a decision framework. It does not prescribe a method from a numerical threshold, because the relevant constraint differs across designs.
No method family has general priority. A designed within-unit comparison can provide evidence about an effect when outcome measurement, phase structure, and threats to the comparison are adequately addressed. Configurational analysis can identify causal packages and deviant cases when condition definitions, calibration, case selection, and limited diversity have been examined. Process tracing, contribution analysis, and realist evaluation can assess proposed processes when their accounts are tested against alternatives and the evidence is not treated as independent merely because it comes from several documents. Diagnostic reasoning can clarify how observations change confidence in competing explanations. Participatory approaches can identify outcomes and evidence that would otherwise be absent, but agreement among participants is not causal validation. Simulation can investigate feedback and scenarios that cannot be observed directly, but it cannot compensate for missing evidence about a real intervention.
These boundaries also explain why mixed-method designs require more than a list of components. Chapter 15 treats integration as an inferential task. The role of each component should be specified before analysis: a within-unit contrast may address the outcome pattern; process evidence may test the proposed mechanism; a configurational analysis may identify the conditions under which implementation differed; participation may challenge the outcome definition; and simulation may examine a dynamic hypothesis. Agreement between components is more informative when they draw on distinct evidence and address distinct threats. Apparent agreement based on the same records, informants, or assumptions may add little.
The quality standards in Chapter 16 follow from the same argument. Transparency about the claim, case universe, source provenance, assumptions, excluded alternatives, and analytic decisions is not an administrative addition to causal inference. It permits a reader to determine what the evidence supports. The relevant quality check depends on the claim. A counterfactual design needs scrutiny of the comparison and outcome series. A configurational analysis needs scrutiny of calibration, consistency, coverage, and case knowledge. A mechanism account needs scrutiny of tests, sequencing, source dependence, and alternative explanations. Participatory work needs scrutiny of representation, substantiation, and power. Simulation needs scrutiny of the model’s structure, inputs, calibration, validation, and uncertainty.
crumbs: 22  Small-n Evaluation as Causal Inquiry

title: 22  Small-n Evaluation as Causal Inquiry
section: 22.2 From evaluation design to evidence use
text:
22.2 From evaluation design to evidence use
The later chapters extend these considerations beyond analysis. Commissioners shape the eventual warrant when they define the evaluation question, allow time for design and data collection, specify access to records, and decide whether the evaluation must inform an immediate decision. A request for an effect estimate cannot be met by adding causal language to a descriptive monitoring exercise after the programme has begun. Where the available design cannot support the requested claim, the terms of reference should state the narrower question that can be answered (Chapter 18).
Translation also requires claim discipline. Policy audiences may need a short, decisive account, but brevity should not remove the intervention, outcome, population, conditions, or uncertainty that define the finding. A brief can say what was observed, what causal conclusion is warranted, what remains uncertain, and what decision follows. It should not turn a conditional configuration or a mechanism proposition into a general estimate of impact. This is particularly important when an evaluation is used to justify continuation, expansion, or withdrawal of a public programme.
Constraints do not remove these obligations. Conflict, displacement, political sensitivity, weak administrative records, and disrupted fieldwork can limit the claims that a design can sustain. They may also alter the ethical and practical costs of data collection. The appropriate response is to revise the claim and design openly, document what has changed, and distinguish missing evidence from evidence of no effect. Chapter 20 shows that a smaller or adapted design may still produce useful evidence, but only if its causal warrant is stated without inflation.
Commissioning, translation, and adaptation under constraint are also where the book engages most directly with the EIPM pathways introduced in Chapter 17: capabilities, structures and processes, and evidence culture. A clearer causal vocabulary and a more explicit terms of reference may change what an organisation asks for and how it appraises what it receives. Whether an organisation adopts that vocabulary, and whether adoption changes a policy decision, are separate questions that this book does not resolve; the framework identifies where such a change would have to occur, not that it will.
Chapter 21 adds a final implication. Evidence synthesis is not the mechanical accumulation of publications under a method label. Studies should be combined only after the reviewer has assessed whether their causal claims, units, outcomes, conditions, and evidential warrants are comparable. The result may be a pooled estimate, a pattern of replications, a refined mechanism proposition, a bounded configuration, a structured account of participant-identified outcomes, or a decision that the evidence should not be combined. Bibliometric mapping can help locate candidate studies and identify ambiguous terminology. It cannot establish that a publication contains an evaluative causal claim or that its result is suitable for synthesis.
crumbs: 22  Small-n Evaluation as Causal Inquiry

title: 22  Small-n Evaluation as Causal Inquiry
text:
22.3 A working discipline
The framework is intended for decisions made before, during, and after an evaluation. Before fieldwork, it asks teams to specify the intervention or causal condition, outcome, population, period, and claim at issue. They then need to identify what variation, comparison, process evidence, and sources of challenge are available. A design should be narrowed or changed where those conditions cannot support the requested claim. This is a substantive decision for commissioners and programme managers, not a technical adjustment to be made after data collection.
During the evaluation, the framework requires a record of analytical choices and changes to the design. New evidence can require a revised programme theory, an amended measure, a different case set, or the abandonment of an infeasible comparison. These changes need not invalidate the work. Their timing, rationale, and consequences should be visible, so that readers can distinguish a response to field conditions from a decision made after an apparent result.
At reporting, the same discipline separates what was observed from what was inferred. An evaluation can be useful when it cannot estimate an effect: it may document implementation, identify a mechanism that requires further testing, establish that outcomes differed across cases, or show that the available records cannot distinguish competing explanations. A qualified conclusion can inform an adaptation, a safeguard, a further data-collection decision, or a later evaluation design. It should not be presented as evidence for scale-up or withdrawal when the claim required for that decision has not been established.
crumbs: 22  Small-n Evaluation as Causal Inquiry

title: 22  Small-n Evaluation as Causal Inquiry
section: 22.4 What the framework does not provide
text:
22.4 What the framework does not provide
The framework does not remove substantive judgement from evaluation. It cannot determine whether a programme objective is desirable, whether the right outcome has been selected, or what level of uncertainty a commissioner should accept. It does not supply a comparison where the programme’s timing, data, or ethics make one unavailable. It does not turn several dependent accounts into independent evidence, or make findings from one setting transportable by calling them generalisable.
Nor does the framework prescribe a uniform sequence. Some evaluations begin with a prospective design and a clear decision point. Others begin after implementation, with incomplete records and a disputed account of what occurred. The questions in this book help teams identify what each situation permits. They may lead to a more demanding design, a narrower claim, a further phase of evidence collection, or a decision that causal attribution cannot be established. That is a result of the evaluation, not a failure to apply the framework.
crumbs: 22  Small-n Evaluation as Causal Inquiry

title: 22  Small-n Evaluation as Causal Inquiry
text:
22.5 Questions that remain
Several methodological and empirical questions remain open. First, evaluation needs clearer approaches to meta-inference across different forms of causal claim. Sequential and nested designs can specify how evidence moves between components, but they do not by themselves determine how a counterfactual result, a mechanism test, and a configurational finding should be weighed when they converge or conflict. This requires more than a generic appeal to triangulation.
Second, there is a need for empirical work on the practice of small-n evaluation. The bibliometric appendix maps a broad literature and the validated subset identifies work that appears relevant to evaluation. It does not establish how consistently evaluations specify their causal claims, document calibration choices, test alternative explanations, address source dependence, or substantiate participant-defined outcomes. Claim-level reviews, using the approach set out in Chapter 21, would provide a firmer basis for describing the field’s strengths and weaknesses.
Third, commissioning and translation require investigation in their own right. The chapters on commissioning and translation set out design principles, but they do not show how frequently commissioners specify causal questions in terms of reference, how evaluators negotiate claims that cannot be supported by the available design, or which forms of communication help decision-makers use qualified findings appropriately. These are empirical questions about evaluation practice, not matters that can be settled by methodological guidance alone.
Finally, the methods need to remain connected to the substantive settings in which they are used. Small-n evaluation is common in international development, but it also arises in education, health, environmental policy, public administration, and organisational change. The relevant causal question is not determined by the sector. It is determined by the intervention, outcome, units, evidence, and decision at hand. Cross-sector applications can therefore test the limits of the framework without treating one sector’s terminology or evidence conventions as universal.
The purpose of this book is modest. It does not offer a substitute for a credible comparison, a complete account of a mechanism, or a common metric for unlike evidence. It offers a way to decide what causal question is being asked, what kind of evidence can answer it, and what the resulting conclusion can support. In small-n settings, that discipline is often the difference between an evaluation that records a plausible story and one that provides a defensible causal account.

title: 23  Supporting simulation literature
text:
Agent-based modelling and system dynamics are supporting modelling traditions, not methods in the book’s comparative small-n corpus. They are retained because they can strengthen a causal analysis when a model is built around an evaluand, its mechanisms, and plausible alternatives. The large number of publications naming either approach cannot be read as evidence that they are widely used in evaluation. Across the two review stages, 73 of 80 sampled records used the intended model term and 24 were coded as applications. The review was stratified to test the search terms, so these figures do not estimate the share of the wider literature that is evaluative.
Figure 23.1 describes the supporting literature only. It counts indexed works that name the relevant model in a title or abstract. It does not count evaluation applications, development evaluations, or uses alongside the core methods. Those claims require record-level screening under the rules set out in the Methods appendix.






Figure 23.1: Indexed literature naming supporting simulation models. Counts are surface mentions, not evaluation applications.



The distinction matters in practice. A model of disease transmission, supply chains, or organisational behaviour may offer relevant background, but it is an evaluation application only when it is used to assess an identifiable intervention or policy choice. Eight sampled applications were coded as development-related. This appendix remains separate from the comparative core-method figures because model mentions do not identify evaluation use.

title: Method-selection aid for small-n evaluation
text:
1. State the decision and the claim
Use this aid before commissioning or beginning fieldwork. It does not choose a method mechanically. It records the claim the evaluation needs to make, the evidence available to support it, and the limits that should be stated in the terms of reference or protocol. The fuller discussion is in 14  A Decision Framework for Method Selection.
Write the decision that will use the findings, who will make it, and when it must be made. Then specify the causal claim in a form that could be wrong.
An effect claim asks whether the outcome would have differed under another intervention state. A configurational claim asks which combinations of conditions are necessary or sufficient in a defined case set. A mechanism claim asks how an intervention contributed to an outcome in a particular context. These claims need different evidence (Three forms of causal claim).

title: Method-selection aid for small-n evaluation
text:
Record
Write before selecting a method




Decision
What decision will use the findings, and by when?


Intervention or causal condition
What changed, for whom, and during what period?


Outcome
What outcome is expected to differ, and when could it be observed?


Primary claim
Effect; configuration; mechanism or contribution; stakeholder-informed account of change; or conditional implication of a formal model


Claim boundary
What conclusion is outside the scope of the proposed evaluation?

title: Method-selection aid for small-n evaluation
text:
2. Identify the available leverage
The number of programme sites is not enough to determine a design. Record which source of leverage is actually available.








Question
Evidence needed
If it is absent




Is an effect claim required?
A comparator, known assignment process, or repeated outcome series with a defensible phase structure
Do not label a before-and-after description as an effect estimate


Are several diverse cases available?
Comparable outcomes and conditions, transparent calibration, and enough diversity to examine configurations
Do not use QCA or CNA merely because cases can be coded


Is a mechanism or contribution claim required?
A chronology, process evidence, a stated theory, and evidence capable of challenging alternatives
Narrow the claim to implementation or description where alternatives cannot be examined


Are participant accounts needed?
Safe participation, a record of who was not represented, and a plan for corroboration or substantiation
Do not treat agreement or selected stories as causal validation


Is a simulation proposed?
A bounded decision question, defensible model structure and inputs, sensitivity analysis, and an empirical role alongside the model
Do not use scenario output as an estimate of programme effect

title: Method-selection aid for small-n evaluation
section: 3. Match the claim to a method role
text:
3. Match the claim to a method role








Primary question
Candidate approach
Minimum claim boundary




Did the intervention cause an outcome difference?
Counterfactual design, including a SCED or a few-unit comparison where assumptions hold
The estimate depends on the stated comparison and does not establish mechanism or transferability


Which combinations of conditions are associated with the outcome?
QCA or CNA, where case and condition variation permit a truth-table analysis
The result applies to the defined cases and does not show the effect of changing one condition


Did the intervention contribute through a proposed process?
Contribution analysis, process tracing, realist evaluation, and diagnostic updating where evidential tests are specified
The account does not estimate an average effect without a counterfactual design


What changes do participants report, and which require further inquiry?
Most Significant Change or outcome harvesting, with selection and substantiation procedures
Counts and selected accounts do not estimate prevalence or attribution


What follows from a proposed feedback structure or set of rules?
System dynamics or agent-based modelling alongside an empirical method
Scenario results remain conditional on the model and its inputs



Methods can be combined only when each has a separate evidential job. The integration protocol should state what each component will establish, how information will pass between components, and how disagreement will be handled (15  Integrating Methods and Causal Claims).

title: Method-selection aid for small-n evaluation
text:
4. Test feasibility before commitment
Record these points in the terms of reference or inception report.







Design condition
Check




Units and exposure
State the unit of analysis, intervention timing, interference or spillover, and which units supply comparison or variation.


Evidence access
List outcome measures, records, documents, observations, interviews, and their timing, quality, and access restrictions.


Alternatives
Name the main rival explanations and the observations that could weaken each one.


Ethics and safety
State which comparisons, questions, or forms of participation are unavailable or unsafe, and how this changes the claim.


Adaptation
Record the conditions that would require a change to the design and how that change will be documented.


Resources
Cost the evidence collection, checking, analysis, and independent challenge needed for the selected approach.

title: Method-selection aid for small-n evaluation
section: 5. Record the conclusion the design can support
text:
5. Record the conclusion the design can support
The final protocol should end with a plain statement in this form:

Given the available units, evidence, and constraints, this evaluation will assess [specified claim] for [population/cases] during [period]. It will use [method and evidence] to examine [stated alternatives or conditions]. It will not establish [claim outside the design].

This statement should be revised openly if the intervention, available evidence, or ethical conditions change. It is a safeguard against reporting a stronger conclusion than the design can support.
